+## 6. Operational usage
+
+### Normal verification
+
+Run the deploy without `--skip-verify`. The output lists every PASS/FAIL with host and check. Treat any FAIL as a release blocker even if the process started.
+
+### Manual rollback of one host
+
+1. List releases:
+
+```bash
+ssh <host>
+ls -1dt /var/www/pg-<role>/releases/*/
+```
+
+2. Choose the previous timestamp and confirm its `shared` environment is compatible. The release-specific app directory has an `.env` symlink to `<remote>/shared/.env`; the shared env is current, not historical. If the env changed, the old code may not match it.
+
+3. Stop and restart the service from the target release, not with `pm2 restart`:
+
+```bash
+TARGET=/var/www/pg-<role>/releases/<previous>
+ln -sfn "$TARGET" /var/www/pg-<role>/current
+"$HOME/.bun/bin/pm2" delete <service> || true
+cd "$TARGET/<backend>"
+PATH="$HOME/.bun/bin:/usr/local/bin:$PATH" pm2 start pm2-compatible-start.js   --name <service> --interpreter /usr/local/bin/bun --update-env
+"$HOME/.bun/bin/pm2" save
+```
+
+The shared PM2 config is regenerated on every deploy and points at the latest release. A plain `pm2 restart` is not sufficient because it reuses the absolute path of the currently running release. Re-running the deploy from the previous commit is the cleanest whole-role rollback.
+
+4. Nginx static files follow `current` immediately; verify the vhost after the switch.
+
+5. Re-run verification for that host or role.
+
+### Rollback of the whole deployment
+
+The reliable path is to check out the previous commit and re-run `./deploy/deploy.sh --update --only=<roles>`. Releases are immutable, but the shared `.env`, PM2 config and Nginx config are rewritten by the new run.
+
+### Database recovery
+
+The pre-migration dump is a `pg_dump -Fc` file in `<CORE_REMOTE_DIR>/shared/backups/pre-migrate-<timestamp>.dump`. It is not restored automatically. Recovery requires an operator decision, a target database and a compatible schema. Migrations are forward-only; restoring an old code release against a migrated schema can fail.
+
+### Backup drill recovery
+
+Use the backup daemon's `/v1/drills/run` or the admin backup control to verify a restore. The drill restores into scratch directories and removes them; it does not restore the live database.
+
+### Common failures
+
+| Symptom | Likely cause |
+| :--- | :--- |
+| `SSH key ... does not exist` | The `*_SSH_KEY_PATH` is wrong or missing on the workstation. |
+| `core /health (mTLS) FAIL` | Core did not start, DB credentials are wrong, or workers/queue are degraded. |
+| `mTLS -> core /internal/... FAIL` | Wrong client CN/cert, core SAN missing the target IP, or core down. |
+| `backup-daemon /health FAIL` | Certificate ownership, missing S3/Barman prerequisite, or daemon config. |
+| Pre-migration dump fails | `pg_dump` is absent on the core host or the primary is unreachable. |
+| PgBouncer connection fails | No `[databases]` mapping in the generated `pgbouncer.ini`. |
+
+### Security notes
+
+- Keep `deploy.env` at 0600 and `deploy/.certs` private; the CA key never leaves the workstation. Secrets are streamed over SSH stdin, but the pre-migration `PGPASSWORD` is embedded in the verbose command and may appear in logs.
+- The core port is private and mTLS-only; edge hosts never receive `DATABASE_URL` or `KMS_MASTER_KEY`.
+- Protect the edge host and make the backup key readable by `pgbackup`.
+- The deploy's `--skip-verify` is not a security control and should not be used for production acceptance.
+
+## 7. Status and deviations
+
+### Implemented
+
+- Core loopback mTLS health.
+- Edge local health.
+- Edge-to-core mTLS channel health across every core URL.
+- Public merchant/checkout vhost probes.
+- Fake Rails backend and vhost probes.
+- PostgreSQL, PgBouncer, Redis, audit/log and backup-daemon probes.
+- Batch-level health gate and final fail-fast verification.
+- Immutable release layout and `current` pointer.

+
+### Partial
+
+- Batch gates are liveness-only for edges and do not test cross-host mTLS.
+- The guide's symlink + `pm2 restart` rollback is incomplete for backend processes.
+
+### Missing / deferred
+
+- Automatic rollback on a failed batch or failed verification.
+- Connection draining and a zero-downtime single-node switch.
+- Blue/green or canary routing.
+- Database down-migrations or an automated point-in-time restore path.
+- Post-deploy alerting or a health history.
+
+### Known bugs, risks and limits
+
+- A single-node service has a restart gap; a core restart can make all edges fail for the cooldown window.
+- A failed verification leaves the new release as `current` on every deployed host.
+- `--skip-verify` can report success with a broken core/edge path.
+- Shared `.env` is not versioned per release; backup probe failures can be cert ownership.

+## 8. Verification and tests

Extends the Payment Gateway Platform proposal (rails, double-entry ledger, maker-checker) and reuses the patterns of the Voucher Provider Management System. ## 1. Summary An operator adds a gateway from the dashboard by describing how to authenticate, what the customer must enter, which HTTP calls start and finish a payment, how the result arrives (OTP response, redirect return, webhook, browser widget callback, polling, statement), how the gateway's status and error codes map to ours, and how the money settles. No release is needed per gateway, exactly as with voucher providers. Where configuration cannot express a gateway, a native adapter plugs into the same registry. A payment gateway is not a voucher provider with a different URL. The customer is in the loop, results arrive late or twice, some gateways run inside the customer's browser, and money may settle days later. The design therefore adds a flow engine, an attempt state machine, a trusted confirmation layer and safer money handling on top of the voucher pattern. ### Headline decisions 1. Four layers instead of one: Gateway (an integration), Credential Set (whose account and secrets, per environment), Rail (what the customer sees, such as Edfali) and Route (which gateway serves which rail, with priority, cost, limits and scope). One gateway serves many rails (aggregators) and one rail can have several routes (Edfali direct, or through an aggregator). 2. Collection mode and confirmation channel are separate axes. What the customer does (OTP, redirect, embedded widget, push approval, QR, pay code, deep link, manual transfer) is independent of how we learn the result (sync response, webhook, return URL, browser callback, polling, statement). Any mode combines with any channel. 3. A declarative flow engine (phases made of steps, with a closed library of transforms) covers the common cases. A native adapter escape hatch covers what configuration cannot express. 4. A browser or return-URL success is never trusted. Money is posted only after a serververified confirmation (signed webhook, inquiry call, synchronous confirm response, or statement match). Page 1 of 44 Dynamic Payment Gateway Management: Design v2 5. Immutable, versioned gateway configuration with a sandbox-to-live lifecycle gated by maker-checker. In-flight attempts stay pinned to the version they started with. 6. Uncertain outcomes become UNKNOWN, are never retried blindly, and are resolved by inquiry, polling or reconciliation. 7. An ownership-aware ledger: per-gateway Clearing Accounts for platform-held funds, and a commission-only posting path for merchant-owned gateway accounts that settle directly to the merchant. 8. Nothing goes live untested: contract tests, a scenario suite per rail, and a built-in mock gateway. ### What changed since Draft v1 |Area|Draft v1|Draft v2| |---|---|---| |Account

Every real flow fits one of eight collection modes, and most need more than one HTTP call (send OTP then confirm; create session, redirect, then verify). 2. The customer's input differs per rail: phone, birth year, card or transaction-card number, OTP, nothing. Forms must be configurable per rail with validation (for example Edfali phones follow a 09xxxxxxxx pattern; MobiCash asks for a card number). 3. Amount handling is not uniform: thousandths for Moamalat, whole or 2-decimal rounding on aggregators, per-gateway and per-merchant limits. Scale, rounding, precision and min/max are gateway settings, and the settled amount is stored apart from the requested amount. Page 7 of 44 Dynamic Payment Gateway Management: Design v2 4. Browser-side success exists and must not be trusted. The Lightbox reports completion to the page; the trustworthy signals are the server notification and the inquiry API. 5. Signatures take many shapes: a hash built from a hex secret (Moamalat), a signature header (MyPay), a callback hash (Plutu card services), IP restriction (T-LYNC, Moamalat). The engine needs a closed transform library and several verification methods. 6. Sessions expire on the gateway's clock (10 to 15 minutes on several rails per Draft v1 research), so our expiry is min(gateway TTL, platform TTL), not a flat 20 minutes. 7. Some rails have no status endpoint, so a timeout on confirm may leave no way to ask. They need stricter UNKNOWN handling and statement reconciliation. 8. The same rail is reachable through different routes with different behavior (Edfali direct as OTP, Edfali through an aggregator as hosted checkout or OTP), and a gateway account can belong to the platform or to the merchant. 9. Limits and ownership change over time (central bank ceilings, the planned move of the national switch). Ceilings cannot be hard-coded, and a rail must be re-routable without touching links. 10. Names collide and spell differently, so identity needs operator, country and aliases. ### 2.5 What could not be confirmed The official Moamalat documentation site, the DPay, Plutu and T-LYNC API specifications, and any merchant API for Numo Pay, GPay, Hawelli, EVO Pay and Libyana's general payments were not reachable or not public. Searches for the EVO wallet merchant API returned only the unrelated international acquirer. Those profiles are marked UNVERIFIED until a partner supplies documents and sandbox credentials. ## 3. Core concepts ### 3.1 Gateway, Credential Set, Rail, Route - Gateway: one integration with an external system. It holds environments (sandbox, live), base URLs, authentication scheme, flow definitions, confirmation channels, status and error mapping, and settings (amount scale, TTL, limits). Examples: Moamalat, DPay, T-LYNC, Plutu, Edfali direct. Identity fields: code, name, operator, country, aliases. - Credential Set: the secrets and identifiers used to talk to a gateway in one environment (merchant id, terminal id, API keys, hex secrets, webhook secrets). It has an owner (PLATFORM or MERCHANT), a settlement target (section 3.2) and its own status. Secrets can be replaced, never revealed. Page 8 of 44 Dynamic Payment Gateway Management: Design v2 - Rail: what the customer chooses, such as Edfali, Sadad or Visa/Mastercard. It owns the customer form, bilingual names, logo, currency, limits and capabilities (refund, partial refund, void, capture). - Route: the link between a rail and a gateway through a Credential Set, with priority, cost model, limits, health and scope. A rail with no active route is hidden. A rail with several routes is ranked like voucher providers (lowest effective cost, then priority) subject to health. A gateway that needs something it cannot express (proprietary encryption, a binary protocol, a multi-leg 3-D Secure exchange) is implemented as a native adapter in code and registered in the Rail Registry with the same contract as a configured gateway. A native adapter supplies only its own flow runner and a typed settings form, and still passes through the same attempt state machine, inbox, verifier and Ledger Poster, so it cannot post money by itself. Money is DECIMAL(18,4): the dinar has three decimal places, so never use floats, and amounts travel as decimal strings. Secret columns are encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM, key id stored per value) and redacted in every log. The database engine is PostgreSQL 18. The Prisma datasource is `provider = "postgresql"`, reached through `@prisma/adapter-pg` on top of the `pg` driver package. Primary keys use native `UUID`, structured values use native `JSONB`, binary payloads use `BYTEA`, money uses `NUMERIC(18,4)`, and Prisma enums become native PostgreSQL enum types. A phase is an ordered list of steps; later steps read the outputs of earlier ones. Step types: HTTP (an outbound call), COMPUTE (transforms only, no network), RENDER (tell the client what to show: OTP prompt, redirect, widget, QR, pay code, deep link, instructions), WAIT (park until an external event or a poll), ASSERT (check a condition, fail if false) and BRANCH (choose the next steps by a condition). Every HTTP step declares: - side_effect: READ_ONLY (inquiry), SENDS_NOTIFICATION (send OTP, push request) or MOVES_MONEY (confirm, capture, refund). - retry_policy: SAFE (read-only), SAFE_WITH_COOLDOWN (re-sending an OTP only after a cooldown and within a cap), NEVER (any step that may have moved money). - idempotency: whether the gateway accepts an idempotency key on this call and where it goes. When it does, the key is derived from attempt id, step and retry counter, so a repeated call is safe. When it does not, retry_policy must stay NEVER. - point_of_no_return: from this step on the attempt is bound to this route. Route fallback is legal only before it. Selectors are dot-notation JSON paths, XPath for XML (parsed with external entities and DTDs disabled), form keys, or header names. A fixed pattern language (RE2-style, no backtracking) is allowed for matches. A required selector that finds nothing is a failure, not a silent null. Callbacks that arrive as form posts (not JSON) are supported by the same selectors. ### 5.4 Success checks and status mapping Many gateways return HTTP 200 with an error in the body. After each step the engine evaluates, in order: 1. HTTP status set (default 2xx). 2. Body checks {selector, equals | exists | not_equals | in}. 3. StatusRules mapping the body to a canonical status and error. Unmapped codes on money-moving steps become UNKNOWN; unmapped codes on read-only steps are logged and retried. 4. ErrorMap supplies the bilingual customer message and whether the failure counts toward OTP lockout. ### 5.5 Template safety Because operators author templates and customers supply values, every substitution is encoded for where it lands: - Customer values may go into BODY, FORM, QUERY or an encoded PATH segment, never into the scheme, host or port of a URL, and never raw into a header (CR and LF are rejected). The requested amount comes only from the link. Where a gateway offers a list of enabled methods or limits (as MyPay does per merchant), a capability probe imports them so the platform's rails match what the account is actually allowed to use. ## 6. Attempt state machine ``` CREATED -> INITIATING -> AWAITING_CUSTOMER -> AUTHORIZING -> VERIFYING -> SUCCEEDED | | (OTP_REQUIRED, REDIRECT_PENDING, WIDGET_OPEN, | | PUSH_PENDING, QR_PENDING, CODE_PENDING, TRANSFER_PENDING) | +--------------------------------------> FAILED, EXPIRED, CANCELLED +--> BLOCKED (velocity or AML) any step -> UNKNOWN -> (inquiry, reconciliation, operator) -> SUCCEEDED or FAILED SUCCEEDED -> PARTIALLY_REFUNDED -> REFUNDED SUCCEEDED -> DISPUTED (chargeback) ``` Rules: 1. Pinned configuration. The attempt stores gateway_version_id, route_id and credential_set_id at creation; edits never change a running attempt. 2. Reservation. Creating an attempt reserves one use of the link inside the same transaction as the guard and velocity checks. The reservation is released on FAILED, EXPIRED or CANCELLED and kept through UNKNOWN. A single-use link cannot have two live reservations. 3. Expiry. expires_at = min(gateway session TTL, platform TTL). After expiry the attempt moves to EXPIRED, but a grace window keeps the inbox open for late events. 4. Terminal states are SUCCEEDED, FAILED, EXPIRED, CANCELLED and BLOCKED. Only a verified late event, reconciliation or an operator can move EXPIRED or FAILED to SUCCEEDED, and that always raises an operator alert. 5. OTP limits. otp_attempts is capped per attempt (for example 3) and per customer identifier per hour; resend has a cooldown and a cap. A lockout never reveals whether the account exists. 6. State only moves forward. A success is never downgraded by a later pending or failure event; a conflicting pair is flagged for review. 7. Each transition writes the audit trail with actor (customer, gateway, worker, admin), time, old and new state, and the step or event that caused it. 8. Ledger posting happens in the same database transaction as the move to SUCCEEDED, guarded by a unique constraint on ledger_entry_id per attempt so a duplicate event cannot post twice. 9. Realtime. Each state change is pushed to the customer page and, for POS, to the POS screen's realtime room. Page 24 of 44 Dynamic Payment Gateway Management: Design v2 ## 9. Money: amounts, fees and the ledger ### 10.1 Amounts The link amount is the single source of truth and is never taken from the client. Per route the engine derives gateway_amount as described in 5.6, and stores requested, gateway and settled amounts. Rail currency must equal link currency or the rail is hidden. Foreigncurrency or cross-currency rails (for example a card rail that settles in another currency) are out of scope until a rate-snapshot design is approved; the schema keeps currency on every record so that extension is possible. ### 10.2 Fee models and bearers Route cost is flat, percent or tiered with a minimum and a maximum, effective-dated and versioned like the Commission Profile. The fee bearer is PLATFORM, MERCHANT or CUSTOMER (a surcharge shown before confirmation). Provider-reported fees from the confirm call or statement overwrite estimates, and differences are tracked as fee variance. ### 10.3 Ledger for platform-held settlement The proposal says every confirmed payment lands in the single Treasury Account. Gateways that pay out later, or into a bank account the platform does not see in real time, break that assumption. Draft v2 keeps one Gateway Clearing Account per gateway, environment and credential set: a receivable representing money the gateway owes us until it settles. Supporting accounts: Gateway Fee Expense, Gateway Fee Accrual (a payable for fees we owe or have been charged), and Suspense (unmatched or held funds). Confirmed payment, 100 LYD, 3% commission, platform-borne gateway fee 0.8 (accrual option on): Page 28 of 44 Dynamic Payment Gateway Management: Design v2 ``` Dr Gateway Clearing (G) 100 Cr Merchant Wallet (M) 97 Cr Income Account 3 Dr Gateway Fee Expense 0.8 Cr Gateway Fee Accrual 0.8 ``` Settlement received, statement shows 99.2 net: ``` Dr Treasury Account 99.2 Dr Gateway Fee Accrual 0.8 Cr Gateway Clearing (G) 100 ``` If the statement fee is 0.9 instead of 0.8, the extra 0.1 posts to Gateway Fee Expense as variance. With the accrual option off, the full fee posts to Gateway Fee Expense at settlement. Customer-borne fee (customer pays 100.8 for a 100 link, gateway deducts 0.8): ``` At confirmation: Dr Gateway Clearing 100.8 / Cr Merchant Wallet 97 / Cr Income 3 / Cr Gateway Fee Accrual 0.8 At settlement: Dr Treasury 100 / Dr Gateway Fee Accrual 0.8 / Cr Gateway Clearing 100.8 ``` For gateways that settle directly into the platform's bank account the same day, the two entries post the same day, so one model covers both. The reconciliation invariant becomes: the sum of debit-balance accounts (Treasury, every Gateway Clearing, Gateway Fee Expense) equals the sum of credit-balance accounts (Wallets, Income, AML Hold, Chargeback Reserve, Suspense, Gateway Fee Accrual, Commission-related payables). A daily check also compares each Clearing balance with the gateway's reported pending settlement, and drift alerts and halts payouts as in the proposal. ### 10.4 Ledger for merchant-owned, directly settled accounts When the Credential Set is owned by the merchant and settles directly to the merchant, no money enters the platform: ``` Confirmed payment 100, commission 3: Dr Merchant Commission Receivable 3 Cr Income Account 3 ``` Commission is collected by netting against the merchant's wallet balance (Dr Merchant Wallet, Cr Commission Receivable), by invoice, or by a card on file, per merchant policy. The merchant wallet is not credited for these payments, but statistics and reports include them, tagged DIRECT. Controls: a per-merchant receivable ceiling, automatic pause of the Page 29 of 44 Dynamic Payment Gateway Management: Design v2 merchant's direct routes when the ceiling is passed, and a clear display that this balance is owed to the platform. Velocity, AML screening and the hold rules still apply to the decision to accept the attempt, but a hold cannot freeze money the platform never received. A held direct payment therefore blocks the link's completion message, flags the merchant and opens an AML case, and the case outcome is operational (notify, suspend, report) rather than a ledger release. ### 10.5 Refunds, voids and chargebacks A rail's capabilities decide what is offered: VOID before settlement, REFUND (full or partial) within refund_window_days, or manual external refund only. Every refund or chargeback is an Adjustment under maker-checker. If the gateway supports an API refund, the executed Adjustment triggers the REFUND flow; a failed or UNKNOWN refund call keeps the Adjustment in an EXECUTING state and uses the same inquiry and reconciliation machinery. Refund evidence (the provider refund reference) is mandatory before the ledger reversal posts for rails that settle externally. A dispute event from a gateway auto-drafts an Adjustment that still needs checker approval. For merchant-direct accounts the refund or dispute happens on the merchant's own gateway account; the platform records it and reverses commission under the commission policy. ### 10.6 Sandbox money Sandbox attempts carry env = SANDBOX, never post to the ledger, are excluded from merchant balances, statistics and AML, and use clearly marked test links visible only to roles with the testing permission. ## 11. Routing, failover and health - Ranking: for a given rail and amount, candidate routes are ACTIVE, healthy, within min and max amount, within the daily cap and maintenance window, in scope for the merchant, application and channel (WEB, API, POS), and backed by a usable Credential Set. They are ordered by effective cost ascending, then priority descending, then a deterministic tiebreak (the voucher comparator). An admin can also choose weighted or strict priority per rail. - One entry per rail at checkout: if a rail has routes with different modes (Edfali direct as OTP, Edfali via an aggregator as hosted checkout), the customer sees one Edfali button and the winning route decides the mode. A rail may instead be configured to expose both as choices. - Failover is allowed only before the point of no return and only on a definitive failure at INITIATE. After the customer has been sent an OTP, a redirect, a widget session, a push request or a QR, the attempt is bound to that route. A customer who restarts gets a Page 30 of 44 Dynamic Payment Gateway Management: Design v2 new attempt (same attempt group) and the old one is cancelled through its CANCEL flow when supported, or left to expire while still being watched. - Circuit breaker per route: opens after N consecutive definitive failures or an error rate above a threshold over a window, counting only gateway-caused failures (customer errors such as a wrong OTP or a per-customer limit do not count). Half-open probes use the credential check or a read-only inquiry. An open breaker hides the route; when no route remains the rail disappears from checkout. - Drain and replace: set a route to DRAINING to move traffic elsewhere without losing in-flight attempts. - Scoping: a route can be limited to certain merchants, applications, channels or risk tiers, so a gateway account that belongs to one merchant is never used for others. - Direct versus aggregator: aggregators launch faster and cover several rails with one contract, but add a party to the settlement chain, a fee layer and a shared failure domain. Direct routes avoid that but need one contract and one profile per gateway. Because both are just routes on the same rail, the choice can differ per rail and change over time without touching links. - Rate limiting: per-route outbound limits and concurrency caps protect gateway accounts that throttle. ## 12. Security - Roles: GATEWAY_ADMIN (draft configs, test), SECURITY_ADMIN (credentials, allowlists, widget scripts, CSP), FINANCE (routes, fees, settlement, statements), OPERATOR (read attempts, trigger inquiry, resolve UNKNOWN), MERCHANT_ADMIN (manage only their own Credential Sets), plus the platform's maker and checker eligibility flags. Revealing a stored credential is impossible; only replacing it is. - Maker-checker scope (added to section 12 of the proposal): create or edit a gateway version, set a route LIVE, change credentials or webhook secrets (platform or merchant), change inbound IP allow-lists, change fees or limits, change statement parsers, enable a native adapter, add a script host to the widget allow-list, resolve UNKNOWN, held or mismatched attempts, confirm MANUAL payments, and any refund. - Secrets: encrypted at rest with key ids for rotation; webhook secrets have overlapping versions (new and old valid together for a window); credentials never appear in logs, exports or error messages; configuration export and import omit secrets. - SSRF: admin-entered and merchant-entered URLs must be https, resolve through DNS, block private, loopback and link-local ranges, disable redirects or re-validate each hop, cap response size, and may be restricted to an allow-list of gateway hosts. Outbound calls leave from fixed egress IPs that can be given to gateways. Page 31 of 44 Dynamic Payment Gateway Management: Design v2 - Inbound endpoints: random path tokens, size and rate limits, strict content types, no reflection of input in responses, and alerts when valid signatures arrive from unlisted IPs. - Card data scope: the platform prefers hosted, redirected or embedded card capture so the PAN never reaches our servers. Some Libyan OTP rails ask for a card or transaction card number; those fields are marked PAN, kept only in memory for the single call, excluded from state, logs, analytics and error reports, and the rail goes through a PCI scope review before launch. - Personal data: phone numbers, birth years and wallet identifiers are personal data. They are masked in the UI, stored encrypted, retained only as long as the regulatory period requires, and never sent to analytics. The retention period must be confirmed with legal counsel and the central bank's requirements. - Embedded widgets: script hosts come from an allow-list; the checkout page uses a per-page CSP that adds only the gateway's hosts; widget iframes use sandbox and postMessage origin checks; the page never trusts a widget's success event. - Checkout hardening: attempt tokens are unguessable, short-lived and bound to the link; CSRF protection on all state-changing calls; frame-ancestors to prevent clickjacking; the redirectUrl must match an allow-list on the Application to prevent open redirects; Arabic-Indic digits are normalized before validation. - Abuse controls: reuse the proposal's velocity rules on OTP sends (per phone, per IP, per link, per rail), generic error messages that do not reveal whether an account exists, and an SMS-pumping guard that caps OTP sends per link and per hour. - Auditing and retention: every configuration change, approval and manual resolution is audited with before and after; raw inbox events and step logs are retained for the regulatory period with sensitive fields redacted at write time. ## 13. Environments and credentials: URLs, auth method, meta, secrets (shown once at entry, never again), inbound IP allow-list, ownership model and settlement target. 3. Customer form: fields, validation, bilingual labels, sensitivity. 4. Flows: step builder per phase with parameters, transforms, success checks, sideeffect, retry and idempotency flags, point of no return. 5. Confirmation: channels, verification method, correlation, dedupe, acknowledgement, polling. 6. Mapping: status rules and error map with bilingual customer messages. Preview and test, then submit for approval. Starter templates exist for each shape (OTP two-step, hosted redirect with signed webhook, embedded widget with hash, push approval, QR or pay code, manual transfer) and for each researched gateway, marked UNVERIFIED until a partner supplies documents. ### 14.2 Lifecycle DRAFT, SANDBOX_VERIFIED, PENDING_APPROVAL, LIVE, then SUSPENDED or RETIRED. A version reaches SANDBOX_VERIFIED only when the required scenario suite passes. Going LIVE needs maker-checker, a named rollback version and, for HIGH RISK gateways, an explicit risk acceptance. Canary rollout can send a configurable percentage or a named merchant allow-list through the new route first. ### 14.3 Test console - Dry-run: builds each request without sending, showing resolved parameters and transform steps with secrets masked. - Live sandbox run: executes a phase against the sandbox and shows the redacted request, response, outputs and status mapping. - Scenario suite per rail: success, wrong OTP, expired OTP, insufficient funds, percustomer limit, customer cancel, gateway 5xx, timeout on confirm, malformed response, duplicate webhook, out-of-order webhook, late webhook, amount mismatch, rounding case, webhook for another environment. - Webhook replay: paste or capture a real event and replay it through the verifier and mapper. Signature methods are validated against a captured real sample before a version can go live. - Statement parser test: upload a sample file and preview the matched columns and rows. - Mock gateway: a built-in simulator that plays scripted responses, used for regression tests when a version changes. - Contract tests run on every new version and nightly in sandbox as health probes. ### 14.4 Merchant-facing credential setup In the Merchant Portal a merchant can add their own gateway account for routes that allow it: a guided form built from the gateway's declared meta fields, a credential check, a status badge (UNTESTED, VERIFIED, FAILING), clear wording on who receives the money Page 41 of 44 Dynamic Payment Gateway Management: Design v2 and how commission is collected, and a maker-checker review on the platform side before the route goes live for that merchant. ## 15.  # Voucher Provider Management System — Technical Design
 
 Final · 10 October 2026 · Technical version (a non-technical management overview is available separately)
 
 ## 1. Overview
 
 This service lets an administrator plug in multiple voucher providers dynamically, with no code change per provider. The admin describes how to authenticate with a provider, which HTTP requests make up a purchase, and how to read the voucher out of the final response. The admin then builds a catalog (a tree of categories and services), attaches providers and product lists to each service, and issues bearer tokens to client applications. Clients browse the catalog and buy vouchers; for every purchase the system ranks the providers (lowest price, then priority) and tries them in order until one succeeds, falling back only when that is safe.
 
 **Goals**
 
 - Data-driven provider integration: authentication, product listing, purchase and extraction are configuration, not code.
 - Best-price routing with admin-controlled priority.
 - Safe money handling: no double purchases, no lost vouchers, full audit trail.
 - Simple back-office UX for providers, catalog, assets, services and tokens.
 
 **Non-goals**: wallets, balances or accounting (client systems keep their own accounts; this system keeps records, audits and logs only), markup or margin (added by client systems), currencies other than LYD, multi-instance deployment (designed for, not built), a scripting language inside provider config.
 
 ## 2. Actors
 
 - **Administrator**: configures everything through the back-office UI.
 - **API client**: external system using a permanent bearer token to read the catalog and purchase vouchers.
 - **Provider**: third-party voucher supplier with its own HTTP API.
 - **Operator**: reads transactions, logs and stats.
 
 ## 3. Architecture
 
 - **Admin API and UI**: CRUD for providers, listings, assets, services, tokens, users; read-only views for transactions, logs, stats.
 - **Public Voucher API**: bearer-token protected catalog and purchase endpoints.
 - **Provider Gateway**: registry of `ApiConsumer` instances (one per provider) handling authentication, token refresh and request execution.
 - **Query Engine**: runs a provider's purchase query stack and extracts the voucher.
 - **Catalog Resolver**: builds the aggregated, ranked product listing for a service and keeps it in a short-lived cache.
 - **Asset, Token and Audit services**.
 - **Storage**: PostgreSQL 18 (money as `NUMERIC(18,4)`, never floats) and file storage for assets. The Prisma datasource is `provider = "postgresql"`, reached through `@prisma/adapter-pg` on top of the `pg` driver package; native `UUID`, `JSONB` and `BYTEA` are used where applicable.
 
 Deployment is a single instance for now. Every in-memory cache (ApiConsumer registry, aggregated listings) sits behind an `InvalidationBus` interface: an in-process emitter today, Redis pub/sub later, with no change to callers.
 
 [embedded content: architecture · components and calls\]
 
 Clients and the admin UI call separate APIs; every outbound provider call goes through the Provider Gateway.
 
 **Configuration**: `API_LISTING_CONCURRENCY` (pool size for collecting API-listed provider products; default 15, typical range 15 to 20), `CATALOG_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS` (default 60), `CURRENCY=LYD`. Purchases use no pool: each purchase runs its own requests.
 
 ## 4. Data Model
 
 All tables have `id`, `created_at`, `updated_at`. All money is LYD, so there are no currency columns. Secret columns (provider credentials, voucher secrets) are encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM, key from environment or KMS).
 
 ### 4.1 Providers
 
 **Provider**
 
 - `name` (unique), `blocked` (bool), `auth_method`: `NONE | PERMANENT_TOKEN | REFRESH_TOKEN | USERNAME_PASSWORD | BASIC_AUTH`.
 - `auth_config` (JSON, validated per method, secrets encrypted; see 5.2).
 - `auth_apply` (JSON): how credentials are attached to each request (default: header `Authorization: Bearer <token>`).
 
 **ProviderMeta** (`provider_id`, `key`, `type` string|number|boolean|json, `value`): free parameters usable by queries and auth, e.g. a merchant id.
 
 **ProviderQuery** (the purchase query stack)
 
 - `provider_id`, `order_index` (lower runs first; unique per provider), `method`, `url` (full), `content_type`, `success_check` (optional, see 6.4), `timeout_ms`.
 
 **ProviderQueryParameter**
 
 - `query_id`, `place` (HEADERS | QUERY | BODY), `type`, `key` (recursive-set path), `selector` (optional), `constant_value` (for CONSTANT).
 
 **ProviderExtraction** (one per provider)
 
 - `secret_selector`, `id_selector`, `serial_number_selector` (all optional, depending on service type), plus rows in **ProviderExtractionMeta** (`key`, `selector`).
 
 A provider with no queries is never used for purchases.
 
 ### 4.2 Catalog
 
 **Asset**: `name`, `mime` (png | svg), `size_bytes`, `storage_key`, `sha256`.
 
 **Listing**
 
 - `parent_id` (null = root), `kind` (SUB\_CATEGORY | SERVICE), `name_ar`, `name_en`, `asset_id` (optional), `priority_index`, `service_id` (only when kind = SERVICE; not unique, so one service can appear under several listings).
 
 **Service**
 
 - `name`, `type` (SECRET | BILL), `blocked`, `form_enabled`.
 - **ServiceMeta** (`key`, `type`, `value`).
 - **ServiceFormField** (`key`, `type` date | date-time | time | number | string | from-list, `label_en`, `label_ar`, `required`, `order_index`, `options` for from-list as `[{value, label_en, label_ar}]`, `rules` optional list of rule descriptors).
 
 **ServiceProvider** (link between a service and a provider)
 
 - `service_id`, `provider_id`, `priority_index` (higher wins ties), `listing_source` (FIXED | API); unique on (`service_id`, `provider_id`).
 
 **FixedProduct** (when FIXED): `service_provider_id`, `amount`, `price` (the provider's price), `face_value` (string), plus **FixedProductMeta** (`key`, `type`, `value`).
 
 **ApiListingConfig** (when API, one per service provider)
 
 - `method`, `url`, `list_selector`, `amount_selector`, `face_value_selectors` (ordered list, joined with a space), `price_selector`.
 - **ApiListingMetaSelector** (`key`, `selector`): copied into the product's meta so it can be passed to the purchase.
 - **ApiListingParameter** (`place`, `key`, `type` PROVIDER\_META | AUTH\_TOKEN | CONSTANT, `selector`). `AUTH_TOKEN` fails validation if the provider's auth method has no token.
 
 ### 4.3 Access and operations
 
 **AccessToken**: `name`, `token_hash`, `last_four`, `ip_whitelist_enabled`, `revoked_at`, `last_used_at`. The plaintext token is never stored. **AccessTokenIp**: `token_id`, `cidr`.
 
 **VoucherTransaction**
 
 - `reference` (our id, unique), `idempotency_key` (unique per token), `token_id`, `client_ip`, `service_id`, `service_provider_id`, `provider_id` (final), `amount`, `price`, `expected_price` (optional), `face_value`, `form_data` (JSON), `status` (PENDING | SUCCEEDED | FAILED | UNKNOWN), `error_code`, `result_ciphertext`, `result_meta`, `started_at`, `finished_at`.
 
 **TransactionAttempt**: one row per provider tried, and per query executed: `transaction_id`, `provider_id`, `query_order`, redacted request, redacted response, HTTP status, duration, outcome.
 
 **AuditLog** (admin actions: who, what, before/after, ip) and **User** (admin users with roles).
 
 ### 4.4 Referential rules
 
 - Provider delete: only when no `ServiceProvider` rows exist.
 - Service delete: only when no `ServiceProvider` rows exist; its listings are removed with it in the same database transaction.
 - Asset delete: only when no listing references it.
 - Listing delete: a service listing (the service itself stays), or an empty sub-category.
 - Transactions are never hard-deleted; they keep a snapshot of names and prices so history survives later edits.
 
 ## 5. Provider Management
 
 ### 5.1 Admin operations
 
 List; add; update name, auth method and details; manage meta (key, type, value); block and unblock (a blocked provider is excluded from listings and purchases); delete when unlinked; manage the purchase query stack (section 6).
 
 ### 5.2 Authentication methods
 
 - **NONE**: no credentials.
 - **PERMANENT\_TOKEN**: `token` string.
 - **REFRESH\_TOKEN**: `refresh_url`, `refresh_method`, `refresh_token`, `refresh_period_ms`, `access_token_selector` (where to read the new access token), and `refresh_parameters` (list of `{type, key, selector, place}`) describing the refresh request. Parameter types: `META`, `REFRESH_TOKEN`, `CONSTANT`.
 - **USERNAME\_PASSWORD**: same as above but the refresh request is built from `USERNAME` and `PASSWORD` parameter types; the access token is extracted with `access_token_selector`.
 - **BASIC\_AUTH**: `username`, `password`; header `Authorization: Basic base64(user:pass)`.
 
 Common settings: `auth_apply` (header name, scheme prefix, or query/body key) because not every provider uses `Authorization: Bearer`; `refresh_period_ms` (default 30 minutes); `refresh_on_error_statuses` (default 401, 403).
 
 ### 5.3 Runtime: ApiConsumer registry
 
 One `ApiConsumer` per provider, cached in a map. It lazily authenticates on first use, keeps the current auth, refreshes on a schedule, and on an auth error refreshes once and retries the request once. Editing a provider's authentication (or its meta) stops the consumer's timer, deletes it from the registry and emits `provider.invalidated` on the bus.
 
 The consumer exposes `request({method, url, query, body, headers})`. Headers the query defines are applied first; auth headers are applied after and win, as in the sample.
 
 ### 5.4 Review of the sample code: required changes
 
 1. **`recursiveSet` overwrites siblings.** It resets `targetObject[setter] = {}` on every call, so setting `a.b` and then `a.c` loses `a.b`. Create the intermediate container only if it does not exist, and do not mutate the passed-in `setter` array (`pop()` does).
 2. **Registry race.** `getProviderApiConsumer` awaits the database before checking the cache, so concurrent callers can create two consumers and leak a timer. Check the map first and store the creation promise.
 3. **Refresh stampede.** Several requests failing with 401 at once each call `updateAuth()`. Use a single-flight promise so one refresh serves all waiters.
 4. **`setInterval` with async work** can overlap. Use a chained `setTimeout` with jitter, and on failure keep the old token and retry sooner.
 5. **No timeouts.** `fetch` needs an `AbortController` with per-request timeouts (defaults: 10s for auth and listing calls, configurable per purchase query).
 6. **Retry on auth error must not duplicate a purchase.** A 401 before the provider processed anything is safe to retry; a timeout or 5xx is not (see 12.4).
 7. **Body is always JSON.** Add `content_type` per query (`json`, `form-urlencoded`) and set the header.
 8. **Auth header is hard-coded as Bearer**, and `isAuthError` defaults to 'retry on every error' when absent. Make both configurable, with a safe default of 401/403.
 9. **Rotating refresh tokens.** If a refresh response returns a new refresh token, persist it, otherwise the next restart fails.
 10. **Not implemented in the sample**: USERNAME\_PASSWORD and BASIC\_AUTH. Specified in 5.2.
 11. **Non-JSON responses** break `result.json()`. Read text first, then parse JSON when the content type says so, and keep the raw text in the redacted log.
 12. **Secrets in logs.** Never log auth headers, passwords or tokens; redact by key list and by known secret values.
 
 ## 6. Purchase Query Stack
 
 ### 6.1 Definition
 
 An ordered list of HTTP queries per provider. Lower `order_index` runs first. The admin can list, add, edit, delete and reorder (reorder is one transactional call that sends the full ordered id list).
 
 ### 6.2 Parameter types
 
 Each parameter writes a value into headers, query or body at `key` (recursive set, dot path; numeric segments create arrays).
 
 - `PROVIDER_META`: `selector` over the provider's meta.
 - `REQUEST_META`: `selector` over the product's meta (the meta captured in the listing).
 - `AMOUNT`, `PRICE`, `FACE_VALUE`: values of the chosen product; no selector.
 - `PREVIOUS_REQUEST_DATA`: `selector` over the previous query's parsed response; creating this on the first query is a validation error (and throws at runtime as a safeguard).
 - `SERVICE_ADDITIONAL_DATA`: `selector` over the submitted `form_data` (for example a meter number on a bill service).
 - Recommended additions: `CONSTANT` (static value) and `TRANSACTION_REFERENCE` (our reference, so a provider that supports it can reject duplicates).
 
 ### 6.3 Execution
 
 ```
 ctx = { providerMeta, productMeta, amount, price, faceValue, formData, reference }
 prev = null
 for query in stack ordered by order_index:
     request = build(query, ctx, prev)       // resolve parameters, compile url + query string
     response = consumer.request(request)    // auth headers applied by the consumer
     assert success(query, response)         // see 6.4
     log attempt (redacted)
     prev = response.data
 voucher = extract(prev, providerExtraction)
 ```
 
 Query strings use `compileUrl` from the sample (indices array format by default). The final response is the extraction source by default; an optional `source_query_order` lets an extraction read an earlier response.
 
 ### 6.4 Success detection
 
 Many providers return HTTP 200 with an error body. Each query therefore has an optional `success_check`: an HTTP status set (default 2xx) and an optional `{selector, equals | exists | not_equals}` check on the body. A missing required selector is a failure, not a silent null.
 
 ### 6.5 Extraction
 
 `secret_selector` (required for SECRET services), `id_selector`, `serial_number_selector` (optional), and meta rows `{key, selector}` stored under `key` with recursive set. Extraction failure after a successful provider call is the worst case: the voucher was bought but not read. The raw redacted response is kept, the transaction is marked UNKNOWN and an alert is raised.
 
 ### 6.6 Validation at save time
 
 Reject: first query using PREVIOUS\_REQUEST\_DATA, duplicate `order_index`, non-absolute URL, invalid selectors, unknown parameter types. Offer a **dry-run** (admin enters sample product and form data, the engine builds requests without sending them) to preview what will be sent.
 
 ## 7. Listings (Catalog Tree)
 
 - A listing belongs to a parent sub-category or to the root (`parent_id = null`).
 - A listing is either a **sub-category** (has children) or a **service listing** (links to one service). Names in Arabic and English are required; the image is optional; `priority_index` sorts siblings (ascending, ties by id).
 - **The same service can appear under several listings.** Each listing has its own names, image and priority; deleting one listing never deletes the service.
 - The admin screen shows one level at a time: root items first, click a sub-category to open the same screen scoped to it, add items inline.
 - Rules: cycles are impossible because parents are only chosen at creation (moving a node must verify the target is not a descendant); maximum depth (suggested 6).
 - Delete: a service listing or an empty sub-category only.
 - **Public visibility** (computed): a service listing is visible when the service is not blocked and it has at least one unblocked provider that has a non-empty query stack and a non-empty product list. A sub-category is visible when it has at least one visible descendant. Admins see everything with a status badge explaining why an item is hidden.
 
 ## 8. Assets
 
 - PNG or SVG with a unique name. Admin can list, add, view in detail (viewer with zoom and metadata), replace the file content, and delete when unreferenced.
 - Upload via `multipart/form-data`. Validate on **both** client and server: extension, declared MIME, **magic bytes**, size limit (suggested 1 MB PNG, 200 KB SVG), and image dimension limit for PNG.
 - **SVG is active content**: sanitize on upload (strip script, event handlers, external references, `foreignObject`), and serve with `Content-Type: image/svg+xml`, `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.
 - Store files under a content-derived key; replacing content writes a new object and swaps the pointer so caches can be busted (`?v=sha256`).
 
 ## 9. Access Tokens
 
 - Admin can list, create, delete (revoke) and manage the IP whitelist per token. Tokens are **shown once**, at creation; they cannot be copied later.
 - Format: `vp_` + 32 random bytes (base64url). Only `sha256(token)` and the last four characters are stored, so a database leak does not expose usable tokens. A lost token is replaced by creating a new one and revoking the old one.
 - **IP whitelist**: when `ip_whitelist_enabled`, the caller's IP must match an entry (IPv4/IPv6, single address or CIDR). Resolve the client IP carefully: only trust `X-Forwarded-For` when the immediate peer is a configured trusted proxy.
 - Tokens grant access to the catalog and purchase APIs only, never to admin routes. Optional later: per-token scopes, rate limits and service allow-lists.
 - Each request updates `last_used_at` (debounced) for visibility.
 
 ## 10. Services
 
 ### 10.1 Management
 
 List, add (`name`, `type` SECRET | BILL), update, delete (only when no providers linked). Detail view: recent transactions, form setup, meta, block and unblock (blocking also removes the service from listings), provider links.
 
 ### 10.2 Service form
 
 - Toggle enabled and disabled; when enabled, purchase requests must include `form_data` valid against the form.
 - Field list: add, edit, delete, reorder. Fields have `key` (name in the submitted body), `type`, bilingual labels, `required`.
 - `from-list` fields carry options `{value, label_en, label_ar}`; submitted value must be one of them.
 - **Rules**: an ordered descriptor list (for example `[{op:'min', value:3}, {op:'regex', value:'^[0-9]+$'}]`) compiled into a zod schema from a whitelist of operations. Never evaluate admin-supplied code. Optional in v1.
 - The compiled schema is cached per service and invalidated on form change; the same descriptor is returned to clients so they can render and validate the form.
 
 ### 10.3 Service meta
 
 Key, type, value rows, available to queries as additional context if needed.
 
 ### 10.4 Provider links
 
 - List, add, update, remove. Add means choosing from providers not already linked and setting `priority_index` (higher is preferred when prices tie).
 - Per link, the admin manages the product list:
   - **FIXED**: add, edit, delete products with `amount`, `price`, `face_value`, and meta rows.
   - **API**: configure `method`, `url`, `list_selector`, `amount_selector`, `face_value_selectors`, `price_selector`, meta selectors, and parameters (list, add, edit, delete). A link with an empty product list is never selected.
 - Switching listing source requires confirmation because it discards the other source's configuration.
 - Provide a **Test fetch** button for API lists that shows the parsed products.
 
 ## 11. Catalog Resolution (Product Listing)
 
 Input: `service_id`. Output: service details, its form definition, and a product list.
 
 [embedded content: catalog resolution · 8 steps\]
 
 The cached, ranked result is what clients see and what purchases read.
 
 1. Middleware: if the service is blocked, respond `404 SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` (same as not found, to avoid leaking state).
 2. Load the service's unblocked providers (with non-empty query stack) from the database; if none, `404 SERVICE_HAS_NO_PROVIDERS`.
 3. Split into FIXED and API sources. FIXED products come straight from the query.
 4. For API sources, fetch product lists in a **bounded concurrency pool** sized by `API_LISTING_CONCURRENCY` (default 15), each with a timeout. A failing provider is skipped and the failure logged, so one slow provider never breaks the listing.
 5. Build a map keyed by `amount` plus `face_value` to `{amount, candidates[]}` where each candidate holds `provider_id`, `service_provider_id`, `priority_index`, `price`, `face_value`, `meta`.
 6. Rank candidates inside each entry with one comparator: **price ascending, then priority descending**.
 7. Drop entries with no candidates and return entries sorted by amount ascending.
 8. Cache the aggregate (TTL 60 s by default), invalidated on provider block, service change or product edit. The cache is also what purchases read (section 12).
 
 **Notes**
 
 - The original notes sort by priority and then by price. Two consecutive stable sorts leave **price as the primary key and priority as the tie-breaker**, which matches the intent 'higher priority wins if prices match'; the comparator above encodes that.
 - **Client response shape**: per entry only `product_key` (opaque), `amount`, `face_value` and the best `price`. Provider ids, provider meta and internal priorities are never exposed to clients.
 
 ## 12. Voucher Purchase
 
 ### 12.1 Request
 
 `POST /v1/purchases` with `service_id`, `product_key`, optional `expected_price`, `form_data` (when the service has a form) and an `Idempotency-Key` header.
 
 Routing is **server-side**: the server reads the ranked candidates for the product from the cached aggregate (rebuilding it through section 11 if missing or expired) and tries them in order until one succeeds. Clients never choose a provider.
 
 [embedded content: purchase flow · 5 steps, 1 decision\]
 
 Section 12.4 defines which failures count as definitive and which end in UNKNOWN.
 
 ### 12.2 Validation
 
 1. Token valid, not revoked, IP allowed.
 2. Service not blocked; `form_data` valid against the service form.
 3. Candidates loaded from the cache; provider and service blocked flags re-checked against the database.
 4. If `expected_price` is provided and the best candidate's price does not match it, respond `409 PRICE_CHANGED` with the current price. If it is omitted, no price check is made.
 5. Idempotency: if the key exists for this token, return the stored result (or `409 IN_PROGRESS`).
 
 ### 12.3 Execution
 
 1. Insert the transaction as PENDING (before any provider call).
 2. Take the best candidate, load its query stack and run the Query Engine (section 6), logging every query. Each purchase makes its own requests; there is no purchase pool.
 3. On success: extract the voucher, encrypt the secret, mark SUCCEEDED, return it.
 4. On failure, apply the fallback rule below.
 
 ### 12.4 Failure handling and fallback
 
 Fallback to the next candidate is allowed **only when the failure is definitive and happened before the provider could have acted**: the failure occurred on the first query and was a connection failure before sending, a 4xx or explicit error body, or an auth failure after the refresh retry. If `expected_price` was provided, a fallback candidate is used only when its price also matches it. In every other case the outcome is ambiguous or partial:
 
 - Timeout or connection reset after sending, 5xx, failure on a later query, or extraction failure: mark the transaction **UNKNOWN**, do not try another provider, return `202`/`502` with the reference, and alert. Resolve through manual reconciliation.
 - All eligible candidates definitively failed: mark FAILED, return `503 NO_PROVIDER_AVAILABLE`.
 
 Never automatically retry a purchase request that may have been accepted.
 
 [embedded content: transaction states · 4 states\]
 
 A transaction leaves UNKNOWN only through manual reconciliation.
 
 ### 12.5 Duplicate protection
 
 The client's `Idempotency-Key` and our own `reference` stop duplicate purchases at our side. The `reference` can be sent to the provider through the `TRANSACTION_REFERENCE` parameter. Whether a provider honours it, and whether it offers an order-status endpoint for reconciliation, is optional and decided per provider later; the design does not depend on it.
 
 ### 12.6 Logging
 
 Store everything needed for investigation: reference, token id, client IP, user agent, service, provider, amounts, form data, per-query redacted request and response, durations, status and error code. Voucher secrets are stored only encrypted and are masked in admin screens; reveal is an audited action.
 
 ### 12.7 Response
 
 ```
 { reference, status, service_id, amount, face_value, price,
   voucher: { secret, id, serial_number, meta } , created_at }
 ```
 
 Provider identity is not returned to clients.
 
 ## 13. Public API Surface
 
 All under bearer-token auth.
 
 - `GET /v1/catalog`: root listing items (visible only).
 - `GET /v1/catalog/{listingId}`: children of a sub-category.
 - `GET /v1/services/{serviceId}/products`: ranked product listing, service details and form definition.
 - `POST /v1/purchases`: purchase (section 12).
 - `GET /v1/purchases/{reference}` and `GET /v1/purchases?from&to&status&page`: transactions of the calling token only. Additional client-based queries are deferred.
 
 Errors use a stable envelope `{ code, message, reference? }`; the codes include `UNAUTHORIZED`, `IP_NOT_ALLOWED`, `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE`, `SERVICE_HAS_NO_PROVIDERS`, `VALIDATION_FAILED`, `PRICE_CHANGED`, `NO_PROVIDER_AVAILABLE`, `IN_PROGRESS`, `PURCHASE_UNKNOWN`.
 
 ## 14. Admin API Surface (summary)
 
 - Providers: `GET/POST /providers`, `GET/PATCH/DELETE /providers/{id}`, `POST /providers/{id}/block|unblock`, `GET/PUT /providers/{id}/meta`, `GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE /providers/{id}/queries`, `PUT /providers/{id}/queries/order`, `PUT /providers/{id}/queries/{qid}/parameters`, `PUT /providers/{id}/extraction`, `POST /providers/{id}/queries/dry-run`.
 - Listings: `GET /listings?parent_id=`, `POST/PATCH/DELETE /listings/{id}`, `PUT /listings/order`.
 - Assets: `GET/POST /assets`, `GET/DELETE /assets/{id}`, `PUT /assets/{id}/file`.
 - Tokens: `GET/POST /tokens` (the token value is returned only by the create response), `DELETE /tokens/{id}`, `GET/POST/DELETE /tokens/{id}/ips`, `PATCH /tokens/{id}` (whitelist flag).
 - Services: `GET/POST /services`, `GET/PATCH/DELETE /services/{id}`, `POST /services/{id}/block|unblock`, `GET/PUT /services/{id}/form`, `GET/PUT /services/{id}/meta`, `GET /services/{id}/transactions`, `GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE /services/{id}/providers`, `GET/PUT /services/{id}/providers/{spid}/products` (FIXED), `GET/PUT /services/{id}/providers/{spid}/api-listing`, `POST .../api-listing/test`.
 - Operations: `GET /transactions` (filters), `GET /transactions/{id}` (attempts), `GET /logs`, `GET /stats`, `GET/POST/PATCH /users`, `GET /audit`.
 
 ## 15. Security
 
 - **Roles**: SUPER\_ADMIN, CATALOG\_ADMIN (listings, assets, services), PROVIDER\_ADMIN (providers, tokens), OPERATOR (read-only transactions and logs). Revealing voucher secrets needs an explicit permission and is audited.
 - **Secrets at rest**: encrypted columns for provider credentials and voucher secrets; client tokens are stored only as hashes; key rotation supported through a key id stored with each ciphertext.
 - **SSRF**: provider URLs are admin-entered. Enforce `https` (optionally allow-list hosts), resolve DNS and block private, loopback and link-local ranges, disable redirects or re-validate on each hop, cap response size.
 - **Rate limiting** per token and per IP on public endpoints; stricter limit on purchases.
 - **Input validation** with zod on every route; selectors and keys validated against a safe path grammar (`[A-Za-z0-9_-]+` segments joined by dots), and prototype pollution guarded (`__proto__`, `constructor`, `prototype` rejected in `recursiveSet`).
 - **Auditing** of all admin mutations with before/after snapshots (secrets masked).
 - **Redaction** of secrets in all stored request and response logs.
 
 ## 16. Observability and Operations
 
 - Structured logs with correlation id (`reference`) across queries.
 - Metrics per provider: success rate, latency percentiles, auth refresh failures, fallback count, UNKNOWN count.
 - Alerts: UNKNOWN transaction, extraction failure, repeated refresh failure, provider error spike.
 - Stats screen: volume by service and provider, success rates, top tokens.
 - Auto-block option (later): temporarily deprioritize a provider after N consecutive definitive failures.
 - Backups include encrypted columns and the key-management plan.
 
 ## 17. Delivery Plan and Decisions
 
 **Phases**
 
 1. Foundations: auth and roles, assets, listings, services and forms, tokens.
 2. Providers: auth methods, ApiConsumer registry, query stack, extraction, dry-run.
 3. Catalog resolution and purchase flow with idempotency, UNKNOWN handling and logging.
 4. Operations: transactions, logs, stats, alerts; then Redis invalidation when going multi-instance.
 
 **Confirmed decisions**
 
 1. `price` is the provider's price; margin and customer-facing prices are added by client systems.
 2. Routing is server-side: the cached ranked list is used and candidates are tried until one succeeds.
 3. Reference-based duplicate protection is required; provider-side idempotency and status endpoints are optional and decided later.
 4. Access tokens are shown once only.
 5. `expected_price` is optional; when provided and not matching, the purchase is rejected with 409.
 6. A service can appear under several listings.
 7. All amounts are LYD; no accounting is kept here, only records, audits and logs.
 8. API-listed products are collected through a configurable pool (default 15, typically 15 to 20); purchases have no pool.

+## 0. Confirmed decisions
+
+1. `project-design/parts/**` is the editable source of truth.
+2. `project-design/PROJECT_DESIGN.md` is generated from the parts as the centralized verbose master document.
+3. `design/**` is kept as a frozen historical/reference archive with a banner and a source map. It is not current authority.

+6. Stale `SCALING_FEATURE.md` and duplicate `notes.md` files in the three frontends are deleted.
+7. `bun scripts/project-design/build.ts --check` is added to the exhaustive runner and PR checklist.
+8. Root `AGENTS.md` is canonical; Claude, Gemini, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot and OpenCode adapters point to it and to `project-design/INDEX.md`.

+- Service READMEs cover operations but not full project usage.
+- `blueprint.md` files are short summaries, not full design documents.
+- Many false/outdated claims remain even after the PostgreSQL pass.

+## 2. Canonical authority model
+
+1. `project-design/` is the only canonical design.
+2. `design/` is historical/reference material only.
+3. Code is the authority for as-built behavior.
+4. Generated appendices are the authority for counts, routes, env keys, schema and tests.
+5. A behavior/contract/config/schema change must update `project-design/` in the same change.
+6. Unimplemented features are explicitly `MISSING` or `DEFERRED`; never mixed into current behavior.
+7. `blueprint.md` files are generated from `project-design/parts/**`; they are not hand-edited.
+8. `README.md` files are hand-written usage manuals, linking to generated appendices.

Verbatim Content: The 12 Books of the Admin Interactive System Guide (`booksPart1.ts` & `booksPart2.ts`) Every Book below MUST be implemented in full inside `admin-front/src/content/guide/` and rendered with its step-by-step diagrams, tables, SOP checklists, and red error-prevention callouts. --- ### BOOK 1: Welcome to the Platform — How Money, Data, and Security Work From Zero #### Chapter 1.1: What Does Our Company Actually Do? (From Zero) When a customer in Tripoli, Benghazi, or Misrata wants to buy something online or in a store—whether a plane ticket, an electronics order, or a clinic bill—they might want to pay using **Sadad** (Almadar), **Edfali** (Bank of Commerce & Development), **Moamalat** (their local debit card on the National Switch), **LYPay / OnePay** (instant bank QR transfer), **MobiCash**, **T-LYNC**, **MyPay**, or **NeomPay**. For an individual store owner (**Merchant**), integrating all 20 of those systems is nearly impossible: each bank speaks a different computer language, uses different mathematical formulas to sign messages, measures Libyan Dinars differently (some in Dinars `10.50`, some in Dirhams `10500`), and settles money on different schedules. **Our platform solves this completely:** 1. **One Unified Integration for Merchants:** A Merchant registers once in our **Merchant Portal** (`merchant-front`), passes our legal & compliance checks (**KYB/AML**), and creates a **Payment Link**, connects their website via **API**, or pairs an in-store **POS Screen**. 2. **One Intelligent Checkout for Customers:** When the customer opens the Payment Link in **Checkout** (`checkout-front`), our system automatically calculates which payment methods (**Rails**) are healthy, allowed, and within limits for that exact amount, and shows a clean Arabic/English screen. 3. **One Zero-Code Engine Behind the Scenes:** When the customer clicks a Rail (e.g., *Sadad*), our isolated core engine (**`core-back`**) translates the request into Sadad's exact format, verifies the result from a trusted server channel, and records the accounting movement in our **Double-Entry Ledger**. #### Chapter 1.2: Why Is Our System Split Into 7 Separate Projects? (The Zero-Trust Model) If you hear engineers mention `core-back`, `admin-back`, `merchant-back`, or `checkout-back`, here is why our platform is built like a high-security bank rather than a single website: ```text [ PUBLIC INTERNET ] ──▶ Checkout Website (checkout-front / checkout-back) ─┐ [ PUBLIC INTERNET ] ──▶ Merchant Portal (merchant-front / merchant-back) ─┼──▶ (mTLS 1.3 Certificate Lock) ──▶ [ CORE ENGINE & DATABASE (core-back) ] [ OFFICE LAN ONLY ] ──▶ Admin Back Office (admin-front / admin-back :8443) ─┘ (Holds All Money, Keys & PostgreSQL 18 database) ``` 1. **The Public Edge Servers Hold Zero Secrets and Zero Database Access:** - The Checkout server (`checkout-back`) and Merchant server (`merchant-back`) face the public internet so customers and merchants can reach them. Because anything on the public internet can be attacked, those servers **do not have the database password, do not have the database software installed, and do not hold any bank secret keys**. 2. **The Admin Portal (`admin-front` / `admin-back`) Is Local-Network (LAN) Only:** - The Admin Back Office you are using right now runs on a private office network port (`:8443`) that is blocked from the public internet at the firewall level. 3. **The Vault (`core-back`) Trusts Nobody Blindly ("The Double-Check Rule"):** - Only `core-back` can talk to the PostgreSQL 18 database, decrypt bank credentials (`Vault`), talk to external banks, or write to the financial ledger (`LedgerPoster`). - Even when `admin-back` or `checkout-back` sends a message to `core-back` using a cryptographic certificate (**mTLS 1.3**), `core-back` **re-checks everything from scratch**: it verifies your login token, your Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), your exact permission flags (`authorities_map`), and ensures that the Maker and Checker on an approval are two different human beings. > **CRITICAL HUMAN ERROR WARNING — NEVER BYPASS NETWORK OR ACCOUNT BOUNDARIES:** > - Never attempt to expose the Admin Portal (`:8443`) or Core Engine (`:4000`) to the public internet or over an unsecured public proxy. > - Never share your Admin account or MFA device with another employee. Every click you make records your `user_id`, IP address, and before/after snapshot in the permanent `audit_log`. --- ### BOOK 2: Roles, Authorities & The Four-Eyes (Maker-Checker) Governance Rule #### Chapter 2.1: Understanding Your Role vs. Your Authorities (`authorities_map`) In our platform, every employee account has two layers of access control: 1. **Your Role (`UserRole`):** Describes your job function (`GATEWAY_ADMIN`, `SECURITY_ADMIN`, `FINANCE`, `OPERATOR`, `COMPLIANCE`, `MLRO`, `SUPPORT`). 2. **Your Authorities Map (`authorities_map`):** The exact list of actions your account is permitted to perform (for example, `case:read`, `dispute:write`, `gateway:write`, `aml:read_confidential`). - **Default-Deny Rule:** If an admin creates a new user account and leaves `authorities_map` empty, that user can see **zero** pages and call **zero** APIs, regardless of their Role title. - **Confidentiality Wall (`AML-CONFIDENTIAL`):** Only `COMPLIANCE`, `MLRO` (Money Laundering Reporting Officer), and `SECURITY_ADMIN` (for audit) can view AML screenings, watch-list matches, or Suspicious Activity Reports. `SUPPORT` and `OPERATOR` staff are blocked from seeing AML reasons so they can never accidentally "tip off" a merchant under investigation. #### Chapter 2.2: How the Four-Eyes (Maker-Checker) System Protects You and the Company Imagine if a tired Finance officer accidentally typed `100,000 LYD` instead of `1,000 LYD` on a manual adjustment, or if a Gateway Admin accidentally pasted a broken URL into a live bank integration. In a normal system, that mistake would immediately break production or lose money. In our platform, **every sensitive action is governed by the Four-Eyes (Maker-Checker) rule**: 1. **Step 1 — The Maker Proposes (`DRAFT -> PENDING_REVIEW`):** - User A (who has `is_maker = true`) fills out the form (e.g., editing a merchant's payout bank account, proposing a refund, changing a commission rate, or promoting a Gateway Version to `LIVE`). - Instead of changing the live database immediately, the system saves an **Approval Request (`approval_requests`)** containing a **JSON-Patch Diff** (a side-by-side comparison of the Old Value vs. the Proposed New Value) and records the entity's current `base_version`. 2. **Step 2 — The Checker Inspects & Decides (`PENDING_REVIEW -> APPROVED -> EXECUTED` or `REJECTED`):** - User B (a **different** person with `is_checker = true` in that domain) opens the **Approvals Queue (`/approvals`)**. - The system enforces **`checker_user_id != maker_user_id`** at three separate levels: in the UI, in the backend middleware, and in a hard PostgreSQL database trigger (`approval_requests_checker_not_maker`). You **cannot** approve your own request. - When the Checker clicks **Approve**, the system verifies that the record hasn't been modified by someone else in the meantime (`base_version` check) and **atomically executes** the change and writes the ledger/audit record in the exact same database transaction. #### Chapter 2.3: The Asymmetry Rule — Emergency Actions (`EMERGENCY_RATIFICATION`) What if a merchant is actively committing fraud at 2:00 AM on a Friday, or an AML rule needs to be tightened immediately to stop an attack, and a second Checker is asleep? - **Actions that REDUCE risk** (Suspending a merchant, tightening a velocity/AML rule, pausing a broken route) are allowed to take effect **immediately** with one authorized person, creating an approval request in **`EMERGENCY_RATIFICATION`** mode with a **24-hour countdown timer (`ratify_due_at`)**. - Within 24 hours, an `MLRO` or `COMPLIANCE` Checker must review and ratify the emergency suspension. If the 24-hour timer expires without ratification, a `P2` alert pages management—and the merchant **stays suspended** (fail-safe, never fail-open) until a human Checker decides. - **Actions that INCREASE risk or MOVE money** (Reinstating a suspended merchant, loosening a rule, releasing an AML hold, approving a refund/cash-out, promoting a gateway to `LIVE`) **NEVER** have an emergency bypass; they always wait for a second human Checker prior to execution. #### Chapter 2.4: Step-by-Step SOP for Checkers Reviewing `/approvals` Before you ever click **Approve** on any row in `/approvals`, complete this 5-point checklist: 1. **Read the Green/Red JSON Diff Line by Line:** Never approve based only on the summary title. Inspect the exact numbers, account IBANs, URLs, or transform pipes changing in the diff viewer. 2. **Check the Currency & Decimal Scale:** Remember that LYD uses 3 decimals (`100.0000` is One Hundred Dinars). Verify that a Maker did not enter `100000` thinking in Dirhams! 3. **Verify External Evidence:** - For a **Bank Account Change (`payout_bank_details_json`)**: Open the merchant's KYB documents and verify the official stamped Bank Letter matches the new IBAN and the merchant's legal name. - For a **Manual Refund / Adjustment**: Verify the `provider_refund_ref` or `external_dispute_ref` against the gateway portal or statement. - For a **Gateway Version Promotion to `LIVE`**: Verify that all **12 Go-Live Gates** show green badges and a valid `rollback_version_id` is selected. 4. **Check the Chargeback Outcome Selector (When Approving a Dispute Adjustment):** Confirm whether the adjustment is escrowing an opened dispute, releasing a `WON` dispute, or finalizing a `LOST` dispute. 5. **Write a Clear Rejection Reason if Anything Looks Wrong:** If even one field is ambiguous, click **Reject**, type the exact correction needed, and let the Maker submit a clean draft. --- ### BOOK 3: The Four-Layer Payment Catalog (`Gateway` -> `Credential Set` -> `Rail` -> `Route`) #### Chapter 3.1: Why Do We Separate Gateways, Credential Sets, Rails, and Routes? New employees often ask: *"Why don't we just have one table called 'Payment Methods'?"* Here is why our 4-layer design is essential in the Libyan market: - Suppose **Edfali** is a payment method that customers love. - We can connect to Edfali **directly** through Bank of Commerce & Development (`Gateway 1: edfali_direct`, which costs us `0.5%`), **or** through the **Plutu Aggregator** (`Gateway 2: plutu`, which costs us `1.2%`), **or** through the **DPay Aggregator** (`Gateway 3: dpay`, which costs us `1.5%`). - Furthermore, a large supermarket chain might have its **own** direct contract with DPay (`Credential Set: Merchant-Owned`), while 500 smaller stores use **our company's** master contract (`Credential Set: Platform-Owned`). By separating the 4 layers, the customer at checkout simply sees **one clean "Edfali" button (`Rail`)**, while our engine automatically picks the best, cheapest, healthy **`Route`** and **`Credential Set`** behind the scenes! ```text Layer 3: RAIL (What the Customer Sees) [ Edfali (إدفع لي) ] ── Owns Logo, Arabic/English Name, Customer Input Form (09xxxxxxxx Phone + OTP) │ ├──▶ Layer 4: ROUTE A (Priority 1, Cost 0.5%, Status: ACTIVE, Health: HEALTHY) │ └──▶ Layer 1: GATEWAY (edfali_direct) + Layer 2: CREDENTIAL SET (Platform Master Account) │ ├──▶ Layer 4: ROUTE B (Priority 2, Cost 1.2%, Status: ACTIVE, Health: HEALTHY — Automatic Backup!) │ └──▶ Layer 1: GATEWAY (plutu) + Layer 2: CREDENTIAL SET (Platform Plutu Account) │ └──▶ Layer 4: ROUTE C (Scoped to Supermarket X Only, Settlement: MERCHANT_DIRECT) └──▶ Layer 1: GATEWAY (dpay) + Layer 2: CREDENTIAL SET (Supermarket X's Own DPay Keys) ``` #### Chapter 3.2: How the "Visible Rails Formula" Decides What Appears at Checkout When a merchant calls support and asks: *"Why isn't Sadad (or Moamalat Card) showing up on my Payment Link?"*, you do **not** have to guess. Our engine evaluates the **Visible Rails Formula** on every checkout load.
