 # merchant-back blueprint
 
 Generated from: `edge.shared`, `edge.merchant`.
 
 ## Shared Core Upstream Client
 
 > Status: `implemented` · Last verified: 2026-11-03
 
 ## 1. Purpose and scope
 
 This part documents the edge-to-core transport used by `admin-back`, `merchant-back` and `checkout-back`. It owns the mTLS agent, the `CORE_BACK_URLS` node pool, node selection, passive failure detection, retries, request identity headers, the `x-pg-min-lsn` consistency hint, path/channel confinement, core error mapping and the SSE stream proxy.
 
 It does not own authorization or business validation. `core-back` remains authoritative for token verification, authorities, maker-checker, amount resolution, idempotency and channel-bound client-certificate checks. The client only guarantees that a request reaches an allowed core channel over an authenticated TLS 1.3 connection.
 
 The implementation exists as three near-identical copies:
 
 - `admin-back/lib/coreInternalClient.ts`
 - `merchant-back/lib/coreInternalClient.ts`
 - `checkout-back/lib/coreInternalClient.ts`
 
 Each copy is 761 lines and differs only in `CORE_SERVICE_NAME` and `CORE_CHANNEL_PREFIX`. There is no workspace package, no generated shared module and no single build artifact for the pool.
 
 ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design)
 
 The historical design requires every edge request to cross a private LAN boundary over mutual TLS 1.3. The edge authenticates with a dedicated client certificate whose CN names the service, and `core-back` binds each internal namespace to that CN. Edge services never receive `DATABASE_URL`, `KMS_MASTER_KEY` or another host's client key.
 
 When `core-back` scales horizontally, each edge receives `CORE_BACK_URLS`. The intended behavior is:
 
 - persistent keep-alive connections to every core node;
 - least-in-flight selection with round-robin tie-breaking;
 - passive removal of a failed node, a cooldown, and a half-open probe after the cooldown;
 - retry of idempotent requests on a different node;
 - propagation of `x-pg-min-lsn` so LSN-aware reads can wait for a replica that has replayed the caller's write;
 - no loss of the edge's identity headers (`x-request-id`, `x-real-client-ip`, `x-client-user-agent`, `x-edge-service`).
 
 The design describes this as enabling rolling core restarts without dropping edge traffic. The implementation provides that only for requests that can be retried and only while at least one other eligible node exists; it does not make an individual single-node core restart seamless.
 
 ## 3. As-built architecture
 
 ### 3.1 Agent and TLS material
 
 `createCoreAgent()` in each copy builds one `https.Agent` per configured node:
 
 - client certificate from `MTLS_CLIENT_CERT_PATH`;
 - client private key from `MTLS_CLIENT_KEY_PATH`;
 - CA from `MTLS_CA_CERT_PATH`;
 - `minVersion` and `maxVersion` fixed to `TLSv1.3`;
 - `rejectUnauthorized: true`;
 - keep-alive enabled with 30-second keep-alive delay and `maxSockets: 64`;
 - the agent-level timeout is `CORE_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`.
 
 Material is loaded synchronously with `fs.readFileSync` when the agent is created. A missing file becomes `MTLS_MATERIAL_UNAVAILABLE` (HTTP 500) rather than a process crash. Because the agent is cached, replacing certificate files on disk does not affect a running process until the pool is rebuilt. The pool is rebuilt when the configured URL signature changes or when `resetCoreAgent()`/`resetCorePool()` is called by tests.
 
 ### 3.2 Pool lifecycle and selection
 
 `ensureNodes()` parses `CORE_BACK_URLS` or falls back to `CORE_BACK_URL`. `parseCoreBackUrls()`:
 
 - splits on commas;
 - rejects empty entries;
 - requires absolute `https:` URLs;
 - de-duplicates by normalized `URL.toString()`;
 - preserves the original trimmed strings for requests.
 
 Each node state tracks `url`, `agent`, `healthy`, `inFlight`, `failures`, `lastFailureAt` and `cooldownUntil`.
 
 `eligiblePool(excluded)` implements the cooldown/half-open state:
 
 1. If any excluded node is unhealthy, has zero in-flight requests and its cooldown has elapsed, return only those half-open nodes. This lets one request probe recovery before the node rejoins the general pool.
 2. Otherwise return every healthy, non-excluded node.
 3. If neither set is non-empty the request fails with `503 CORE_UNAVAILABLE`.
 
 `selectNode()` picks the minimum in-flight count and uses a monotonic round-robin cursor to break ties. The cursor advances on every selection and is reduced modulo the tied set size. A node selected for an attempt is added to the request-local `attempted` set, so a retry never targets the same URL within one logical call.
 
 ### 3.3 Failure marking and retries
 
 `markNodeFailure()` sets `healthy=false`, increments `failures`, records `lastFailureAt` and sets `cooldownUntil = now + CORE_FAILURE_COOLDOWN_MS` (5 seconds). `markNodeHealthy()` clears all failure state.
 
 Retry eligibility is controlled by `retryAttemptsFor()`:
 
 - idempotent methods default to retrying: `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`;
 - `POST` and `PATCH` do not retry by default;
 - `retryIdempotent: true` forces retries; `retryIfUnavailable: true` allows a non-idempotent call to retry;
 - `maxAttempts` defaults to 2 and is floored to at least 1; there is no upper cap.
 
 `request()` marks a node failed and retries when the node returns HTTP `502` or `503`, or when the request throws a connection/TLS error. Any other status, including other `5xx` responses, marks the node healthy and is returned to the caller. If every attempt ends in a `502`/`503`, the last response body is returned rather than converted to a local error. If every node has already been attempted and no eligible node remains, the call fails with `CORE_UNAVAILABLE`.
 
 `mapCoreTransportError()` maps transport failures to stable edge errors:
 
 | Transport condition | Edge error |
 | :--- | :--- |
 | `ETIMEDOUT`, `ESOCKETTIMEDOUT` | `504 CORE_TIMEOUT` |
 | `ECONNREFUSED`, `ECONNRESET`, `EPIPE`, `EHOSTUNREACH` | `502 CORE_UNREACHABLE` |
 | `ENOTFOUND`, `EAI_AGAIN` | `502 CORE_DNS_FAILURE` |
 | TLS error codes | `502 CORE_TLS_ERROR` |
 | other failures | `502 CORE_CONNECTION_ERROR` |
 
 ### 3.4 Headers and consistency
 
 `buildCoreHeaders()` emits:
 
 - `x-request-id`: the resolved edge request id;
 - `x-real-client-ip`: the client IP resolved from the trusted proxy;
 - `x-client-user-agent`: the caller's user agent, possibly empty;
 - `x-edge-service`: `admin-back`, `merchant-back` or `checkout-back`;
 - `accept: application/json`;
 - `content-type: application/json` when a JSON body exists, or the supplied raw content type;
 - `authorization` when present;
 - every caller-supplied header, lowercased;
 - `x-pg-min-lsn` when `minLsn` or `consistencyLsn` is non-empty.
 
 `consistencyHeader(lsn)` is a helper that returns the same header or an empty object. The client does not generate an LSN. Callers must obtain one from a write response or another trusted source. `x-pg-min-lsn` is passed through to `core-back`, where `lib/storageEngine` converts it into an `atLeastLsn` read constraint with a 250 ms wait.
 
 ### 3.5 Path and channel confinement
 
 `assertCorePath()` rejects:
 
 - empty paths and non-rooted paths;
 - protocol-relative paths (`//...`), embedded `://` and backslashes;
 - invalid percent escaping;
 - decoded `.` or `..` segments;
 - any path outside the service's channel prefix.
 
 The prefixes are:
 
 | Service | Prefix |
 | :--- | :--- |
 | `admin-back` | `/internal/admin` |
 | `merchant-back` | `/internal/merchant` |
 | `checkout-back` | `/internal/checkout` |
 
 `resolveCoreUrlAgainst()` pins the result to the configured base origin and appends the path to the base pathname. `resolveCoreUrl()` exposes the same behavior for callers and tests. This is a client-side guard only; `core-back` independently enforces the certificate CN with `requireEdgeIdentity()` in `core-back/api/middleware/mtlsGuard.ts`.
 
 ### 3.6 SSE streams and fallback behavior
 
 `openCoreStream()` is the streaming counterpart of `request()`:
 
 - sets `accept: text/event-stream` and `cache-control: no-cache`;
 - uses the same node selection, retry count, cooldown and attempted-node set;
 - increments `inFlight` until the stream ends, closes or errors;
 - if a node answers `502`/`503` and another attempt is possible, drains that response into a buffer, records it as `lastStream`, and tries the next node;
 - if retries are exhausted, returns `lastStream` or maps the transport error.
 
 `proxyCoreStream()` converts a non-2xx upstream into the normal core HTTP error, then copies the stream to the express response with `cache-control: no-cache, no-transform`, `connection: keep-alive` and `x-accel-buffering: no`. On client disconnect it aborts the upstream request.
 
 There is no true fallback to polling at the edge. Checkout and POS SSE are implemented by the core endpoint polling PostgreSQL on a timer; an established edge stream that breaks is ended, not resumed. The buffered `lastStream` fallback only preserves a failed handshake response body for retry purposes.
 
 ## 4. Contracts and invariants
 
 - Every core URL must be an absolute `https:` URL. Plain HTTP is not accepted by the edge configuration schema.
 - TLS 1.3 is the only accepted protocol version.
 - The client cert CN must match the channel; the client path guard prevents accidental cross-channel calls, and `core-back` prevents forged ones.
 - A call never retries against the same URL twice.
 - A default retry only applies to idempotent methods.
 - A `502`/`503` from any node is interpreted as node unavailability even if generated by application code.
 - Request identity headers and `authorization` are forwarded verbatim; the edge does not mint or re-sign tokens.
 - The pool does not load-balance SSE streams after establishment; selection happens once per stream open.
 - LSN hints are propagated, not validated. A malformed value is passed to core, where the storage layer decides how to handle it.
 - The client never receives or uses `DATABASE_URL`, `KMS_MASTER_KEY`, or another service's certificate.
 
 ## 5. Data / API / config / deployment surface
 
 ### Environment
 
 | Key | Required | Used by | Meaning |
 | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
 | `CORE_BACK_URL` | yes | all BFFs | First core URL and fallback when `CORE_BACK_URLS` is unset. |
 | `CORE_BACK_URLS` | no | all BFFs | Comma-separated core pool. |
 | `MTLS_CLIENT_CERT_PATH` | yes | all BFFs | Client certificate. |

 ### Deployment surface

 The deploy engine installs only the CA and the edge's own client certificate on an edge host. Certificate paths in the generated `.env` are relative (`shared/certs/...`) and are expanded to the release directory by `absoluteEnv()`.
 
 ## 6. Operational usage
 
 - When adding a core node, add it to `CORE_NODES` or set `CORE_BACK_URLS`; re-deploy the edge tiers so their process environment changes. The pool itself would notice a changed environment only if the process configuration changes, which requires a restart in a deployed environment.
 - When rotating certificates, restart or redeploy the edge processes. Replacing files in place is not sufficient for a running pool.
 - Check `/health` on the edge only for process liveness; it does not probe core. Use `deploy/lib/healthVerifier.ts` or a manual mTLS request to check the upstream.
 - Use `x-request-id` to correlate an edge failure with core logs. The edge maps core envelopes and preserves `code`, `message`, `details` and `reference`.
 - To debug node selection, inspect `CORE_BACK_URLS` in the generated `.env`, the edge logs and the core health endpoint. There are no exported pool metrics or a status endpoint.
 
 ## 7. Status and deviations
 
 ### Implemented
 
 - Per-node keep-alive TLS 1.3 agents with client certificates and CA verification.
 - Least-in-flight selection with round-robin tie-breaking.
 - Passive failure marking with a 5-second cooldown.
 - Half-open selection: one zero-in-flight request probes an unhealthy node after cooldown.
 - Idempotent retries and explicit non-idempotent retry opt-in.
 - `x-pg-min-lsn` propagation and header helper.
 - Channel path confinement and URL origin pinning.
 - Core envelope and transport error mapping.
 - SSE stream proxying with pre-establishment retry and buffering of failed handshake responses.
 
 ### Partial
 
 - The "shared" client is a copy-paste implementation. Behavior is consistent today, but a change must be applied three times.
 - Certificate rotation requires a restart; there is no file watcher or hot reload.
 - The SSE fallback preserves a failed response but does not resume an interrupted stream.
 
 ### Missing / deferred
 
 - No circuit-breaker metrics, pool introspection, or administrative pool status endpoint.
 - No request hedging or per-attempt deadline separate from the overall timeout.
 - No automatic retry for `POST`/`PATCH` unless a caller opts in.
 - No jitter on cooldown or randomized selection.
 
 ### Known bugs / risks
 
 - Treating every upstream `502`/`503` as a node failure can evict a healthy core node that legitimately returned a gateway-style `502`/`503`.
 - A half-open node is preferred over healthy nodes while any half-open candidate exists. With several recovering nodes this can concentrate probe traffic rather than spread it.
 - `maxAttempts` can exceed the number of nodes; the attempted set then stops the loop early.
 - A pool with an empty URL list throws `CORE_UNAVAILABLE`; there is no startup-time rejection of an empty `CORE_BACK_URLS` beyond the fallback to `CORE_BACK_URL`.
 - The stream path does not retry after response headers are delivered; a mid-stream core restart is visible to the browser.
 
 ### Code gap versus documentation
 
 The historical design describes zero-downtime rolling core restarts. The client enables retry-based continuity for idempotent one-shot calls and for stream establishment, but it does not guarantee zero downtime for non-idempotent calls, established SSE streams, or a single core node. This document records the as-built behavior.

 ## Merchant Edge BFF
 
 > Status: `partial` · Last verified: 2026-11-03
 
 ## 1. Purpose and scope
 
 `merchant-back` is the public merchant edge. One Bun/Express process serves two audiences:
 
 - the authenticated merchant portal under `/api/v1/merchant/*`;
 - the merchant server API under `/api/v1/external/*`, authenticated by a `pg_live_` bearer token and a core-side IP allowlist.
 
 It owns request validation, edge translation to the canonical core contract, upload verification, rate limiting, the public merchant API shape and mTLS forwarding to `/internal/merchant/*`. It owns no database connection, no Prisma client, no `DATABASE_URL`, no `KMS_MASTER_KEY` and no authority decisions.
 
 The merchant vhost serves the SPA through Nginx. The backend itself binds to loopback in deployment.
 
 ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design)
 
 The design splits the merchant experience into a portal API and a server-to-server API. The portal covers registration, identity verification, login/MFA, KYB onboarding, wallets, applications, links, POS terminals and cashier screens, payments, disputes, cash-outs, API tokens, credential sets, team users and overview statistics. The external API covers link creation/inspection/cancellation and payment lookup using a long-lived merchant token.
 
 All operations are forwarded over mTLS 1.3 with `CN=merchant-back`. The edge validates multipart KYB documents for MIME type, magic bytes and size before forwarding raw bytes to core. The portal may accept amounts and currencies when the merchant owns link creation; the edge never performs money arithmetic and core re-validates every monetary field. The external API is meant to enforce a `pg_live_` bearer token and an IP allowlist, with core as the authority.
 
 ## 3. As-built architecture
 
 ### 3.1 Process, listener and middleware
 
 `merchant-back/index.ts`:
 
 - disables `x-powered-by`;
 - sets `trust proxy` to false;
 - enables CORS with any origin and no credentials;
 - installs request logging;
 - serves unauthenticated `GET /health`;
 - parses JSON and URL-encoded bodies with `MAX_JSON_BODY_BYTES`;
 - mounts `/api/v1`;
 - adds the shared 404 and error handlers.
 
 The listener binds to `BIND_HOST` (default `0.0.0.0` in the service schema). The deploy engine overrides this to `127.0.0.1`; direct exposure of port 4102 is a configuration error.
 
 Middleware layers:
 
 | Layer | Behavior |
 | :--- | :--- |
 | `authLimiter` | Fixed 15-minute window, `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_MAX` (default 20), on `/api/v1/merchant/auth`. |
 | `onboardingLimiter` | 60-second window, `API_RATE_LIMIT_MAX` (default 300), on `/api/v1/merchant/onboarding`. |
 | `apiLimiter` | 60-second window, `API_RATE_LIMIT_MAX` (default 300), on the protected merchant router. |
 | `externalLimiter` | 60-second window, `EXTERNAL_RATE_LIMIT_MAX` (default 120), on `/api/v1/external`. |
 | `requirePgLiveToken` | Requires `Authorization: Bearer pg_live_...` by prefix only. Applied to the whole external router. |
 | `coreForward` `requireAuth` | Rejects a missing `Authorization` header for protected portal routes. Defaults to required; auth/onboarding routes opt out with `requireAuth: false`. |
 | `requireBearer` | Helper used by dispute evidence and merchant user routes to require a header before multipart work. |
 | `requireAuthHeader` | Exported from `api/public/auth.ts` but a no-op; it is not a security control. |
 
 There is no edge session parser, role guard or token verifier in `merchant-back`. An arbitrary non-empty bearer token reaches core for every protected portal route.
 
 ### 3.2 Forwarding behavior
 
 `merchant-back/api/forward.ts` implements a stricter forwarder than admin's:
 
 1. Requires `Authorization` unless `requireAuth === false`.
 2. Validates route params and query with Zod.
 3. Validates the public body with `schema`.
 4. Applies `bodyMapper()` to translate product vocabulary into the core body.
 5. Applies `bodyFrom()` when the route replaces the body entirely.
 6. Re-validates the translated body with `coreSchema` when configured, so a request that core would reject is stopped at the edge.
 7. Calls `callCoreResponse()` with request id, resolved client IP, user agent and the bearer token.
 8. Returns the core body with the declared status, or the core status when `relayStatus: true`.
 
 The external router also has its own PG-live prefix check. It does not hash or validate the token; core does the authoritative token lookup and IP check.
 
 ### 3.3 Uploads
 
 `merchant-back/api/upload.ts` uses Multer memory storage with `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`, one file and at most 32 fields. `forwardUpload()` and the dispute route call `assertAllowedUpload()`:
 
 - checks the declared MIME type against `UPLOAD_ALLOWED_MIME`;
 - checks magic bytes for PNG (`89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A`), JPEG (`FF D8 FF`) and PDF (`25 50 44 46 2D`);
 - enforces the size cap;
 - computes SHA-256;
 - forwards raw bytes with `x-upload-filename`, `x-upload-content-type`, `x-upload-sha256`, `x-upload-size` and base64url `x-upload-metadata`.
 
 Dispute evidence is converted into a canonical JSON body (`toCoreDisputeEvidence`) rather than raw bytes. The max evidence size is defined in `merchant-back/api/contract.ts`.
 
 ### 3.4 Route map
 
 Portal auth is mounted under `/api/v1/merchant/auth`:
 
 | Method | Path |
 | :--- | :--- |
 | POST | `/register`, `/verify-identity`, `/accept-invitation`, `/login`, `/google`, `/mfa/verify` |
 | GET | `/me` |
 
 Onboarding is mounted under `/api/v1/merchant/onboarding`:
 
 | Method | Path |
 | :--- | :--- |
 | GET, PUT | `/join-request` |
 | GET | `/kyb-revalidations`, `/beneficial-owners` |
 | POST | `/kyb-documents` (multipart), `/beneficial-owners`, `/submit` |
 | DELETE | `/beneficial-owners/:id` |
 
 The protected portal API is mounted under `/api/v1/merchant`:
 
 | Area | Routes |
 | :--- | :--- |
 | Wallets | `GET, POST /wallets`, `GET /wallets/:id`, `GET /wallets/:id/balance`, `GET /wallets/:id/statements`, `GET /wallets/:id/statements/:month/export` |
 | Applications | `GET, POST /applications`, `GET, PATCH /applications/:id` |
 | Links | `GET, POST /links`, `GET /links/:id`, `POST /links/:id/cancel`, `GET /links/:id/attempts` |
 | POS | `GET, POST /pos/terminals`, `GET, PATCH /pos/terminals/:id`, `POST /pos/terminals/:id/screens`, `GET /pos/screens/:screenCode/stream` (SSE) |
 | Payments | `GET /payments` |
 | Disputes | `GET /disputes`, `GET /disputes/:id`, `POST /disputes/:id/evidence` (multipart) |
 | Cash-outs | `GET, POST /cashouts` |
 | Tokens | `GET, POST /tokens`, `PUT /tokens/:id/ips`, `DELETE /tokens/:id` |
 | Credential sets | `GET, POST /credential-sets`, `GET, PUT /credential-sets/:id` |
 | Team | `GET, POST, PATCH /users`, `PATCH /users/:id` |
 | Stats | `GET /stats/overview` |
 
 `merchant-back/api/protected/options.ts` exports `optionsRouter` for `GET /options/:kind`, but the router is not imported by `api/protected/index.ts` and has no live mount.
 
 The external merchant server API is mounted under `/api/v1/external`:
 
 | Method | Path |
 | :--- | :--- |
 | POST | `/links`, `/links/:key/cancel` |
 | GET | `/links/:key`, `/payments/:reference` |
 
 ### 3.5 Authentication behavior and the Google gap
 
 Portal auth routes are public at the edge (`requireAuth: false`) and forward to `/internal/merchant/auth/*`:
 
 - `POST /register` validates phone/email, password, name and optional identity fields, then creates a registration.
 - `POST /verify-identity` validates an identity type, number, phone and OTP code.
 - `POST /accept-invitation` validates an invitation token and password.
 - `POST /login` validates an identifier and password.
 - `POST /google` validates a Google `idToken` shape and forwards it, but `core-back` answers `501 NOT_IMPLEMENTED` with `Google sign-in requires a configured OIDC provider` (`core-back/api/internal/merchant.ts:853`). The capability is not implemented at the core.
 - `GET /me` and `POST /mfa/verify` forward the supplied bearer/challenge state to core.
 
 The merchant portal session is a core-issued token. The edge never verifies its signature, expiry, revocation, MFA state or merchant status. Core verifies the signature, expiry, user status and authorities; it does not re-check MFA or a session revocation list on every call.
 
 ## 4. Contracts and invariants
 
 - All portal business routes require an `Authorization` header at the edge; its validity is decided by core.
 - The external API requires a `pg_live_` prefix at the edge; access-token validity, revocation and source-IP allowlist are decided by core.
 - Every forwarded path stays under `/internal/merchant`; the shared client enforces this and core re-checks `CN=merchant-back`.
 - The edge never accepts arbitrary core paths.
 - Link creation accepts decimal-string amounts and ISO 4217 currencies; the edge does not do arithmetic and core re-validates amount, currency and fee model.
 - Checkout money semantics do not apply here: merchant link creation is an owning operation.
 - Uploaded KYB and dispute files are validated for MIME, magic bytes and size before the core call.
 - Team/user and credential-set operations are forwarded with the caller's bearer token; the core enforces merchant roles and maker-checker where applicable.
 - The POS SSE route requires a bearer header, then proxies the core stream.

 ## 6. Operational usage
 
 ```bash
 cd merchant-back
 bun install
 bun run start
 bun run dev
 bun test
 bun run typecheck
 ```
 
 - Public reachability is through `https://merchant.<domain>/api`; the backend port must stay loopback-only.
 - For POS issues, verify the Nginx stream route disables buffering and the proxy read timeout exceeds the cashier idle window.
 - For upload failures, check `UPLOAD_ALLOWED_MIME`, magic bytes, `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` and the core-side upload limits.
 - For external API `401 INVALID_API_TOKEN`, the edge did not see a `pg_live_` bearer; for a core rejection, inspect the core token/IP state.
 - Google login currently returns 501 by design of the core; use password or invitation flows.
 
 ## 7. Status and deviations
 
 ### Implemented
 
 - Two-audience routing with separate rate limits and external token prefix gate.
 - Full portal and external route surface, including multipart KYB and evidence uploads.
 - Public-to-core schema validation and canonical body mapping.
 - MIME/magic-byte/size validation and hashed raw upload forwarding.
 - mTLS pool, retries, LSN header propagation and channel confinement.
 - POS SSE proxy with buffering disabled.
 
 ### Partial
 
 - Portal authentication is only a presence check at the edge; all session and authority enforcement is in core.
 - External token validation is prefix-only at the edge.
 - Google sign-in is exposed but not implemented by core.
 
 ### Missing / deferred
 
 - Google OIDC provider integration in core.
 - Edge session revocation/MFA cache.
 - Route-level merchant role guards at the edge.
 - A live `GET /options/:kind` mount for the merchant portal.
 - SSE resume/replay or polling fallback at the edge.
 
 ### Known bugs / risks
 
 - `requireAuthHeader` is a no-op and should not be mistaken for a guard.
 - The auth limiter uses a hard-coded 15-minute window; `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS` has no effect.
 - `x-real-client-ip` is preferred over `x-real-ip` in `merchant-back/lib/net/index.ts`. When the backend is loopback-bound this is safe; if it is ever exposed and a direct peer is inside `TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`, the peer can spoof its client IP.
 - The options router is dead code; a frontend calling `/api/v1/merchant/options/:kind` receives a 404.
 - The external prefix check is not a credential check; do not log or expose token values.

 - **Decision:** `project-design/parts/**` is the editable source of truth. `PROJECT_DESIGN.md`, `STATUS.md`, appendices and `*/blueprint.md` are generated. `design/**` is historical/reference only.
 - **Rationale:** The historical design corpus mixes normative design, delivery logs, aspirational plans and obsolete engine versions. A single generated master plus part metadata gives one authoritative answer and a machine-checkable status.
 - **Consequences:** Agents must update part docs and `TRACKER.md` with code changes. Generated files are never hand-edited.
 
 ## ADR-0002 — PostgreSQL 18 is the only runtime database
 
 - **Date:** 2026-11-03
 - **Status:** accepted
 - **Decision:** PostgreSQL 18 (`@prisma/adapter-pg` + `pg`) is the only supported runtime engine. MySQL/MariaDB runtime support and legacy migration history are removed.
 - **Consequences:** Historical MySQL notes remain only in `design/**` with historical labels. `deploy.env` defaults to PostgreSQL 18.
 
 ## ADR-0003 — Storage/backup design is as-built, not aspirational
 
 - **Date:** 2026-11-03
 - **Status:** accepted
 - **Decision:** Storage/backup/search/seeder design parts must distinguish implemented behavior from partial/missing features. Read models, replica routing, keyset pagination, audit/log retention and backup drill behavior are documented as they exist, not as the blueprint originally proposed.
 - **Consequences:** P0/P1 gaps stay visible in `TRACKER.md` until the code changes.
+
+## 2026-11-03 — Two-machine lab is disposable and marker-gated
+
+- **Decision:** `deploy/test-matrix/**` owns the T1-T8 lab. Bootstrap writes `/etc/pg-lab-matrix`; teardown only drops PostgreSQL clusters when that marker exists.
+- **Why:** the lab intentionally creates and destroys `main`, `replica_*`, `audit` and `log` clusters on both hosts. Without a marker, a teardown could destroy a non-lab database.
+- **Consequence:** live certification requires HOST_B reachable and the marker present. Config generation and unit tests do not need HOST_B.

Purpose and scope The repository is a multi-rail payment gateway and payment-links platform built around a single database-owning core service. It lets an operator add a gateway by declarative configuration instead of a code release, lets a merchant create payment links and onboard through KYB/AML, and lets an anonymous payer complete a payment through one of the visible rails and collection modes. This part owns the product-level overview: the workspaces, product scope, the seven-service topology plus the optional Fake Rails tier, the implemented versus unimplemented capabilities, and the lineage from the historical design corpus to the current code. It does not own the detailed contracts of the core API, the rail engine, the ledger, storage, deploy or any individual frontend; those are owned by the later parts. The primary users are: - Platform operators in the admin back office: onboarding review, KYB, AML, approvals, gateways/rails/routes, reconciliation, finance, disputes and backups. - Merchants and merchant staff in the merchant portal and through the external `pg_live_` server API: onboarding, wallets, applications, links, POS, payments, disputes, cash-outs, tokens and credentials. - Anonymous payers on the hosted checkout: link resolution, rail selection, customer fields, OTP/redirect/embedded/QR/push flows and status polling. - Internal edge services, which are not human users but callers whose identity is a client certificate common name. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The historical corpus describes a national payment switch for the Libyan market with a first-party wallet rail, plus direct and aggregator integrations for the roughly twenty researched gateways. The product is not a simple redirect wrapper: the customer is in the loop, confirmations arrive late, twice, through a browser or through a statement, and money may settle days after the payment attempt. The design therefore adds a declarative flow engine, an attempt state machine, a trusted-confirmation layer and an ownership-aware double-entry ledger on top of the voucher-style provider pattern. The stable design intent, corrected where the code has moved on, is: 1. **Four catalog layers.** A `Gateway` is one technical integration. A `CredentialSet` is whose account and secrets are used, per environment, with an ownership and settlement target. A `Rail` is what the customer sees and chooses. A `Route` binds a rail to a gateway through a credential set with priority, cost, limits, health and scope. 2. **Two independent axes.** Collection mode is what the customer does: `OTP_PULL`, `REDIRECT`, `EMBEDDED`, `PUSH_APPROVAL`, `QR_DISPLAY`, `PAY_CODE`, `DEEP_LINK`, `MANUAL`, `HYBRID`. Confirmation channel is how the platform learns the result: sync response, webhook, inquiry/poll, return URL, browser callback, statement, operator confirmation. 3. **Zero-trust split.** `core-back` is the only service with database credentials, the KMS master key, ledger-posting authority and outbound gateway execution. The edge backends have no database drivers or credentials and call core only over mutual TLS. 4. **Declarative engine plus escape hatch.** The engine supports a closed transform library and declarative phases. A native adapter is the escape hatch for proprietary protocols, but it still goes through the same attempt state machine, inbox, verifier and ledger poster. 5. **Nothing browser-side is trusted.** Widget callbacks and return URLs are hints that trigger a server inquiry. Money is posted only after the trusted-success facts match. 6. **Immutable configuration.** Gateway versions are snapshots; an attempt pins its gateway version, route, credential set and commission profile at creation. 7. **Uncertain outcomes become `UNKNOWN`.** A timeout, reset, 5xx or extraction failure on a money-moving step is not retried blindly. 8. **Ownership-aware ledger.** Platform-held settlement uses gateway clearing accounts; merchant-direct settlement books commission only; internal rails clear through treasury. 9. **Governance and compliance.** Maker-checker, KYB, beneficial-owner screening, AML rules, confidential AML access, disputes, adjustments, cash-outs, reconciliation and reporting are part of the product, not add-ons. 10. **Operational safety.** Durable workers, a webhook inbox, statement reconciliation, backups/PITR drills, and horizontal deployment are part of the architecture. The target scale stated in the historical design is a national switch with tens to hundreds of millions of records, `1..N` compute nodes per tier, `0..N` PostgreSQL streaming replicas, PgBouncer in transaction mode, Redis for cache/velocity, dedicated audit and log databases, and 5 to 30+ dedicated hosts. The code supports the horizontal arrays and the storage ports; no production-shaped scale run is recorded in the repository. ### Design lineage - `design/Dynamic-Payment-Gateway-Management-Design-v2.md` introduced the four catalog layers, the two collection/confirmation axes, the declarative engine, the ownership-aware ledger and the `UNKNOWN` rule. - `design/payment-gateway-refined-design-v4.1.md` restored the operational/compliance program: roles, four-eyes matrix, onboarding/KYB, AML, disputes, ledger-derived reporting and the 140-case catalog. - `design/payment_gateway_final_design-v5.md` is the consolidated multi-service production narrative. It is authoritative for intent but stale on counts, route lists and some runtime behavior; this part set corrects those. - `design/opencode_technical_delivery_design.md` is a delivery tracker and historical verification log, including the PostgreSQL 18 storage/backup/scaling delivery run (section 28). - `design/payment_gateway_deployment_and_guides_architecture.md` is the deployment topology, PKI, firewall and pipeline source. - `design/performance-efficiency/storage_driver_postgres18_backup_and_scaling_architecture.md` is authoritative for the storage/backup/scaling intent, with the DDL/read-model/LSN drift corrected by the storage part. - `design/fake_payment_rails_service_architecture.md` and the Fake Rails code define the optional emulator. - `design/**` remains historical/reference only. Canonical current behavior is `project-design/parts/**` and the code. ## 3. As-built architecture The workspace contains four backend services, three Vue 3 + Vuetify 3 + TypeScript frontends, an optional Fake Payment Rails emulator (backend and portal), a deployment engine with a backup daemon, tests and the canonical design tree. | Workspace | Runtime | Role | Evidence | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `core-back` | Bun + Express 5 + native TLS server | PostgreSQL owner, domain engine, ledger, governance, workers, backup control client, synthetic seeder | `core-back/index.ts`, `core-back/api/**`, `core-back/engine/**`, `core-back/lib/**` | | `admin-back` | Bun + Express 5 | LAN-only admin edge BFF; validates and forwards to `/internal/admin/*` | `admin-back/index.ts`, `admin-back/api/**`, `admin-back/lib/coreInternalClient.ts` | | `merchant-back` | Bun + Express 5 | Public merchant portal API and external `pg_live_` API; forwards to `/internal/merchant/*` | `merchant-back/index.ts`, `merchant-back/api/**` | | `checkout-back` | Bun + Express 5 | Public checkout, SSE proxy and raw webhook intake; forwards to `/internal/checkout/*` | `checkout-back/index.ts`, `checkout-back/api/public/**` | | `admin-front` | Vue 3 + Vuetify 3 + Vite | LAN admin back office SPA | `admin-front/package.json`, `admin-front/src/**` | | `merchant-front` | Vue 3 + Vuetify 3 + Vite | Merchant portal SPA | `merchant-front/package.json`, `merchant-front/src/**` | | `checkout-front` | Vue 3 + Vuetify 3 + Vite | Hosted payer checkout SPA | `checkout-front/package.json`, `checkout-front/src/**` | | `fake-rails-back` | Bun + Express 5 + SQLite | Optional standalone rail emulator with hosted pages, SDK shims, chaos and webhook dispatch | `fake-rails-back/index.ts`, `fake-rails-back/api/**`, `fake-rails-back/engine/**` | | `fake-rails-front` | Vue 3 + Vuetify 3 + Vite | Optional tester portal for Fake Rails | `fake-rails-front/package.json`, `fake-rails-front/src/**` | | `deploy` | Bun | Multi-host provisioning, PKI, firewall, PM2/nginx templates, backup daemon | `deploy/deploy.ts`, `deploy/lib/**`, `deploy/provisioners/**` | | `tests` | Playwright/Vitest | Cross-workspace and live-stack journeys | `tests/**` | The seven-service topology is therefore `core-back`, the three edge backends and the three frontends. Fake Rails is an eighth and ninth workspace only when enabled. The core is private-LAN only on port `4000`; the admin edge listens on `4101` and is normally reached through a LAN-only nginx vhost on `8443`; merchant and checkout edge backends listen on `4102`/`4103` behind public TLS reverse proxies. Ports are deployment-configured, with the defaults above in the deploy schema. The product scope implemented in code includes: - Payment links with single-use and multi-use slots, link cancellation, visible rails and fee breakdowns. - A universal rail engine with seven runtime phases, a separate credential-check phase, 39 transforms, crypto profiles and a scoped SSRF guard. - A PostgreSQL 18 schema with 75 models and 105 enums at schema version 8, and four migrations: baseline, storage engine, CQRS read models and storage hardening. - A double-entry ledger, 17 `LedgerScenario` values and 11 GL account types, with sharded system GL accounts. - Merchant onboarding, KYB documents, beneficial owners, screening, AML rules/cases, regulatory reports, disputes, adjustments, cash-outs and reconciliation. - Admin and merchant authentication with password login, optional MFA challenge, session JWTs and merchant `pg_live_` API tokens. - Admin maker-checker approvals, with the executable-handler coverage described in `01-core-back/01-api-surface.md`. - Durable workers for expiry, polling, inbound inbox, notification outbox, ledger invariants, join-request expiry, periodic screening, KYB expiry, retention and the background job queue. - Storage engine ports for unit-of-work, replica reads, Redis cache/velocity, dedicated audit and dedicated logs. - Backup control through the mTLS `pg-backup-daemon`, with catalog, trigger, drill and policy routes. - Optional Fake Rails emulator and tester portal. - Deploy engine with horizontal compute/storage node arrays, PKI, firewall, nginx/PM2 templates and ordered pipeline. The product scope intentionally not implemented is tracked in section 7 and in `project-design/appendices/stale-claims-register.md`. In particular, the voucher provider system exists only as design, guide v2 is future work, Google OIDC is a 501 stub, and `CAPTURE`/`SETTLEMENT_FETCH` are reserved enum values. ## 4. Contracts and invariants The platform-level non-negotiables are: 1. **PostgreSQL 18 is the only runtime database.** The Prisma datasource is `provider = "postgresql"`; the runtime uses `@prisma/adapter-pg` and `pg`; `DATABASE_URL`, replica URLs, audit and log URLs are validated as PostgreSQL URLs in `core-back/lib/env/index.ts`. MySQL and MariaDB support have been removed. 2. **Money is decimal.** Runtime money uses `Decimal`/`decimal.js` and Prisma `NUMERIC(18,4)`; the transform library forbids `to_number` on monetary outputs. 3. **Database exclusivity.** Only `core-back` holds `DATABASE_URL`, database drivers, `KMS_MASTER_KEY`, ledger authority and outbound gateway credentials. Edge backends' package manifests and environment schemas contain no database driver or database URL; their only upstream is `CORE_BACK_URL` / `CORE_BACK_URLS`. 4. **mTLS and channel identity.** `core-back` requires a client certificate signed by the internal CA and binds each internal namespace to one common name: `/internal/admin/*` only `admin-back`, `/internal/merchant/*` only `merchant-back`, `/internal/checkout/*` only `checkout-back`. 5. **Authorities are enforced by core.** Edge checks are advisory. `core-back` re-authenticates the bearer credential, re-reads the user/merchant/authority state from the database, and re-validates payloads. 6. **Maker-checker is server-side.** The approval route and governance execution require a human user, a checker authority, and a checker different from the maker; the database also has a check constraint and a trigger on `approval_requests`. 7. **Atomic critical writes.** The ledger, outbox and audit outbox are written in one transaction on the critical path; the storage engine's `UnitOfWork` owns the commit LSN. 8. **Secrets and confidential data never reach logs.** Vault redaction covers sensitive field names, literal decrypted secrets and Luhn-valid PANs. Edge services never receive the KMS key or database credentials. 9. **Bilingual catalogues stay in sync.** User-facing text is maintained in English and Arabic. 10. **Deploy-time UI flags are runtime-controlled.** The deploy engine writes `showChecklists`/`showSnapshotExportChecklist` and `showHelpPanels` into the admin runtime config and injects the matching `VITE_*` build constants; source builds fall back to the documented defaults. ## 5. Data / API / config / deployment surface The platform surface is split by trust boundary: - **Human frontends:** `admin-front` calls `admin-back`; `merchant-front` calls `merchant-back`; `checkout-front` calls `checkout-back`. None of them calls core directly. - **Edge HTTP surfaces:** - Admin edge: `/api/v1/admin/*` (auth routes plus protected router). - Merchant edge: `/api/v1/merchant/auth/*`, `/api/v1/merchant/onboarding/*`, `/api/v1/merchant/*`, `/api/v1/external/*`. - Checkout edge: `/api/v1/pay/*`, `/api/v1/return/*`, `/api/v1/inbound/*`. - **Core internal surfaces:** `/internal/admin/*`, `/internal/merchant/*`, `/internal/checkout/*`, plus an `/api/public` mount with a rate limiter and no registered routes. - **Core data surfaces:** PostgreSQL primary and replicas, optional PgBouncer, Redis cache/velocity, `pg_audit_db`, `pg_logs_db`, `pg-backup-daemon`. - **Deployment surface:** `deploy/deploy.env` with compute node arrays, PostgreSQL primary/replicas/PgBouncer, Redis nodes, audit/log nodes, backup node, mTLS PKI, firewall and nginx/PM2 templates; `deploy/backup-daemon` is provisioned from the same config. The request paths are: - Payer: browser -> `checkout-front` -> public TLS -> `checkout-back` -> mTLS -> `core-back` `/internal/checkout/*` -> PostgreSQL and, for payment execution, an external gateway through `ApiConsumer`. - Merchant portal: browser -> `merchant-front` -> public TLS -> `merchant-back` `/api/v1/merchant/*` -> mTLS -> `core-back` `/internal/merchant/*`. - External merchant server: HTTPS + `Authorization: Bearer pg_live_...` -> `merchant-back` `/api/v1/external/*` -> mTLS -> `core-back` `/internal/merchant/external/*`; core checks the token hash, revocation and optional CIDR allowlist. - Admin: LAN browser -> LAN-only nginx `:8443` -> `admin-back` `:4101` -> mTLS -> `core-back` `/internal/admin/*`. - Gateway callback: gateway -> public `checkout-back` `/api/v1/inbound/{gateway}/{env}/{pathToken}` with the raw body -> mTLS -> `core-back` `/internal/checkout/inbound/...`. - Return URL: payer browser -> `checkout-back` `/api/v1/return/{attemptToken}` -> core inquiry -> status redirect. - Backups: admin UI -> `admin-back` `/api/v1/admin/system/backups/*` -> core backup router -> mTLS backup daemon `:4090`. ## 6. Operational usage Typical local verification follows the service READMEs: ```bash cd core-back bun run generate-mtls-certs bun run migrate-generate bun run migrate-deploy bun run db-seed bun run start ``` Each edge backend requires `CORE_BACK_URL` (or `CORE_BACK_URLS`) and its client certificate, key and CA paths. Purpose and scope This part describes the runtime service graph: which processes exist, how they listen, which network boundary they sit in, which channels are mutual-TLS, which component owns the database, and how requests travel from a browser or gateway to core and back. It also describes the horizontal-node arrays in the deploy engine and the optional Fake Rails tier. This part does not repeat the API contracts (`01-core-back/01-api-surface.md`), the security controls (`00-platform/02-security-and-mtls.md`), the full env schema (`00-platform/03-runtime-and-config.md`) or the deploy pipeline (`07-deploy/**`). It provides the topology those parts depend on. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The historical design defines a seven-service split: 1. `core-back`: private-LAN mTLS server, sole database owner, KMS and secret owner, dynamic rail engine, ledger, workers and outbound gateway calls. 2. `admin-back`: LAN-only edge BFF with no database driver. 3. `merchant-back`: public-SSL merchant edge BFF with no database driver. 4. `checkout-back`: public-SSL checkout and webhook edge with no database driver. 5. `admin-front`: LAN-only admin SPA. 6. `merchant-front`: public merchant SPA. 7. `checkout-front`: public hosted-checkout SPA. `fake-rails-back` and `fake-rails-front` are an optional eighth and ninth workspace used for sandbox and testing; they are not part of the production seven-service core. The design also defines the network zones: - Public internet reaches only the merchant and checkout reverse proxies on `80/443`. The proxies serve the matching SPA and forward `/api` to the matching edge backend. - The admin reverse proxy is bound to a private LAN interface on a non-forwarded port, normally `8443`. It serves the admin SPA and forwards `/api` to `admin-back`. - All three edge backends call `core-back` over a private LAN with mTLS 1.3 client certificates. - `core-back` is never published by a reverse proxy and has no public listener. - `core-back` reaches PostgreSQL, Redis, the audit database, the log database and external gateways. - The backup daemon is a separate mTLS control plane, normally `:4090`, with backup storage in S3/MinIO/R2 and an optional secondary vault. The historical target for compute is `CORE_NODES`, `ADMIN_NODES`, `MERCHANT_NODES` and `CHECKOUT_NODES` arrays, each entry shaped `nodeId@sshHost:sshPort:privateIp:servicePort`. Storage is declared separately with `PG_PRIMARY_NODE`, `PG_REPLICA_NODES`, `PGBOUNCER_*`, `REDIS_NODES`, `AUDIT_DB_NODE`, `LOG_DB_NODE` and `BACKUP_NODE`. The design supports a single all-in-one host, combined compute hosts, fully distributed hosts and horizontal compute. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 Process and listener inventory | Process | Default listener | Exposure | Database | Upstream | Entry point | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `core-back` | `127.0.0.1:4000` (`HOST`/`PORT`) | Private LAN only, TLS 1.3 server, client certificate required | PostgreSQL primary/replicas, Redis, audit/log DBs | External gateway HTTPS endpoints, backup daemon mTLS | `core-back/index.ts` | | `admin-back` | `127.0.0.1:4101`, behind LAN nginx `:8443` | Private LAN only; `enforceLanAccess` on `/api/v1/admin` | None | `CORE_BACK_URL(S)` over mTLS | `admin-back/index.ts` | | `merchant-back` | `0.0.0.0:4102` | Public reverse proxy `80/443` | None | `CORE_BACK_URL(S)` over mTLS | `merchant-back/index.ts` | | `checkout-back` | `0.0.0.0:4103` | Public reverse proxy `80/443` | None | `CORE_BACK_URL(S)` over mTLS | `checkout-back/index.ts` | | `admin-front` | static build behind nginx `:8443` | LAN | None | `admin-back` HTTP API | `admin-front/src/**` | | `merchant-front` | static build behind public nginx | Public | None | `merchant-back` HTTP API | `merchant-front/src/**` | | `checkout-front` | static build behind public nginx | Public | None | `checkout-back` HTTP API | `checkout-front/src/**` | | `fake-rails-back` | `127.0.0.1:4104` (`HOST`/`PORT`) | Optional, behind `fake-rails` nginx `:8444` | Its own SQLite store | Core inbound URL for synthetic webhooks | `fake-rails-back/index.ts` | | `fake-rails-front` | static build behind the Fake Rails vhost | Optional | None | `fake-rails-back` portal API | `fake-rails-front/src/**` | The ports above are schema defaults; every deployment can override them. `deploy/lib/configSchema.ts` derives the edge pool from `CORE_NODES` unless `CORE_BACK_URLS` is set explicitly. ### 3.2 Core composition `createApp()` builds one Express app for both the TLS server and tests. The middleware order is: 1. `app.disable("x-powered-by")`. 2. `app.set("trust proxy", env.TRUST_PROXY)`. 3. `requestIdMiddleware`. 4. `requestLoggerMiddleware`. 5. `rawBodyMiddleware` for opaque upload/webhook paths. 6. `express.json({ limit: "1mb" })`. 7. `express.urlencoded({ extended: true, limit: "1mb" })`. 8. `GET /health`. 9. `app.use("/internal", internalRouter)`. 10. `app.use("/api", apiRouter)`. 11. The terminal error handler. `internalRouter` mounts each channel behind `requireEdgeIdentity`: ```text /internal/admin -> requireEdgeIdentity("admin-back") -> adminInternalRouter /internal/merchant -> requireEdgeIdentity("merchant-back") -> merchantInternalRouter /internal/checkout -> requireEdgeIdentity("checkout-back") -> checkoutInternalRouter ``` `apiRouter` mounts `publicRouter` at `/api/public`; that router currently installs only a rate limiter and registers no endpoint. Inside the admin router, `/health` is public over the mTLS channel; authentication starts at `router.use(requireAuthentication)`, and the backup router is mounted under `/system/backups` after that guard. Inside the merchant router, `/health` and the auth routes before the `requireAuthentication` line are public within the channel; onboarding and the remaining merchant routes require a bearer credential. The checkout router has no bearer authentication because the link key and attempt token are the payer capability. ### 3.3 Edge composition All three edge backends use the same pattern: - Express 5 app, `x-powered-by` disabled, `trust proxy` false, CORS enabled with `origin: true, credentials: false`. - A request logger and a `/health` endpoint returning service name and uptime. - Body parsers with a per-edge JSON limit: admin `4 MiB`, merchant `2 MiB`, checkout `1 MiB`. - A request validator at the edge and a second validator inside core (the Double-Check Rule). - A mTLS HTTPS agent built from `MTLS_CLIENT_CERT_PATH`, `MTLS_CLIENT_KEY_PATH` and `MTLS_CA_CERT_PATH`, with `minVersion` and `maxVersion` fixed to TLS 1.3 and `rejectUnauthorized: true`. - `CORE_BACK_URLS` parsed into an ordered pool; `CORE_BACK_URL` remains the first-node compatibility value. - Least-in-flight selection with a round-robin tie-break, a 5-second failure cooldown, passive health marking on transport errors and `502`/`503`, and retries for idempotent methods (or when `retryIfUnavailable` is set). - Forwarded headers: `x-request-id`, `x-real-client-ip`, `x-client-user-agent`, `x-edge-service`, and `authorization` when present. `x-pg-min-lsn` is propagated when a route declares a consistency LSN. `admin-back` adds `enforceLanAccess`, which resolves the client IP through trusted proxy CIDRs and checks `ADMIN_LAN_CIDRS`. `merchant-back` adds rate limits for auth, portal API and external API. `checkout-back` mounts the raw inbound router before the JSON parser so webhook bytes and signature headers survive. ### 3.4 Storage and data topology `core-back` boots exactly one `StorageEngine` per process. `createStorageEngine()` constructs: - A Prisma client for the primary from `DATABASE_URL`. - Zero or more Prisma clients for `DATABASE_REPLICA_URLS`, each with a health/lag state. - A `PostgresReplicaReadStore` with `READ_REPLICA_MAX_LAG_MS`, LSN monitor and primary fallback. - A `PostgresUnitOfWorkAdapter` that owns `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`, sorted `gl_account_shards` locking and the post-commit WAL flush LSN. - A Redis cache/velocity adapter when `REDIS_URL` or the first `REDIS_NODES` entry is set; otherwise an in-memory adapter. - A dedicated audit driver over `AUDIT_DATABASE_URL` when set. - A dedicated log sink over `LOG_DATABASE_URL` when set; without it, logs are kept in a bounded in-memory buffer. PostgreSQL is the only runtime database. The data plane also includes PgBouncer when `PGBOUNCER_ENABLED=true`, streaming replicas, the 16-way system GL shard table, the outbox/read-model tables, and the audit/log databases. Redis is never authoritative for money. The backup control plane is core -> `BACKUP_DAEMON_URL` (mTLS when HTTPS) -> `pg-backup-daemon` -> WAL-G/Barman -> primary S3 and optional secondary vault. The daemon also exposes `/health`, `/v1/overview`, `/v1/backups/trigger`, `/v1/drills/run`, `/v1/policy`, `/v1/runs` and `/v1/drills`. ### 3.5 Fake Rails tier `fake-rails-back` is intentionally independent: it reads its own env, owns a SQLite store and never touches the gateway database. It listens on `127.0.0.1:4104` by default and is published on a separate nginx vhost, default `:8444`. It exposes hosted pages, rail routers, SDK shims, portal APIs, chaos scenarios and a webhook dispatcher that calls `CORE_INBOUND_BASE_URL` (default `http://127.0.0.1:4103/api/v1/inbound`). Core can reach a Fake Rails host only through a three-part allowlist: `ALLOW_FAKE_RAILS_HOSTS=true`, the host in `FAKE_RAILS_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, and the same host in the gateway version's `allowed_hosts`. This is an SSRF exception scoped to the exact host; it is not a general private-network allowance. The `FAKE_RAILS_ENABLED` and `FAKE_RAILS_ALLOW_IN_PRODUCTION` flags are separate from the SSRF allowlist. ## 4. Contracts and invariants ### 4.1 Channel binding - `/internal/admin/*` accepts only a certificate whose subject CN is exactly `admin-back`. - `/internal/merchant/*` accepts only `merchant-back`. - `/internal/checkout/*` accepts only `checkout-back`. - A valid certificate from the internal CA on the wrong channel gets `403 FORBIDDEN_SERVICE_IDENTITY`. - An unauthorized or missing client certificate is rejected by TLS (`rejectUnauthorized: true`) and, defensively, by `requireEdgeIdentity` with `401 MTLS_UNAUTHORIZED`. ### 4.2 Database exclusivity - `DATABASE_URL`, `DATABASE_REPLICA_URLS`, `AUDIT_DATABASE_URL`, `LOG_DATABASE_URL`, `REDIS_URL` and `KMS_MASTER_KEY` are core-only. - Edge env schemas do not contain those keys; edge packages do not depend on `pg` or Prisma. - Edge services can only mutate state through core's internal API. - The frontend packages list `@prisma/client` as a dependency, but no frontend source imports Prisma and no frontend receives a database URL; it is not a data-plane credential. ### 4.3 Request consistency - A core route may set `x-pg-min-lsn` on a write response. The edge passes the header on a subsequent read, and core routes that use `readThroughReplicaOrPrimary` wait for a replica at or above that LSN, falling back to the primary. - The commit LSN for an attempt is kept in an in-process map in `PlatformRuntime` and consumed once by the checkout confirm route. It is not shared across core nodes. ### 4.4 Health contracts - Core `GET /health` is always on the mTLS listener and reports queue health; it is not a public liveness endpoint. It returns `status: "ok"` or `status: "degraded"` with HTTP 200 in both cases. - Each channel also has a trivial `GET /health` inside its internal router (`admin`, `merchant`, `checkout`), reachable only after the channel identity guard. - Edge `GET /health` is unauthenticated and reports `{ status: "ok", service, uptime }`. - The backup daemon has its own `/health` and is not proxied through core's `/health`. ### 4.5 Horizontal nodes - `CORE_NODES`, `ADMIN_NODES`, `MERCHANT_NODES` and `CHECKOUT_NODES` are comma-separated `nodeId@sshHost:sshPort:privateIp:servicePort` entries. - The core certificate SAN includes every core private IP; edge client certificates are shared per edge role. - Edge pools are per-process and built lazily from `CORE_BACK_URLS`. A failed node is cooled down for five seconds and retried; another eligible node is selected when available. - Rolling deployment updates one batch of nodes at a time and health-checks each batch before continuing. The previous release remains on disk when a batch fails. ## 5. Operational usage ### 6.1 Local seven-service run 1. Generate the PKI with `bun run generate-mtls-certs` in `core-back`. 2. Start PostgreSQL, apply migrations and seed. 3. Start `core-back` on `127.0.0.1:4000`. 4. Start `admin-back` with `CORE_BACK_URL=https://127.0.0.1:4000` and the admin client certificate. 5. Start `merchant-back` and `checkout-back` with their own certificates. 6. Start the three frontends against the matching edge API URLs. The core certificate SAN and the edge `CORE_BACK_URL` hostname must agree with the agent's `servername`; the edge sets `servername` only when the base URL host is not an IP literal. ### 6.2 Adding a core node 1. Add the node to `CORE_NODES` and its private IP to the core certificate SAN generation. 2. Deploy the same release to the new node. 3. Set `CORE_BACK_URLS` to the full ordered pool, or let the deploy engine derive it from `CORE_NODES`. 4. Health-check the node over mTLS before rolling the next batch. ### 6.3 Failure behavior - Edge-to-core transport failure: the node is marked unhealthy and cooled down; the pool retries another node for idempotent calls. Non-idempotent POSTs are not retried unless `retryIfUnavailable` is explicitly set by the route. - Core database failure: `GET /health` stays HTTP 200 but reports `QUEUE_HEALTH_UNAVAILABLE` and `status: "degraded"`. - Worker disabled: core refuses to boot when `WORKER_ENABLED` or `WORKER_BACKGROUND_JOBS_ENABLED` is false, because queue-only routes would accept work that no worker can drain. - Backup daemon unavailable: backup writes return `503 BACKUP_DAEMON_NOT_CONFIGURED`; the local catalog remains readable. ### 6.4 Request path diagrams ```text Payer: browser -> checkout-front -> public nginx -> checkout-back -> mTLS /internal/checkout/* -> core-back -> PostgreSQL / external gateway Merchant: browser -> merchant-front -> public nginx -> merchant-back -> mTLS /internal/merchant/* -> core-back Admin: browser -> LAN nginx :8443 -> admin-back -> mTLS /internal/admin/* -> core-back Webhook: gateway -> checkout-back /api/v1/inbound/:gateway/:env/:pathToken -> raw bytes over mTLS -> core-back -> inbound_events + callback verifier + engine Backup: admin-front -> admin-back -> /internal/admin/system/backups/* -> mTLS backup daemon -> WAL-G/Barman -> S3/secondary vault ``` ## 7. Status and deviations ### Implemented - The seven production services, their listeners and their channel bindings exist in code. - The core has database exclusivity and the three client-certificate guards. - Edge pools implement least-in-flight selection, round-robin tie-break, cooldowns and idempotent retry. - The storage engine, replicas, Redis, audit/log databases and backup client are composed at core startup. - The deploy engine defines horizontal node arrays, host plans, PKI SANs, firewall rules and a 14-step pipeline. - The optional Fake Rails backend and portal exist and are independently configured. ### Partial - **Multi-host verification.** The topology code and unit tests exist, but no production-shaped deployment, replica failover, rolling batch or backup restore is recorded in this repository state. - **Storage mTLS.** Deploy generates storage certificates; PostgreSQL and Redis configuration do not consume them, so the storage-plane certificate chain is not an enforced channel today. - **Backup daemon mTLS.** Core reads `BACKUP_DAEMON_CA_CERT_PATH`, `BACKUP_DAEMON_CLIENT_CERT_PATH` and `BACKUP_DAEMON_CLIENT_KEY_PATH`; the daemon reads `BACKUP_DAEMON_CERT_PATH`, `BACKUP_DAEMON_KEY_PATH` and `BACKUP_DAEMON_CA_CERT_PATH`. The provisioner mapping is not aligned in the current tree, so a staging verification is required. - **Core node identity.** All core nodes share the same server certificate role; there is no node-specific identity or leader election inside core. Workers rely on database `SKIP LOCKED` claims and conditional updates. ### Missing / deferred - No service mesh, sidecar, centralized proxy or runtime service discovery. Purpose and scope This part records the actual security controls of the platform: the TLS and mutual-TLS configuration, channel-bound certificate identity, bearer authentication and authority checks, MFA and revocation behavior, maker-checker enforcement, secret storage and redaction, SSRF protections, webhook verification, edge LAN controls and the deployment PKI. It describes what the code enforces, not what the historical designs aspired to. Where the historical documents claim a control that is only partially wired, the limitation is stated explicitly. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The historical design is a zero-trust seven-service architecture: - `core-back` is the only service with database and KMS access and the only service that executes outbound money-moving calls. - The three edge backends are untrusted from core's point of view. They authenticate to core with distinct client certificates whose common names are bound to namespaces: `admin-back`, `merchant-back`, `checkout-back`. - Core independently re-validates every payload, token, user/merchant state, authority, amount, link state and maker-checker invariant. Compromising an edge must not be enough to move money or elevate authority. - Fifteen engineering safeguards are specified: prototype-pollution-safe `recursiveSet`, promise-cached consumers, single-flight token refresh, jittered refresh timers, atomic rotated-refresh persistence, per-step timeouts, strict money-step retry boundaries, raw-text-first parsing, multi-layer secret redaction, SSRF/DNS-rebinding protection, host-pinned credentials, distributed invalidation, destination-correct encoding, final-URL re-validation, and edge-to-core double validation. - Maker-checker is enforced at the database constraint/trigger, the approval service and the HTTP middleware. A checker must differ from the maker; system automation can never check. - Browser callbacks and return URLs are untrusted hints. Webhooks are verified with constant-time signatures across active secret versions, source IP allowlists and replay windows. - Secrets are write-only to clients, encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM, bound to a key id, redacted from logs, and never exported in configuration. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 TLS 1.3 server and client `core-back/createHttpsServer()` reads the server key, server certificate and internal CA from `MTLS_SERVER_KEY_PATH`, `MTLS_SERVER_CERT_PATH` and `MTLS_CA_CERT_PATH`. A missing file aborts startup with a message instructing the operator to run `bun run generate-mtls-certs`. The server is created with Node's `tls.createServer`: ```ts tls.createServer({ key: readSecretFile("mTLS server key", env.MTLS_SERVER_KEY_PATH), cert: readSecretFile("mTLS server certificate", env.MTLS_SERVER_CERT_PATH), ca: [readSecretFile("internal CA certificate", env.MTLS_CA_CERT_PATH)], requestCert: true, rejectUnauthorized: true, minVersion: "TLSv1.3", }); ``` A plain `http.Server` is created around the Express app, and every `secureConnection` socket is fed into it. TLS handshake errors are logged without certificate material. `x-powered-by` is disabled. The edge backends use `https.Agent` with: - `cert`, `key` and `ca` read from their client certificate paths. - `minVersion: "TLSv1.3"` and `maxVersion: "TLSv1.3"`. - `rejectUnauthorized: true`. - keep-alive with 30-second keep-alive and 64 maximum sockets. - the request timeout from `CORE_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`. The edge sets SNI `servername` only when the core URL host is not an IP literal. A core server certificate must therefore contain the DNS/IP identity used by `CORE_BACK_URLS`. ### 3.2 Channel-bound common-name guard `requireEdgeIdentity(expectedCn)` runs before every internal namespace router. It: 1. Reads `request.socket` as a `TLSSocket`. 2. Rejects with `401 MTLS_UNAUTHORIZED` if `socket.authorized` is false. 3. Reads the peer certificate subject CN; array CNs use the first entry. 4. Rejects with `401 MTLS_UNAUTHORIZED` if the CN cannot be inspected. 5. Rejects with `403 FORBIDDEN_SERVICE_IDENTITY` if the CN differs from the expected edge name. The bindings are exactly: ```text /internal/admin/* -> admin-back /internal/merchant/* -> merchant-back /internal/checkout/* -> checkout-back ``` There is no mapping from a certificate to a specific core node or tenant. One certificate per edge role is the trust unit. ### 3.3 Bearer authentication `authenticate()` resolves a bearer token in two modes: 1. **`pg_live_...` API token.** - SHA-256 hashes the token and looks up `AccessToken` by `tokenHash`. - Rejects an unknown token with `401 ACCESS_TOKEN_INVALID`. - Rejects a revoked token with `401 ACCESS_TOKEN_REVOKED`. - Reads scopes from `AccessToken.scopes`. - If `ipWhitelistEnabled`, resolves the client IP from `x-real-client-ip` first and checks it against `AccessTokenIp.cidr` entries; failure is `403 ACCESS_TOKEN_IP_NOT_ALLOWED`. - Updates `lastUsedAt`. - Returns a principal with `kind: "apiToken"`, `role: "MERCHANT_API"`, the token merchant/application, and the scopes as both authorities and scopes. 2. **Session JWT (anything else).** - Verifies the HS256 signature, issuer `payment-gateway-core` and audience `payment-gateway-edge`. - Rejects an invalid or expired token with `401 SESSION_INVALID`. - Loads the user and rejects a missing user with `401 SESSION_USER_MISSING`. - Rejects a non-`ACTIVE` user with `403 SESSION_USER_INACTIVE`. - Reads `authoritiesMap` from the database, not from the JWT; empty authorities are rejected with `403 SESSION_AUTHORITIES_EMPTY`. - Returns `kind: "session"`, user id, role, merchant id, authorities and `sessionId` equal to the JWT subject. The session key and MFA-challenge key are derived with HKDF-SHA256 from `KMS_MASTER_KEY` using the purposes `session-signing` and `mfa-challenge`. Session lifetime is 12 hours; MFA challenge lifetime is 10 minutes. The JWT includes a `mfa` boolean claim and an `appScopeIds` array. ### 3.4 Actual MFA, revocation and IP behavior | Control | Admin | Merchant | API token | Notes | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Password login | Yes | Yes | N/A | bcrypt cost 12 | | MFA challenge issued when `user.mfaRequired` | Yes | Yes | N/A | 6-digit code, HMAC stored in challenge token, notification row queued | | MFA enforced on every request | No | No | N/A | `resolveSessionPrincipal` does not inspect `claims.mfa` | | Session revocation | No per-session revocation | No per-session revocation | Yes, `revokedAt` | Disabling a user blocks the next request because the user is re-read; changing a password does not invalidate existing JWTs | | IP allowlist | Edge LAN CIDR only | API token CIDR only | Yes | Core does not enforce an admin IP list | | Authority source | DB `authoritiesMap` | DB `authoritiesMap` | Token scopes | Session JWT authorities are not trusted for authorization decisions | | Google OIDC | N/A | 501 | N/A | Merchant `/auth/google` is a stub | The `pg_live_` token IP check trusts `x-real-client-ip` without checking that the immediate peer is a trusted proxy. That is acceptable only because core is expected to be reachable solely through the mTLS edge and a private network; a direct core access path would make the header spoofable. The admin edge also enforces `ADMIN_LAN_CIDRS` through `enforceLanAccess`, resolving the client IP through `TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`. That is an edge control; core itself has no admin IP guard. ### 3.5 Authority enforcement Most admin internal routes call `requireAuthorities(request, [...])` per handler. The semantics are OR: any one of the listed authorities (or `*`) satisfies the requirement. The authority list is read from the database-backed principal. Examples: - `security:read` for users/audit/backups overview. - `merchant:read` / `merchant:write` for merchant surfaces. - `kyb:read` / `kyb:write`, `compliance:read` / `compliance:write`. - `approval:read` and `approval:check` / `approval:write`. - `gateway:read` / `gateway:write`, `gateway:test`. - `settings:read` / `settings:write`, `finance:read` / `finance:write`, `cashout:read` / `cashout:review`. - `case:read` / `case:write`, `operator:read` / `operator:write`. Not every authenticated admin route has a specific authority. `GET /stats/overview`, `POST /stats/export-audit`, `GET /options/:kind` and the current-user academy progress routes require only a valid admin session. See `01-core-back/01-api-surface.md`. The admin edge's `requireAuthorities` parses unverified JWT claims only to hide/deny screens early. It normalizes a small role-to-authority alias map for `COMPLIANCE`/`MLRO`. Core is the authority. Merchant internal routes do not call `requireAuthorities`. They authenticate, require a `merchantId` binding, and use `merchantIdOf(request)` to scope queries. API-token scopes are stored but not checked per endpoint. `requireMerchantScope` is exported from the merchant router but has no production caller. This is a material authorization gap relative to the design. Checkout internal routes are intentionally unauthenticated: the long link key and attempt id are capabilities, and the payer must not need an account. The checkout edge validates the shape and forbids monetary fields; core re-validates and resolves the amount from `payment_links.amount`. ### 3.6 Maker-checker enforcement There are three enforcement layers: 1. **Database:** `approval_requests_checker_not_maker_insert` is a `CHECK` constraint, and `approval_requests_checker_not_maker_update` is a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger. Both are in the PostgreSQL baseline migration. 2. **Middleware:** `actorFromRequest` requires a human user id, rejects `SYSTEM_AUTOMATION` as an actor, and computes `isChecker` from `approval:check`. `assertCheckerIsNotMaker` rejects equal or missing maker/checker ids. `assertCheckerAuthority` requires the checker authority. 3. **Execution:** `executeApprovalSubject` re-checks that the checker is not the system automation principal, that a checker exists and that maker != checker before dispatching to a subject-specific handler. The approval endpoint additionally applies domain checks: - An admin-assisted join request prepared by the same operator cannot be checked by that operator. - Merchant approvals restrict the checker role by payload domain via `merchantApprovalCheckerAllowed`. - Backup policy approvals require the daemon to be configured and are executed out of band by the backup route. The executable subject coverage is uneven. `executeApprovalSubject` handles `AML_CASE`, `OPERATOR_CASE`, `ADJUSTMENT`, `REGULATORY_REPORT`, `REPORTING_RULE`, `AML_RULE`, `JOIN_REQUEST`, `MERCHANT`, `COMMISSION_PROFILE`, `VELOCITY_RULE`, `USER` and `GATEWAY_VERSION`. Any other subject type throws `409 NO_EXECUTABLE_SUBJECT`. `BACKUP_POLICY` is handled specially in the approve route. `APPLICATION` approvals are created by the merchant route but have no handler, so they remain `PENDING_REVIEW` and cannot be executed. Cash-out processing and some settings/commission/velocity writes execute under a single authority-holding actor rather than through the approval queue; see `01-core-back/01-api-surface.md` for the exact list. ### 3.7 Secrets and cryptographic material - The vault encrypts with AES-256-GCM, a random 12-byte IV and the key id as additional authenticated data. The payload is `keyId:iv:authTag:ciphertext` in base64 segments. - The master key resolution supports `KMS_MASTER_KEY` as a 32-byte value, a base64 32-byte value, a `keyId:base64key` value, or a JSON key map. `KMS_KEYS_JSON` can hold multiple direct 32-byte keys. - A non-32-byte master secret is SHA-256 hashed once; per-key material is derived with HKDF-SHA256 using the key id and the context `payment-gateway:vault:aes-256-gcm:v1`. - Redaction covers exact sensitive names (`password`, `secret`, `token`, `otp`, `cvv`, `pan`, `authorization`, `apikey`, `webhooksecret`, `clientsecret`, `privatekey`), a broad sensitive-name pattern, literal decrypted secrets (longest first), and Luhn-valid 12-19 digit sequences. - Credential sets store encrypted entries in `entriesCiphertext`; the API never returns a secret, only write/replace/verify operations. - KMS material is core-only. Edge services receive only their client certificate, key and CA. Deploy writes database and KMS values only to the core host. `CryptoEngine` implements the signing side of the declarative crypto profiles: HMAC-SHA256/512, RSA-SHA256 and SHA-256, with UTF8/HEX/BASE64 key decoding and HEX_LOWER/HEX_UPPER/BASE64 output. Canonicalization modes include `MOAMALAT_SECURE_HASH`, `DPAY_WEBHOOK_VERIFY`, `PLUTU_CALLBACK_HASH`, `MYPAY_RAW_BODY`, `SORTED_KEY_VALUE_AMP`, `TIMESTAMP_DOT_RAW_BODY`, `SORTED_VALUES_HASH`, `TEMPLATE_STRING`, `JSON_CANONICAL` and `RAW_BODY`. Signature comparison is constant-time via SHA-256 hashing plus `timingSafeEqual`. ### 3.8 SSRF and outbound hardening Outbound gateway calls run through `StepExecutor` and/or `ApiConsumer`. Both enforce: - **HTTPS only**, except for the explicitly scoped Fake Rails host. - **Host allowlist:** the final URL host must appear in the gateway version's `allowed_hosts` when the list is non-empty. - **No userinfo, no fragments, no backslashes, no encoded path separators, no `.`/`..` traversal.** - **No control characters** in URLs, headers, query keys/values. - **No redirects:** fetch uses `redirect: "manual"` and a 3xx response becomes `GATEWAY_REDIRECT_BLOCKED`. - **DNS resolution guard:** for a hostname, every resolved address must be public. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The historical design requires: - A private-LAN `core-back` process that reads its database and KMS configuration only from its own env. - Edge processes with no database or KMS variables; their only upstream configuration is the core URL pool and their mTLS material. - PostgreSQL 18 through `@prisma/adapter-pg` and `pg`; no MySQL/MariaDB runtime path. - A unified storage engine with `UnitOfWork`, `ReadStore`, cache/velocity, audit and log ports. - Durable workers that start with core and claim work with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. - A queue-drainability guard: queue-only routes must not accept work when no worker can drain it. - Redis Pub/Sub invalidation across core nodes when Redis is available, with a local fallback. - Request IDs propagated from edge to core and returned in responses. - Dedicated audit and log databases; logging must never block or fail a payment. - Build-time UI flags injected by the deploy engine and runtime-config values written into the deployed release. ## 3.
