Purpose and scope This part owns the stateless background loops that drain durable work in `core-back`: attempt expiry and polling, inbound inbox processing, notification delivery, ledger invariant checks, onboarding expiry, periodic screening, KYB lifecycle, record retention, the durable background-job queue, the transactional outbox relay, and the audit shipper. It also documents the production worker composition and the startup/health contract. It does not own the business logic that a worker invokes. The workers call the engine, repositories, screening service, notification transport, and ledger. The ledger and governance invariants are documented in their own parts. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The design requires stateless worker processes that use PostgreSQL as the durable timer and queue: - `payment_attempts.expires_at` and `next_check_at` are polled by stateless workers using `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`; an expiring attempt is asked (`inquire`) before it expires when the route supports inquiry. - `inbound_events` is drained by an inbox worker so webhook processing is inbox-first and deduplicated; `notifications` is a transactional outbox drained by a sender. - Terminal transitions are applied at most once with a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE terminal_at IS NULL`, and the double-entry invariant is checked continuously. - Statement reconciliation and dispute/adjustment execution use a durable queue with leases, backoff, and crash recovery. - The retention worker removes evidence after the configured period without moving a balance; the transactional outbox maintains read models, and the audit outbox ships audit rows to a dedicated audit database with a hash chain. The design also presents realtime fan-out as event-driven. The as-built behavior differs in several places: inbound handling is synchronous on the request path, checkout/POS SSE streams poll the database, and the ledger outbox does not project a read model. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 Worker base `BaseWorker` (`core-back/engine/workers/workerRuntime.ts:40`) provides: - a `start`/`stop` lifecycle with a single in-process timer chain; - `setTimeout` scheduling with ±10% jitter (`jitter`), not `setInterval`; - `unref()` on the timer so the timer does not keep the process alive; - one `tick` at a time in a process: the next tick is scheduled only after the current tick resolves; - error isolation: a failed tick is logged and the loop continues; - `runOnce()` for tests and manual ticks. The loop is not a distributed lock by itself. Cross-node safety comes from `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` claims plus conditional updates (or from leases for background jobs). ### 3.2 Production composition `createProductionWorkerRuntime` (`core-back/engine/workers/productionRuntime.ts:207`) builds the workers and connects their ports: - inquiry port -> `platform.engine.inquire`, so an expired or due attempt is asked before a terminal decision; - inbound handler -> `platform.engine.verifyCallback`; - notification sender -> `NotificationTransport` (webhook when `NOTIFICATION_WEBHOOK_URL` is set, otherwise the log transport); - storage engine -> outbox relay and, only for a dedicated audit store, the audit shipper; - background-job handlers -> reconciliation and adjustment/dispute execution. `core-back/index.ts:259` starts the runtime when `WORKER_ENABLED` is true. `assertBackgroundJobQueueDrainable` refuses to boot if workers or background jobs are disabled, because statement upload and dispute intake answer `202` and would otherwise strand work (`productionRuntime.ts:121`). `WORKER_ENABLED` and `WORKER_BACKGROUND_JOBS_ENABLED` therefore default to true and cannot be safely disabled in the current API configuration. ### 3.3 Worker inventory | Worker | Trigger and default cadence | Claim / concurrency | Behavior | Status | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `ExpirySweeperWorker` | `expires_at <= now`, every `WORKER_POLL_INTERVAL_MS` (5 s) | `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, batch `WORKER_BATCH_SIZE` (50) | Inquires inquiry-capable routes first; It refreshes route inquiry support once per tick. For each attempt: - if the route supports inquiry and an inquiry port exists, it calls `inquire`; a definitive terminal outcome (`SUCCEEDED`, `FAILED`, `EXPIRED`, `CANCELLED`) is applied with a conditional update; non-terminal outcomes update status/substatus and continue; - an inquiry error moves the attempt to `UNKNOWN` with `nextCheckAt = now + 60 s`; - otherwise it transitions to `EXPIRED` with a conditional `WHERE terminal_at IS NULL`, releases the link slot, and writes an audit row. The production inquiry port calls `DynamicRailEngine.inquire`, which performs the VERIFY phase and posts the confirmation ledger when the inquiry returns a trusted success. The sweeper itself does not post a ledger entry. ### 3.5 Poll worker `PollWorker` (`core-back/engine/workers/PollWorker.ts`) selects attempts with `next_check_at <= now` in the pollable statuses, including `UNKNOWN`. It first reconciles persisted inquiry schedules (`reconcileGatewayInquiries`). For each attempt: - a route `stopOnStates` match clears `nextCheckAt` and completes the active schedule; - a manual inquiry schedule owns its own window start; otherwise the attempt creation time is the reference; - `computeBackoffDelaySeconds` returns the next step or `null` when the 900 s default window elapses; an elapsed window expires the schedule and clears `nextCheckAt`; - the query calls `Platform.engine.inquire`; terminal states are applied with a conditional update; non-terminal states are stored with a new `nextCheckAt`; - `FAILED` and `CANCELLED` release the link slot; `EXPIRED` and `BLOCKED` do not. The schedule metadata (`GatewayInquirySchedule`) records source, status, window start, next run, attempts, last result/error, and completion/cancellation. The poll worker marks a schedule `RUNNING` before the inquiry and updates it to `COMPLETED`, `RETRYING`, `EXPIRED`, or leaves it for reconciliation. ### 3.6 Inbound inbox `InboundInboxWorker` (`core-back/engine/workers/InboundInboxWorker.ts`) is a complete inbox drainer: it selects unprocessed events, calls the handler, marks processed/skipped/failed, retries only `RetryableInboundError`, and opens an `UNKNOWN` operator case on a terminal failure. It also exposes `persistInboundEvent` with a dedupe lookup and raw insert. The actual checkout inbound route does **not** use the worker. `POST /internal/checkout/inbound/:gateway/:env/:pathToken` (`core-back/api/internal/checkout.ts:1477`) validates the channel, gateway, environment, and dedupe key, inserts the `inbound_events` row, correlates the attempt, calls `engine.verifyCallback` synchronously, and marks the event processed in the same request before returning the configured acknowledgement. The worker's handler is wired, but no producer enqueues unprocessed rows for it. This is the main design deviation for this part. The synchronous route stores the raw body and a redacted header subset, not the full header set. It marks `verificationError = VERIFICATION_PENDING` initially and records the final verification result. The separate `persistInboundEvent` helper is not called by the route. ### 3.7 Notification outbox `OutboxNotificationWorker` (`core-back/engine/workers/OutboxNotificationWorker.ts`) drains the `notifications` table, not `outbox_events`. For each queued row it: 1. finds the template by code/channel/language; 2. records a delivery failure when the template is missing; 3. calls `assertNoTippingOff` and records a delivery failure when a non-`INTERNAL` template references AML variables; 4. redacts AML-like payload keys for non-`INTERNAL` classes; 5. renders subject/body; 6. calls the sender; 7. writes `SENT` or `DELIVERED`, or re-queues with exponential backoff up to 8 attempts. The production sender uses the webhook transport when `NOTIFICATION_WEBHOOK_URL` is configured and the log transport otherwise. The log transport reports `SENT`, never `DELIVERED`; `IN_APP` notifications are delivered by the notification row itself. The rendered body of an `INTERNAL` template is never written to the log. ### 3.8 Ledger invariant worker `LedgerInvariantWorker` runs `InvariantVerifier` every 60 seconds. On non-zero drift it logs the left/right sides, calls the optional `onDrift`, and opens a single open `MISMATCH`/`P1` case with a four-hour SLA. It does not halt payouts itself; the operator case and the admin invariant panel are the control surface. ### 3.9 Onboarding expiry `JoinRequestExpiryWorker` expires abandoned `DRAFT` rows older than 30 days and expires overdue reviews in `SUBMITTED`, `IN_REVIEW`, or `INFO_REQUESTED` whose `sla_due_at` has passed, explicitly excluding `PENDING_CHECKER`. It uses direct SQL updates and does not write an audit row or queue a notification. The batch is limited for overdue reviews, but the draft expiry is a single update. ### 3.10 Periodic screening and KYB `PeriodicScreeningWorker` (`core-back/engine/workers/PeriodicScreeningWorker.ts`) selects active merchants whose latest merchant screening is older than the rescreen interval using `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, re-checks the due condition under the merchant row lock, screens the merchant and active owners with trigger `PERIODIC`, applies owner statuses, and handles only a `CONFIRMED_MATCH`: it raises one case (prefix `SCREENING_CONFIRMED_MATCH`) and suspends an active merchant with `AML_CONFIRMED_MATCH`. A potential match does not suspend or open a case here; it remains for the screening queue. `KybExpiryWorker` (`core-back/engine/workers/KybExpiryWorker.ts`) performs five bounded passes: 1. mark accepted/uploaded documents whose `expires_on` passed as `EXPIRED`; 2. queue 30-day and 7-day `KYB_DOC_EXPIRING` notices using unique event keys; 3. suspend an active merchant whose required document is past the grace period with no replacement, setting `KYB_EXPIRED` and queuing `KYB_EXPIRED_SUSPENSION`; 4. start periodic revalidation requests for due merchants and advance `nextKybReviewAt`; 5. expire overdue revalidation requests. ### 3.11 Retention `RetentionWorker` (`core-back/engine/workers/RetentionWorker.ts`) is disabled by default (`WORKER_RETENTION_ENABLED=false`) because it removes evidence. It resolves the period from an explicit option, then platform setting `OD-4`, then a five-year default. It supports a dry run. It purges, in dependency order and bounded transactions: - `notifications` older than the cutoff; - `inbound_events` received before the cutoff; - `attempt_step_logs` older than the cutoff and belonging to an attempt older than the cutoff; - `audit_log` and `detail_change_logs` older than the cutoff; - terminal attempts older than the cutoff whose journal entry is retained, together with their adjustments, disputes, operator cases, inbound events, step logs, and free attempt groups. It deliberately never purges `journal_entries` or `journal_lines`, because deleting a line without folding it into a checkpoint would silently change a merchant balance while the system-wide invariant still balanced. AML cases, screenings, KYB documents, KYB revalidations, regulatory reports, platform settings, background jobs, `outbox_events`, and `audit_outbox` are not in the retention scope. ### 3.12 Background job queue `BackgroundJobWorker` (`core-back/engine/workers/BackgroundJobWorker.ts`) is the durable queue for statement reconciliation and dispute/adjustment execution: - `claimDueJobs` selects `QUEUED` jobs whose `available_at <= now`, marks them `RUNNING` and sets `locked_at` inside one transaction; the row locks are held until the mark commits; - `recoverExpiredLeases` re-queues `RUNNING` rows whose `locked_at` is older than the lease (default 300 s); - a missing handler or thrown error increments attempts and re-queues with exponential backoff (30 s base, 30 min cap) until `maxAttempts` (default 5), then marks `FAILED`; - success marks `SUCCEEDED`, `completed_at`, clears `locked_at`, and logs the job id/type/reference. Handlers (`core-back/engine/workers/BackgroundJobHandlers.ts`): - `RECONCILIATION_RUN` parses the uploaded statement, matches items, posts settlement sweeps for batch sources, and posts fee variance true-ups. - `ADJUSTMENT_EXECUTION` handles `kind: DISPUTE_INTAKE` through `openDisputeWithDraftedAdjustment`, and `kind: ADJUSTMENT_EXECUTION` through `executeApprovalSubject` using the approval id and recorded checker. The job payload never carries an independent checker; the executed adjustment uses the checker recorded on the approval request. ### 3.13 Outbox relay and audit shipper `OutboxRelayWorker` (`core-back/lib/storageEngine/outboxWorkers.ts:134`) claims unprocessed `outbox_events` with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and marks `processed_at` after the handler. Default handlers: | Topic | Handler | | :--- | :--- | | `attempt.transitioned` | Projects `rm_merchant_daily_stats` and `rm_route_daily_volumes` using the event kind (`created` vs terminal), status, merchant, route, currency, gross, and net. | | `ledger.entry_posted` | No-op. No ledger-driven read model is projected. | | `merchant.updated` | No-op. | | `kyb.document_uploaded` | No-op. | | `reconciliation.completed` | No-op. | | `config.invalidated` | No-op. | The relay is instantiated only when a storage engine is supplied. Outbox rows are marked processed, never deleted; there is no outbox retention job. `AuditShipperWorker` is instantiated only when `options.storage.auditStore` is a `DedicatedAuditDatabaseDriver`. It claims unshipped `audit_outbox` rows, appends them to the dedicated audit database's SHA-256 hash chain, and marks `shipped_at`. It is idempotent on the source id. Shipped rows are retained, not deleted. `writeAudit` only writes `audit_outbox` when `AUDIT_DATABASE_URL` is configured; otherwise `audit_log` is the only sink. ### 3.14 Realtime fan-out reality The engine publishes attempt transition events on the invalidation bus, and the AML resolution path also publishes. The checkout status SSE (`core-back/api/internal/checkout.ts:1292`) and merchant POS SSE (`core-back/api/internal/merchant.ts:2392`) do **not** subscribe to that bus. They poll `payment_attempts` every 2 seconds (checkout, 10-minute deadline) or every 3 seconds (POS, 15-minute deadline) and write `event: status` / `event: attempts` frames. This is polling SSE, not a transition subscription. ### 3.15 Startup and health `GET /health` (`core-back/index.ts:76`) reports `OK`/`DEGRADED` and a `queue` object with: - whether workers and background jobs are enabled; - queued job count; - oldest queued job age; - threshold (`WORKER_BACKGROUND_JOBS_MAX_QUEUE_AGE_MS`, default 300 s); - degraded flag. It degrades when workers are disabled, the queue cannot be read, or the oldest queued job exceeds the threshold. It does not report per-worker liveness, tick age, notification backlog, inbound backlog, outbox lag, or audit-chain status. `readBackgroundJobQueueHealth` only reads `background_jobs`. ## 4. Contracts and invariants 1. A worker tick must not overlap with itself in the same process. Multiple nodes are allowed; claims use `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. 2. Terminal attempt transitions are conditional on `terminal_at IS NULL`, so the same attempt is not expired, failed, or cancelled twice. 3. An `AML_HOLD` attempt is excluded from expiry sweeping, and the sweeper has a defense-in-depth check on `substatus`. 4. An expiring inquiry-capable attempt is asked before it is expired. An inquiry failure keeps it open (`UNKNOWN`/deferred) rather than silently expiring it. 5. A background job is executed at most once per claim, but handlers must be idempotent because a lease can expire and re-queue a job after a crash. 6. A notification delivery failure re-queues with backoff up to the attempt cap; a missing or tipping-off template is retried up to that cap and then marked `FAILED`. 7. The invariant worker opens at most one open `MISMATCH`/`P1` case for drift. 8. Retention never deletes ledger entries or lines and never deletes a terminal attempt whose ledger entry is missing; it stops rather than risk orphaning evidence. 9. Statement upload and dispute intake are queue-only; the service refuses to start if no background-job drain is enabled. 10. The notification worker never sends an AML variable to a non-`INTERNAL` template. 11. Outbox processing marks `processed_at`; the audit shipper marks `shipped_at`. Neither deletes rows. 12. SSE stream contract: checkout status ends on a terminal status or a 10-minute deadline; POS stream ends on a 15-minute deadline; both poll the database. ## 5. There is no worker-control or per-worker metrics endpoint. ## 6. Operational usage ### Starting and stopping `core-back` is a single process that starts the HTTP(S) server and the worker runtime. `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` stops the workers, clears storage/log sinks, closes Redis, shuts down the storage engine, and closes the server. There is no separate worker-only entrypoint in this repository. ### Observing 1. Check `GET /health` for queue depth, oldest queued age, and degraded state; for a stuck queue inspect `background_jobs` by `state`, `available_at`, `locked_at`, `attempts`, and `last_error`. 2. For expiry/poll issues inspect `payment_attempts.expires_at`, `next_check_at`, `terminal_at`, `substatus`, and `gateway_inquiry_schedules`; for notifications inspect `notifications.status`, `attempts`, `next_attempt_at`, and the template class. 3. For outbox/read-model lag inspect `outbox_events.processed_at`, `audit_outbox.shipped_at`, and the `rm_*` tables; for retention run with `RETENTION_DRY_RUN=true` first. ### Tuning - Increase `WORKER_BATCH_SIZE` for throughput; the base worker still runs one tick at a time per process. - Increase `WORKER_BACKGROUND_JOBS_BATCH_SIZE` carefully because each job may parse a statement or execute a refund, and increase the lease only when a legitimate handler can exceed it. - Keep `WORKER_BACKGROUND_JOBS_MAX_QUEUE_AGE_MS` below the operational SLA; do not rely on `WORKER_CONCURRENCY`, which has no runtime effect. ### Adding a worker 1. Extend `BaseWorker`, implement `tick`, and use a claim query with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` or a conditional update; make every state change idempotent. 2. Add the worker to `createProductionWorkerRuntime`; gate evidence-destroying work behind an explicit env flag and a dry run. 3. Add a fake-DB test and a live PostgreSQL test where locking matters, and document its health/backlog surface. ## 7. Status and deviations ### Implemented - Expiry sweeper with inquiry-first behavior, AML-hold exclusion, and conditional terminal updates; poll worker with route backoff, inquiry schedules, and terminal handling. - Notification outbox with template lookup, tipping-off guard, redaction, rendering, backoff, and delivery states; ledger invariant worker and P1 operator case. - Periodic screening (L2), KYB lifecycle, durable background-job queue with claim/lease/retry/handlers, outbox relay for attempt transitions, and audit shipper for a dedicated audit database. - Startup guard for queue-only routes and queue health payload. ### Partial - **Inbound inbox** — the worker is implemented and wired, but the checkout route processes synchronously and marks the event processed; the worker has no producer. The inbox-first asynchronous design is not in force. - **Retention** — opt-in, dry-run capable, bounded, and ledger-safe, but the scope excludes AML/KYB/reporting evidence and the default is off. - **Join-request expiry** — expires drafts/reviews but writes no audit row and sends no merchant notification. - **Outbox relay / audit shipper** — only `attempt.transitioned` has a projection (`ledger.entry_posted` and four other topics are no-ops); the audit shipper only runs with a dedicated audit DB and never deletes shipped rows. - **Realtime fan-out** — transition events are published, but checkout/POS clients receive polling SSE, not subscriptions. ### Missing / deferred - Asynchronous webhook inbox processing on the request path. - Transition-bus-backed SSE/WebSocket fan-out. - Outbox and audit-outbox retention. - Per-worker health, tick latency, backlog, and last-success metrics; separate worker deployment/entrypoint and real `WORKER_CONCURRENCY`. - AML/KYB/report retention passes and batch/deferred AML monitoring worker. ### Known bugs / risks - **Code gap:** `PollWorker` releases a link slot for `FAILED` and `CANCELLED` but not for `EXPIRED` or `BLOCKED`, unlike the expiry sweeper's terminal release path. A poll-discovered expiry can leave a slot reserved. - **Code gap:** the synchronous inbound route marks the event processed even when verification fails; the event is not retried by the inbox worker. Verification failure is recorded but there is no asynchronous replay. - **Code gap:** `InboundInboxWorker` retries `RetryableInboundError` on the next tick with no delay, so a persistent retryable failure can burn its attempt cap quickly. - **Code gap:** merchant fallback balance reads can double count a checkpoint; this is documented in `core.ledger` but affects worker-written ledger balances too. - **Risk:** retention and audit shipping are independent: retention purges `audit_log` and `detail_change_logs` on its own schedule without consulting `audit_outbox.shipped_at`, and the outbox rows are never purged. - **Risk:** `OutboxRelayWorker` marks an unknown topic processed without a handler, so a newly added event type can be silently dropped until a handler is deployed. - **Documentation gap:** the design describes an event-driven realtime and inbox-first system; the as-built system is synchronous on inbound and polling on SSE. ## 8. Purpose and scope The storage engine is the boundary between domain code and PostgreSQL 18, Redis, the dedicated audit database and the dedicated log database. It owns: - the `StorageEngine` composition object and its ports; - the transactional unit of work that couples domain writes, `outbox_events` and `audit_outbox`; - the post-commit WAL flush watermark used by LSN-aware reads; - primary/replica read routing and replica health tracking; - Redis cache and sliding-window velocity counters, with an in-memory fallback; - the dedicated audit hash-chain append adapter and audit query adapter; - the buffered operational step/access log sink; - GL account shard arithmetic and shard-aware ledger writes; - the transactional outbox relay and audit shipper workers; - the read-model projection for `rm_merchant_daily_stats` and `rm_route_daily_volumes`; - the mTLS backup-control client used by `core-back` to reach `pg-backup-daemon`; - the storage health snapshot API. It does not own the Prisma schema or migration workflow (`core.storage` is paired with `core.data`), the backup daemon implementation (`07-deploy`), the global-search provider catalogue (`core.search`), or domain ledger/attempt decisions. Dependent systems: `engine/**` through the platform runtime, `api/internal/{admin,merchant,checkout,backups}.ts`, the worker runtime, the global search route, and the storage-engine and backup-admin test suites. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The historical storage blueprint defines a thin, ACID write path for a high-volume switch: - A payment or ledger write touches the operational row, one `gl_account_shards` balance row, one `outbox_events` row and one `audit_outbox` row in a single transaction. - The unit of work reports a commit WAL position so a caller can ask for a replica that has replayed at least that position. - System GL accounts are split into 16 deterministic shards; merchant wallets use a single shard. Shard rows are locked in stable sorted order to avoid deadlocks. - Outbox events project read models asynchronously so dashboards do not aggregate the ledger on the write path. - Replica reads are selected by lag and LSN, with primary fallback. - Redis provides L2 cache and Lua-backed velocity windows; it is never authoritative for money. - Audit is shipped asynchronously to a dedicated append-only database with a SHA-256 hash chain and immutable rows. - Operational step/access logs go to a separate log database so logging cannot block a payment. - Backups are controlled through an mTLS daemon that wraps WAL-G or Barman. The blueprint's implementation claims must not be repeated as current behavior. The actual code differs in these material ways: - `ledger.entry_posted` is registered but its handler is a no-op; only `attempt.transitioned` projects read models. - The two read models are written but not read by dashboards or list endpoints. - `AuditShipperWorker` marks `audit_outbox.shipped_at`; it never deletes shipped rows. - Replica routing is used by global search and three merchant list endpoints, not by all dashboards, lists and exports. - Pagination is offset-based, not keyset-based. - Access logs record zero database query metrics. - There is no `gateway_wire_logs` table and no disk spool for the log sink. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 Composition root `core-back/lib/storageEngine/index.ts` builds one `StorageEngine`: - `createStorageEngine` resolves `DATABASE_URL`, `DATABASE_REPLICA_URLS`, `AUDIT_DATABASE_URL`, `LOG_DATABASE_URL` and Redis from the environment (`index.ts:56-71`). - It creates the primary Prisma client and one Prisma client per replica URL (`index.ts:72-80`). - It constructs `PostgresReplicaReadStore` and starts the LSN monitor (`index.ts:82-87`). - It constructs `PostgresUnitOfWorkAdapter` with an optional post-commit callback (`index.ts:89-92`). - It selects `RedisCacheAdapter` when a Redis URL exists, otherwise `MemoryCacheAdapter` (`index.ts:94-98`). - It creates `DedicatedAuditDatabaseDriver` from a dedicated `pg.Pool` and `DedicatedPostgresLogSink` from a separate `pg.Pool` (`index.ts:100-114`). - It exposes `uow`, `readStore`, `cache`, `auditStore`, `logSink`, `primary`, `health()` and `shutdown()` (`index.ts:116-209`). - It exports `readThroughReplica` and `readThroughReplicaOrPrimary` helpers (`index.ts:227-268`) and a process-wide singleton (`index.ts:214-225`). `core-back/index.ts` gets the singleton, installs it into the platform runtime, and installs the log sink into the request logger before listening (`index.ts:255-260`). Shutdown stops the LSN monitor, closes the log sink and cache, disconnects clients and ends both pools (`index.ts:198-207`, `core-back/index.ts:285-291`). ### 3.2 Ports and adapters `core-back/lib/storageEngine/ports.ts` defines the contracts: - `UnitOfWorkPort.run(fn, options)` returns `{ data, commitLsn, durationMs }`. - `StorageTx` exposes `db`, `outbox`, `audit` and `lockGlAccountShardsSorted`. - `ReadStorePort.execute(consistency, fn, options)` returns `{ data, servedBy, replicaLagMs? }`. - `CachePort` exposes `get`, `getOrLoad`, `set`, `del`, `incrWindowCounter`, optional `publishInvalidation` and `close`. - `AuditStorePort` exposes audit query, count, hash-chain verification and detail lookup. - `LogSinkPort` exposes step/access log writes, attempt step-log queries, `flush` and `close`. - `StorageEngine` aggregates the ports plus primary client, `health()` and `shutdown()`. The concrete adapters are `PostgresUnitOfWorkAdapter`, `PostgresReplicaReadStore`, `MemoryCacheAdapter`, `RedisCacheAdapter`, `DedicatedAuditDatabaseDriver`, `DedicatedPostgresLogSink` and `BackupControlClient`. ### 3.3 Unit of work, outbox and audit outbox `PostgresUnitOfWorkAdapter.run` opens a Prisma interaction transaction (`uowAdapter.ts:25-152`): 1. It sets a local statement timeout at least one second long and 250 ms below the transaction timeout (`uowAdapter.ts:26-30`). 2. It buffers outbox and audit envelopes in memory during the callback. 3. It deduplicates and sorts requested GL shard targets by account id and shard id, then selects them with `FOR UPDATE` in that order (`uowAdapter.ts:52-97`). 4. It runs the caller callback. 5. It inserts all buffered outbox events with `createMany` and all buffered audit rows with `createMany` inside the same transaction (`uowAdapter.ts:102-137`). 6. It reads `pg_current_wal_lsn()` inside the transaction (`uowAdapter.ts:139-142`). 7. After commit it calls the optional `onAfterCommit` wake-up, swallowing wake-up failures (`uowAdapter.ts:154-159`). 8. It reads `pg_current_wal_flush_lsn()` on the primary and replaces the in-transaction LSN when available (`uowAdapter.ts:161-172`). This is the post-commit flush LSN that makes an `atLeastLsn` replica read safe. The audit id is generated by `uuidv7()` inside `StorageTx.audit.record` and preserved by the shipper for idempotent append (`ports.ts:24-51`, `uowAdapter.ts:46-50`). ### 3.4 Outbox relay and audit shipper `OutboxRelayWorker` (`outboxWorkers.ts:134-248`) claims up to `batchSize` unprocessed rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, runs a handler, then updates `processed_at`. Registered handlers (`outboxWorkers.ts:149-157`): | Topic | Handler | | :--- | :--- | | `attempt.transitioned` | `projectAttemptTransition` updates both read models | | `ledger.entry_posted` | no-op | | `merchant.updated` | no-op | | `kyb.document_uploaded` | no-op | | `reconciliation.completed` | no-op | | `config.invalidated` | no-op | `projectAttemptTransition` validates the payload shape defensively and uses `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` for `rm_merchant_daily_stats` and `rm_route_daily_volumes` (`outboxWorkers.ts:68-132`). It treats rows without an `event` marker as `created`, preserving the historical "every attempt counted at creation" behavior (`outboxWorkers.ts:82-90`). `AuditShipperWorker` (`outboxWorkers.ts:268-385`) claims unshipped rows, appends them through `DedicatedAuditDatabaseDriver.appendBatch`, and then updates `shipped_at = now()` by id. The append is idempotent on the source id, so a crash between append and mark re-appends safely. There is no delete. ### 3.5 Replica read router `PostgresReplicaReadStore` keeps one handle per replica with `healthy`, `lastReplayLsn`, `lagMs` and `consecutiveFailures` (`readStoreAdapter.ts:6-13`). A 150 ms interval monitor reads `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()` and `now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp()` (`readStoreAdapter.ts:31-76`). A replica becomes unhealthy after two consecutive monitor failures. Selection is round-robin over healthy replicas: - `"primary"` bypasses replicas. - `"replica"` accepts a healthy replica whose `lagMs` is at or below `READ_REPLICA_MAX_LAG_MS`. - `{ atLeastLsn, maxWaitMs }` accepts a replica whose replay LSN is at least the requested watermark, polling and refreshing watermarks until the deadline (`readStoreAdapter.ts:78-120`). - If no replica qualifies, or the chosen replica throws, the query runs on the primary (`readStoreAdapter.ts:165-192`). A query failure marks the replica unhealthy. Current replica call sites are: - global search: `core-back/api/internal/admin.ts:687`; - merchant wallet list: `core-back/api/internal/merchant.ts:1323`; - merchant link list: `core-back/api/internal/merchant.ts:1661`; - merchant payment list: `core-back/api/internal/merchant.ts:1744`. No dashboard aggregate, export or other list uses the router. ### 3.6 Redis cache and velocity `MemoryCacheAdapter` is a process-local map with TTLs, single-flight `getOrLoad`, prefix deletion and sliding windows (`redisCacheAndVelocityAdapter.ts:42-141`). It is the fallback when Redis is unavailable or not configured. `RedisCacheAdapter` adds a local L1 cache, a JSON L2 cache with `EX` TTL, prefix deletion and a preloaded Lua velocity script (`redisCacheAndVelocityAdapter.ts:168-345`). The script: - removes entries older than the window; - adds the current amount/sequence member; - sums amounts from member prefixes; - returns count, amount, count-violation and amount-violation flags; - refreshes the key TTL. On any Redis error, `incrWindowCounter` falls back to the in-memory adapter (`redisCacheAndVelocityAdapter.ts:326-328`). `del` uses Redis `KEYS` followed by `DEL` (`redisCacheAndVelocityAdapter.ts:269-280`), which is a blocking scan on a large keyspace and is not production-safe at scale. `getOrLoad` exists but is not used by the core read paths; the main cache consumer is the attempt guard velocity store (`core-back/engine/guards/AttemptGuardPipeline.ts:1205-1216`). Redis invalidation is published through a separate invalidation bus, not `CachePort.publishInvalidation`. ### 3.7 Audit database adapter `DedicatedAuditDatabaseDriver` (`auditAndLogAdapters.ts:99-331`) appends with `pg` directly: - It opens a transaction and takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(tableName:hash-chain))` to serialize chain appends. -- It reads the last `row_hash`, starts from `"0" * 64`, skips ids already present, computes a SHA-256 hash over previous hash, id, timestamp, actor, action, entity type/id and stable before/after JSON, then inserts. +- It skips ids already present, inserts the audit fields without `prev_hash`/`row_hash`, and reads the values computed by the audit database BEFORE INSERT trigger (`pg_advisory_xact_lock(994001)` serializes all core nodes). - It queries with SQL filters, cursor and offset support, caps `limit` at 5,000 and orders by `created_at DESC, id DESC`. - It exposes `verifyHashChainIntegrity(limit?)`, recomputing each row and returning the first broken id. The audit table itself is provisioned by `deploy/provisioners/auditAndLogDbProvisioner.ts` with an append-only trigger that rejects `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `TRUNCATE`, plus least-privilege grants. ### 3.8 Operational log sink `DedicatedPostgresLogSink` (`auditAndLogAdapters.ts:333-524`) buffers step and access rows in memory: - The step buffer is bounded by `STORAGE_LOG_BUFFER_MAX`; when full it drops the oldest row (`auditAndLogAdapters.ts:368-371`). - It keeps the last 500 step logs per attempt for in-memory fallback and caps remembered attempts at 1,000 when no log DB is configured (`auditAndLogAdapters.ts:372-383`). - It flushes every `STORAGE_LOG_FLUSH_INTERVAL_MS`, when the step buffer reaches 250 rows, or on `close`. - Flush batches up to 500 rows per table and uses multi-row inserts; step logs use `ON CONFLICT (id, created_at) DO NOTHING`. - On a database error the step batch is put back if it still fits; the access batch is not explicitly requeued, so a failed flush can lose access-log rows. - With no log DB, step logs are remembered in memory and access logs are dropped. There is no disk spool. There is no `gateway_wire_logs` table. The request logger always supplies `dbQueries: 0` and `dbDurationMs: 0` (`core-back/lib/requestLogger/index.ts:185-203`). ### 3.9 Sharding and ledger writes `shardBalances.ts` defines 16 default shards, excludes `MERCHANT_WALLET`, uses FNV-1a over the attempt/reference id and computes `shardId = hash % count`; unsharded accounts use shard 0 (`shardBalances.ts:1-32`). `ledgerShardWriter.ts` upserts `gl_account_shards` with a signed delta (`credit` negative, `debit` positive) and can pre-create all shards for an account (`ledgerShardWriter.ts:8-51`). `createLedgerPoster` wires the shard writer and an optional `ledger.entry_posted` outbox writer (`ledgerPosterFactory.ts:17-40`). The hardening migration adds a `0 <= shard_id < 16` check. ### 3.10 Read models The CQRS migration creates `rm_merchant_daily_stats` and `rm_route_daily_volumes` with composite primary keys and a day index. Only `projectAttemptTransition` writes them. There is no `rm_merchant_dashboard_stats` and no `rm_wallet_statements` table. The read models are write-only in current application code. ### 3.11 Backup control client `BackupControlClient` (`backupControlClient.ts:145-308`) is an HTTP client for the daemon: - base URL from `BACKUP_DAEMON_URL`; - keep-alive agents, TLS 1.3 minimum for HTTPS, optional CA/client cert/key from the environment; - explicit JSON serialization, timeout handling, 502/504 error mapping and a typed `BackupDaemonNotConfiguredError`. It exposes `overview`, `health`, `triggerBackup`, `runDrill`, `updatePolicy`, `listRuns` and `listDrills`. The internal backup router uses it for overview, trigger, drill and policy. There are no automatic retries or circuit-breaker semantics. ### 3.12 Health `StorageEngine.health()` probes the primary with `SELECT 1`, each replica, cache set/get, audit pool and log pool with short timeouts (`index.ts:123-197`). It returns `StorageHealth` with primary latency, replica lag/watermarks, cache driver and audit/log configured flags. The public `GET /health` in `core-back/index.ts:76-115` does not call `StorageEngine.health()`. It reports only background-job queue health. The storage snapshot is currently consumed by tests (`core-back/test/storage-engine/engine-factory.test.ts`) rather than by an operational endpoint. ## 4. Contracts and invariants - Domain writes that use the UoW and both outbox writers commit the business row, `outbox_events` and `audit_outbox` atomically. A failure rolls back all three. - The reported `commitLsn` is the post-commit `pg_current_wal_flush_lsn()` when readable; callers can treat an `atLeastLsn` replica as having replayed the commit. - GL shard locks are taken in `(gl_account_id, shard_id)` order. Callers must pass all targets before making balance-dependent decisions. - Audit ids are UUIDv7 generated in the UoW; the audit chain is append-only and idempotent by id. -- The audit hash chain uses stable JSON key ordering. Any change to the hashed field list or canonicalization invalidates historical verification. +- The audit hash chain canonicalizes JSONB with PostgreSQL `before_json::text`/`after_json::text`; verification reads the same text form. Any change to the trigger field list or canonicalization invalidates historical verification. - Outbox handlers must be idempotent: a claimed batch is retried after a crash because `processed_at` is updated only after the handler completes. - The outbox relay processes rows in ascending id order and never deletes them. - Read consistency is one of `primary`, `replica` or `{ atLeastLsn, maxWaitMs? }`. A replica query failure falls back to the primary; callers must not assume a replica served the read. - Cache contents are not authoritative. A Redis failure must not fail a payment; velocity falls back to local memory. - The in-memory velocity fallback is per process and does not coordinate across core nodes. - The log sink is best-effort. It may drop the oldest step log when its buffer is full, may drop access logs on a failed flush and does not spool to disk. - `gl_account_shards.shard_id` is limited to `0..15`; the default shard count is 16 and `MERCHANT_WALLET` is always one shard. - Backup daemon calls are mTLS when the base URL is HTTPS; a missing client certificate is not silently replaced by an insecure channel. - `StorageEngine.shutdown()` must be called on process shutdown so monitors, buffers and pools are released. ## 5. Data / API / config / deployment surface ### Schema models `GlAccountShard`, `OutboxEvent`, `AuditOutbox`, `BackupCatalogRun`, `BackupRestoreDrill`, `RmMerchantDailyStat` and `RmRouteDailyVolume` are the storage-engine-native models. The journal, attempt and audit-log tables are defined by the broader schema (see `core.data`). ### Internal APIs - `GET /internal/admin/system/backups/overview` - `POST /internal/admin/system/backups/trigger` - `POST /internal/admin/system/backups/drill` - `PUT /internal/admin/system/backups/policy` - `GET /internal/admin/system/backups/catalog` - `POST /internal/admin/search` (delegates to the read store, see `core.search`) ### Environment | Key | Purpose | Default | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `DATABASE_URL` | Primary PostgreSQL 18 URL | required | | `DATABASE_REPLICA_URLS` | Comma-separated replica URLs | empty | | `READ_REPLICA_MAX_LAG_MS` | Maximum acceptable replica lag | `2000` | | `AUDIT_DATABASE_URL` | Dedicated audit DB URL | unset | | `LOG_DATABASE_URL` | Dedicated log DB URL | unset | | `REDIS_URL` / `REDIS_NODES` | Redis cache/velocity | unset / empty | | `STORAGE_QUERY_TIMEOUT_MS` | Default query timeout budget | `5000` | | `STORAGE_LOG_BUFFER_MAX` | Log buffer bound | `5000` | | `STORAGE_LOG_FLUSH_INTERVAL_MS` | Log flush interval | `250` | | `STORAGE_SHARD_COUNT` | GL shard count, max 16 | `16` | | `BACKUP_DAEMON_URL` | Daemon base URL | unset | | `BACKUP_DAEMON_CA_CERT_PATH` | Daemon CA | unset | | `BACKUP_DAEMON_CLIENT_CERT_PATH` | Daemon client cert | unset | | `BACKUP_DAEMON_CLIENT_KEY_PATH` | Daemon client key | unset | | `BACKUP_DAEMON_TIMEOUT_MS` | Daemon request timeout | `15000` | ### Deployment `deploy/lib/hostPlanner.ts` injects the core environment with the primary/replica/audit/log URLs and backup daemon client paths. Storage mTLS consumption by PostgreSQL and Redis is not implemented (see `07-deploy/05-storage-provisioners.md`). ## 6. Operational usage - Start `core-back` with the primary URL; replica URLs are optional. Replica routing degrades to primary when none is configured. - Watch `READ_REPLICA_MAX_LAG_MS` when adding lagging replicas; an oversized value makes stale reads more likely. - Run the outbox relay and audit shipper through `createProductionWorkerRuntime` when `WORKER_ENABLED` is true. Without the audit store the shipper is not registered. - Send writes through `UnitOfWorkPort`; do not write `outbox_events` or `audit_outbox` directly in new code. - Use `readThroughReplicaOrPrimary` with the `x-pg-min-lsn` request header for read-after-write consistency. The header is consumed by the search route and the three merchant list routes. - Inspect the storage snapshot through `getStorageEngine().health()` or the tests; do not assume `/health` includes storage checks. - Treat Redis as disposable. If Redis is down, velocity evaluation uses process-local memory and does not coordinate across nodes. - Monitor `audit_outbox` growth directly. The shipper marks rows shipped but does not remove them, so a retention job is required outside this code. - Use `scripts/run-benchmarks.sh` with a real PostgreSQL 18 test database and, optionally, Redis to reproduce write-path numbers. ## 7. Status and deviations ### Implemented - Ports/adapters and singleton composition (`ports.ts`, `index.ts`). - Atomic UoW with transactional outbox, transactional audit outbox and sorted GL shard locks. - Post-commit `pg_current_wal_flush_lsn()` watermark. - Outbox relay with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, idempotent retry semantics and attempt read-model projection. - Audit shipper with idempotent append and audit hash-chain verification. - LSN/lag-aware replica router with primary fallback. - Redis cache adapter with Lua velocity and memory fallback. - 16-way shard arithmetic and shard-aware ledger writer. - Dedicated audit DB and log DB adapters. - Backup control client with TLS/mTLS support and typed errors. - Storage health snapshot API. - Read model tables and writer. - Test coverage for primitives, UoW, read store, outbox workers, audit chain, log sink, shards, engine factory and performance thresholds. ### Partial - Read-model adoption: `rm_*` tables are written but no dashboard or list reads them. - Outbox projection: only `attempt.transitioned` has an effect; `ledger.entry_posted` and four other topics are no-ops. - Replica routing: only global search and three merchant list endpoints use it. - Cache: Redis/L1 is used primarily by velocity; `getOrLoad` is available but not used by core read paths. - Audit/log retention: log partitions have a deploy-side retention function, but core `audit_outbox`, `outbox_events` and the dedicated audit table have no application-level retention job. - Backup control: the client is implemented and tested, but deployment certificate ownership and daemon-side gaps remain (see `core.backup`). ### Missing / deferred - Keyset pagination. `core-back/lib/listQuery.ts:220` returns `skip`/`take`; no cursor pagination exists. - `gateway_wire_logs` table and any raw gateway wire-log persistence. Evidence is stored in redacted step logs only. - On-disk log spool and durable log backpressure. The buffer drops instead of spooling. - Storage health endpoint. `StorageEngine.health()` is not wired to HTTP. - Automatic outbox and audit-outbox pruning/archival. - Distributed velocity counters when Redis is unavailable. - A real multi-node cache invalidation path through `CachePort.publishInvalidation` (the method is optional and unused). - Read models for merchant dashboards or wallet statements. Only the two attempt-derived tables exist. - A structural benchmark for sustained 1,000+ TPS, deep search or restore throughput (see `core.tests`). ### Known bugs / risks - `AuditShipperWorker` retains every shipped `audit_outbox` row. At high audit volume this becomes an unbounded primary-database table. Code gap. - `OutboxRelayWorker` retains every processed `outbox_events` row. The partial index makes the unprocessed scan cheap, but storage still grows. Code gap. - A failed log flush requeues step logs but not access logs, so access-log rows can be silently lost. Code risk. - The replica LSN monitor runs per process and each core node probes every replica every 150 ms. At many nodes this is measurable probe load. Code risk. - `readThroughReplica` falls back to the primary on any thrown error, including a caller bug, which can hide query errors. Code risk. - Audit chain appends serialize on a single advisory lock. Operational risk. - `lockGlAccountShardsSorted` returns only rows that already exist; missing shard rows are not created by the lock call. A caller that assumes a complete map can under-lock. Code risk; `ensureAccountShards` must have run. - `StorageEngine.health()` returns `audit.ok = false` when the audit store is not configured, which conflates "not configured" with "unhealthy". Code risk in monitoring semantics. - The backup client creates a keep-alive agent once from the environment. Certificate rotation requires a process restart or singleton reset. Operational risk. ## 8. Purpose and scope This part owns the PostgreSQL 18 relational model, the committed migration history, the schema-version guard and the deterministic seeders that populate a baseline platform. It covers: - `core-back/prisma/schema.prisma` — 75 Prisma models and 105 enums; - `core-back/prisma/migrations/**` — four committed migrations; - `core-back/prisma/schemaVersion.ts` and `core-back/prisma/client/index.ts` — schema version 8 and the boot guard; - `core-back/prisma/migrateDev/index.ts` — the migration creation/adoption workflow; - `core-back/prisma/seed.ts`, `seedBlueprints.ts`, `seedGlAccounts.ts`, `seedGuides.ts` and `seedFakeRails.ts` — deterministic baseline data; - `core-back/prisma/syntheticSeeder/**` — the optional multi-year synthetic history (documented separately in `core.seeder`). It does not own domain state machines, ledger templates, API behavior, storage adapter behavior or backup policy. Those are documented in `core.engine`, `core.ledger`, `core.storage` and `core.backup`. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The historical design treats PostgreSQL 18 as the only runtime database and the schema as the durable contract for the switch: - money is stored as `DECIMAL(18,4)` and never as floating point; - payments, ledger entries and audit/outbox records are written atomically; - the ledger is append-only and enforced by constraints and shard projections; - maker-checker is a database-enforced rule, not only an application convention; - the append-only journal is range-partitioned by month for retention and maintenance; - read models and the dedicated audit/log databases are separate physical targets; - migrations are versioned and checked at boot so an outdated database cannot serve traffic. The blueprint's stale counts are corrected here: - the schema is not 64 models and 100 enums; it is 75 models and 105 enums; - the schema version is 8, not 5 or 6; - there is not one migration that creates shards, outboxes and all tables. The baseline creates the tables, the storage migration adds indexes, the CQRS migration adds read models, and the hardening migration adds partitions, checks and search indexes; - `rm_merchant_dashboard_stats` and `rm_wallet_statements` do not exist. The actual read models are `rm_merchant_daily_stats` and `rm_route_daily_volumes`. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 Schema size and layout `core-back/prisma/schema.prisma` contains: - 75 `model` declarations; - 105 `enum` declarations; - 188 `@@index` / `@@unique` declarations in the datamodel; - PostgreSQL provider configured through `DATABASE_URL` and the Prisma 7 `@prisma/adapter-pg` runtime. The models are grouped by domain: | Domain | Representative models | | :--- | :--- | | Merchant and onboarding | `Merchant`, `User`, `UserIdentity`, `JoinRequest`, `KybDocument`, `KybRevalidationRequest`, `BeneficialOwner`, `Application`, `Wallet`, `AccessToken`, `AccessTokenIp` | | Payment collection | `PaymentLink`, `PosTerminal`, `PosScreen`, `AttemptGroup`, `PaymentAttempt`, `AttemptStepLog`, `InboundEvent`, `OperatorCase`, `GatewayInquirySchedule` | | Ledger and balances | `GlAccount`, `JournalEntry`, `JournalLine`, `GlAccountShard`, `CommissionProfile` | | Gateway catalogue and flow | `Gateway`, `GatewayVersion`, `GatewayVersionEvidence`, `GatewayEnvironment`, `GatewayAuth`, `GatewaySetting`, `CredentialSet`, `Asset`, `Rail`, `RailField`, `RailRoute`, `CryptoProfile`, `Flow`, `FlowStep`, `StepParameter`, `StepOutput`, `StatusRule`, `ErrorMap`, `ConfirmationChannel`, `PollPolicy`, `WidgetDefinition`, `RedirectDefinition`, `StatementSource`, `ManualInstruction` | | Risk and collection operations | `VelocityRule`, `AmlCase`, `AmlScreening`, `AmlScreeningMatch`, `AmlRule`, `ReportingRule`, `RegulatoryReport`, `Dispute`, `Adjustment`, `CashoutRequest`, `ReconciliationRun`, `ReconciliationItem` | | Governance and audit | `ApprovalRequest`, `DetailChangeLog`, `AuditLog`, `NotificationTemplate`, `Notification`, `PlatformSetting`, `BackgroundJob` | | Health and operations | `GatewayHealthSample`, `BackupCatalogRun`, `BackupRestoreDrill` | | Write-path infrastructure | `OutboxEvent`, `AuditOutbox` | | Read models | `RmMerchantDailyStat`, `RmRouteDailyVolume` | `core-back/generated/prisma/**` is the committed generated client. It must be regenerated with `bun run migrate-generate`, not hand-edited. ### 3.2 Schema version `core-back/prisma/schemaVersion.ts` exports `REQUIRED_SCHEMA_VERSION = 8`. `core-back/prisma/client/index.ts:17-37` implements `ensureSchemaVersion()`: - it connects through the base client; - it reads `schema_versions.version` where `id = 1`; - it throws when the row is missing or does not equal 8; - it caches the successful check and resets the cached promise after a failure so a later call can retry. `core-back/prisma/seed.ts`, `seedFakeRails.ts` and `syntheticSeeder/index.ts` call `ensureSchemaVersion()` before writing. A stale database is therefore rejected by these seeders and by any caller that explicitly asserts the version. The core HTTP start path does not call it. ### 3.3 Migration history There are exactly four committed migrations: | Migration | Purpose | | :--- | :--- | | `20261103000000_postgres18_init` | Creates 74 tables: all baseline Prisma model tables plus the `schema_versions` support table. Creates enums and the initial indexes/FKs. Inserts schema version 7. | | `20261103120000_postgres18_storage_engine` | Adds `pg_trgm` and `btree_gin`; replaces outbox/audit indexes with partial/BRIN indexes; adds covering/BRIN journal indexes; adds worker-claim partial indexes; adds attempt reference indexes and trigram search indexes. | | `20261103130000_cqrs_read_models` | Creates `rm_merchant_daily_stats` and `rm_route_daily_volumes` plus their day indexes. | | `20261103180000_storage_hardening` | Adds `pg_stat_statements` when available; sets `gl_account_shards.shard_id` default and range check; converts `journal_lines` to monthly range partitions; adds partition maintenance function; adds broader trigram indexes; updates schema version to 8. | The baseline creates the tables, not the storage migration. The storage migration is index-only. The hardening migration is the one that rewrites `journal_lines` into a partitioned table: - it renames the old table to `journal_lines_unpartitioned`; - it creates the new partitioned parent with primary key `(id, created_at)`; - it creates monthly partitions from 2023-01 through the 2028-11 partition and a default partition; - it copies existing rows; - it re-adds foreign keys and the positive-amount check; - it recreates the covering and BRIN indexes; - it creates `ensure_journal_line_partitions(months_ahead)` and runs it for 18 months. The deploy engine installs a daily cron at `JOURNAL_LINE_PARTITION_MAINTENANCE_CRON = "30 1 * * *"` that calls `ensure_journal_line_partitions(18)` (`deploy/provisioners/backupEngineProvisioner.ts:333-336`). Partition creation outside that cron is not automatic. A write that falls outside all monthly ranges goes to the default partition. ### 3.4 Indexes The index strategy has four layers: 1. Foreign-key and uniqueness indexes from the baseline. 2. Partial indexes for worker claim loops: - `outbox_events_unprocessed_idx` on `id` where `processed_at IS NULL`; - `audit_outbox_unshipped_idx` on `(created_at, id)` where `shipped_at IS NULL`; - `payment_attempts_active_expiry_partial_idx` and `payment_attempts_active_poll_partial_idx` for non-terminal attempts; - `inbound_events_unprocessed_partial_idx`, `background_jobs_queued_partial_idx` and `notifications_queued_partial_idx`. 3. Covering and BRIN indexes: - `journal_lines_account_id_cov_idx` includes direction, amount and created_at; - BRIN indexes on `journal_lines.created_at`, `payment_attempts.created_at`, `outbox_events.created_at` and `audit_outbox.shipped_at`; - `payment_attempts_merchant_keyset_cov_idx` exists even though the application does not yet use keyset pagination. 4. Trigram GIN indexes for search candidates on merchants, attempts, join requests, users, gateway inquiries, approvals, KYB documents, disputes, adjustments, reconciliations, AML cases/screenings/rules, regulatory reports, gateways, rails and `audit_log`. ### 3.5 Constraints and triggers The database enforces the invariants that must not depend on a caller: | Constraint | Definition | Purpose | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `journal_lines_amount_positive` | `amount > 0` | Rejects zero/negative journal lines | | `attempt_groups_single_success` | `success_count <= 1` | One success per attempt group | | `payment_links_slot_reservation_invariant` | `infinite_use = true OR confirmed_count + active_locked_count <= use_count` | Prevents slot over-reservation | | `approval_requests_checker_not_maker_insert` | `checker_user_id IS NULL OR checker_user_id <> maker_user_id` | Maker-checker on insert | | `gl_account_shards_shard_id_range` | `shard_id >= 0 AND shard_id < 16` | Shard range | | `journal_lines_entry_id_fkey` | FK to `journal_entries` with `ON DELETE RESTRICT` | No orphan ledger lines | | `journal_lines_gl_account_id_fkey` | FK to `gl_accounts` with `ON DELETE RESTRICT` | No orphan account lines | The baseline also creates the `approval_requests_checker_not_maker` trigger function and `approval_requests_checker_not_maker_update` before-update trigger, which raises when a checker is set equal to the maker. Unique indexes further enforce: - `journal_entries(ref_type, ref_id)` — one journal entry per domain reference; - `payment_attempts(reference)`, `payment_attempts(ledger_entry_id)` and `payment_attempts(link_id, idempotency_key)`; - `inbound_events(channel_id, dedupe_key)`; - `users(email)`, `user_identities(kind, identifier_normalized)` and `user_identities(provider_subject)`; - `payment_links(key)`, `access_tokens(token_hash)`; - `gateways(code)`, `gateway_versions(content_hash)` and `gateway_versions(gateway_id, version_number)`; - `adjustments(dispute_id)` and `adjustments(journal_entry_id)`; - `reconciliation_runs(file_hash)` and `platform_settings(key, scope, version)`. ### 3.6 UUID and timestamp conventions - IDs are UUIDs stored as native PostgreSQL `uuid` (`@db.Uuid`). - Most models declare `@id @default(uuid(7))`. The application also generates UUIDv7 directly through `core-back/lib/storageEngine/uuid.ts` for audit ids; `uuidv7()` is monotonic within a millisecond and preserves B-tree insert locality. - Some infrastructure tables use non-UUID keys: `OutboxEvent.id` is `BigInt @default(autoincrement())`; `HttpAccessLog` (dedicated log DB, outside Prisma) and `AuditRecord` use their own identity/primary-key conventions. - `createdAt` is `DateTime @default(now()) @map("created_at")`; `updatedAt` is `DateTime @updatedAt` on models that mutate. - Core domain tables use `TIMESTAMP(3)` (without time zone), matching Prisma's default mapping in the baseline. Storage-engine tables such as `gl_account_shards`, `outbox_events`, `audit_outbox`, `backup_catalog_runs` and the two read models explicitly use `@db.Timestamptz(3)`. - `schema_versions` uses `TIMESTAMPTZ(3)` directly in raw SQL. - Column names are snake_case through `@map` / `@@map`; the Prisma client exposes camelCase fields. The mixed timestamp convention is real. Any query that compares a core `TIMESTAMP(3)` column to `now()` relies on the session time zone; storage-engine tables compare absolute instants. New tables should use `TIMESTAMPTZ(3)` unless there is a documented reason not to. ### 3.7 Baseline seeders `core-back/prisma/seed.ts` is the main baseline seeder. It is idempotent by lookup for most rows and covers: - platform settings (`OD-1` through `OD-11` plus `join_request.four_eyes_policy`, `onboarding.required_documents`, `join_request.volume_threshold`, `kyb.refresh_policy`); - system GL accounts via `seedSystemGlAccounts(client)`; - the blueprint catalogue (`seedBlueprints(client)`) — gateways, versions, rails, routes, flows, steps, status/error maps and related definitions; - platform credential sets via `seedPlatformCredentialSets(client)`; - bilingual notification templates; - reporting rules for the CBL large-transaction and suspicious-activity references; - checkout support configuration and per-rail help guides via `seedCheckoutSupport` and `seedRailHelpGuides`. `core-back/prisma/seedFakeRails.ts` is a separate bridge that points seeded gateways at the Fake Rails emulator, rewrites environment base URLs and allowed hosts, updates widget definitions to the emulator SDK, and derives inbound verification secrets from the shared seeder token. It is not a full domain seed. `core-back/prisma/syntheticSeeder/index.ts` is the optional multi-year history seeder. It requires the Fake Rails safety gate and is described in `core.seeder`. ### 3.8 Migration workflow The normal workflow is: ```bash cd core-back bun run migrate-dev # create a new migration from the schema and apply it bun run migrate-deploy # apply committed migrations bun run migrate-reset # drop and recreate the database, then apply all migrations bun run migrate-generate # regenerate the Prisma client bun run prisma:validate # validate the datamodel ``` `core-back/prisma/migrateDev/index.ts` wraps Prisma: 1. It lists migration directories before the operation. 2. It runs `prisma migrate dev --create-only --name init`. 3. If Prisma created a migration, it patches the SQL: it removes the `DROP TABLE "schema_versions"` statement and appends the schema-version table DDL plus an upsert to `REQUIRED_SCHEMA_VERSION`. 4. It runs `prisma migrate deploy`. The patch exists because `schema_versions` is managed outside the Prisma datamodel. It is string-based and assumes the generated Prisma SQL contains the exact `DROP TABLE "schema_versions";` statement. A Prisma output change that renames or reformats that statement would silently leave the drop in place or skip the upsert. Review the patched SQL before committing a migration. ## 4. Contracts and invariants - PostgreSQL 18 is the only runtime database. MySQL/MariaDB must not be reintroduced. - Money columns are `DECIMAL(18,4)` (or Prisma `Decimal` with the same precision). Application code uses `Decimal`/`decimal.js`; no floating-point arithmetic is allowed for money. - The Prisma schema is the source of the datamodel. Migrations are the source of applied DDL. Never edit `PROJECT_DESIGN.md`, generated appendices or the generated Prisma client as if they were the schema source. - Every migration must be forward-applicable to the committed history. There are no down migrations; recovery is restore/PITR or a new forward migration. - The schema-version row is single-row (`id = 1`) and must equal `REQUIRED_SCHEMA_VERSION` before the application or seeder proceeds. - `journal_lines` is append-only and partitioned by `created_at`. The primary key includes `created_at` because PostgreSQL requires the partition key in every unique key. - `journal_lines.amount > 0`; direction carries the sign. - `payment_links` slot accounting must satisfy the check invariant at all times. - `approval_requests` must have `checker_user_id <> maker_user_id` when a checker is present, on insert and update. - `gl_account_shards.shard_id` must be in `0..15`. - FK actions are deliberate: ledger and shard references use `RESTRICT`; optional relationships use `SET NULL` or `CASCADE` where the dependent row has no independent meaning. - UUIDv7 is the preferred identifier for new domain rows. Do not use random UUIDv4 for high-volume insert paths without a measured reason. - Seeders must be safe to rerun. Baseline seeders use existence checks; the synthetic seeder uses a completed-run marker and `skipDuplicates`. - The Fake Rails bridge requires `FAKE_RAILS_SEEDER_TOKEN`; it must not silently fall back to an empty secret. - `rm_*` tables are derived data, not the source of truth. A rebuild must be possible from the outbox/ledger. ## 5. Data / API / config / deployment surface ### Prisma and generated surfaces - Datamodel: `core-back/prisma/schema.prisma`. - Generated client: `core-back/generated/prisma/**`. - Migration lock: `core-back/prisma/migrations/migration_lock.toml` (`provider = "postgresql"`). - Schema version constant: `core-back/prisma/schemaVersion.ts`. - Boot guard: `core-back/prisma/client/index.ts`. - Migration wrapper: `core-back/prisma/migrateDev/index.ts`. ### Environment | Key | Purpose | | :--- | :--- | | `DATABASE_URL` | Primary PostgreSQL 18 connection used by Prisma, migrations and seeders | | `POSTGRES_TEST_DATABASE_URL` / `STORAGE_TEST_DATABASE_URL` | Alternative test database URLs used by test helpers | | `FAKE_RAILS_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` | Base URL used by `seedFakeRails.ts` | | `FAKE_RAILS_SEEDER_TOKEN` | HMAC seed for Fake Rails secrets and seeder authentication | | `FAKE_RAILS_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | Allowed hosts written into gateway environments | | `SYNTHETIC_SEED_*` | Synthetic seeder controls (see `core.seeder`) | ### Scripts | Script | Action | | :--- | :--- | | `bun run migrate` | `prisma migrate deploy` | | `bun run migrate-dev` | Create + patch + apply a migration | | `bun run migrate-deploy` | Apply committed migrations | | `bun run migrate-reset` | Drop/recreate the database and apply migrations | | `bun run migrate-generate` | Regenerate the Prisma client | | `bun run db-seed` | Run the baseline seed | | `bun run seed-fake-rails` | Point seeded gateways at Fake Rails | | `bun run seed-synthetic-history` | Run the synthetic history seeder | ### Deployment surfaces - The deploy engine provisions PostgreSQL 18 on the primary, replicas and optional PgBouncer. - The partition cron is installed on the primary by `backupEngineProvisioner.ts`. - The audit and log databases have their own DDL in `deploy/provisioners/auditAndLogDbProvisioner.ts`; they are not Prisma models. - Backups capture the core database, audit database and optional Redis snapshot (see `core.backup`). ## 6. Operational usage - Apply migrations before starting a new core build. The boot guard will reject a schema version other than 8. - Use `bun run migrate-dev` only in development. For production, review and commit the generated migration, then run `bun run migrate-deploy`. - After changing `schema.prisma`, run `bun run migrate-generate` before typechecking or starting the application. - Keep the `schema_versions` patch logic in `migrateDev/index.ts` under review. It is the only place that updates the version for newly created migrations. - Run partition maintenance by installing the deploy cron or by calling `SELECT ensure_journal_line_partitions(18)` on a schedule. The default partition is a safety net, not a substitute for monthly maintenance. - Run `bun run db-seed` once per environment. It is idempotent for the platform settings, system accounts, blueprints, credential sets, templates, reporting rules and guides. - Run `bun run seed-fake-rails` only in environments that intentionally point at the emulator. It rewrites gateway base URLs and allowed hosts. - For a test server, set the synthetic seeder safety variables and run `bun run seed-synthetic-history` after the baseline seed and Fake Rails blueprints. - To inspect the schema, read the generated `project-design/appendices/schema-catalog.md` and `migration-catalog.md`; regenerate them with `bun scripts/project-design/build.ts`. ## 7. Status and deviations ### Implemented - 75 models and 105 enums in the Prisma datamodel. - Schema version 8 with an equality check used by the seeders. - Four committed migrations with the intended separation: baseline, storage indexes, CQRS read models, hardening. - Monthly range partitioning of `journal_lines` with historical/future partitions and a default partition. - Partial, covering, BRIN and trigram indexes for the write path, workers and search. - Maker-checker insert check and update trigger, slot invariant, positive journal amount, shard range and reference uniqueness. - UUIDv7 defaults and application UUIDv7 generation. - Baseline seeders for settings, GL accounts, blueprints, credential sets, templates, reporting rules and guides. - Fake Rails bridge seeder. - Synthetic seeder integration with the schema-version guard. - Schema, constraint, trigger and index test suites. ### Partial - Timestamp semantics: core domain tables use `TIMESTAMP(3)` while storage tables use `TIMESTAMPTZ(3)`. This is consistent inside each area but mixed globally. - Seed coverage is complete for platform fundamentals and blueprints, not for every optional model. Business history is delegated to the synthetic seeder. - Migration guard coverage: the schema-version check runs in the seeders, not in the core HTTP start path; the migration wrapper patches new migrations, but there is no general runtime guard around every script. ### Missing / deferred - Down migrations or automated rollback. Intentional forward-only design. - Automatic partition creation inside the application. Deferred to the deploy cron. - A hand-maintained schema table in the design docs. Purpose and scope Global search is the admin back-office deep-search feature that finds records across 20 domain groups and links the operator to the canonical page or drawer for the record. It owns: - the server-side provider registry in `core-back/lib/globalSearch.ts`; - the query parser, token classification, match scoring and result sanitization in `core-back/lib/search/engine.ts`; - the core internal route `POST /internal/admin/search`; - the mTLS admin BFF proxy `POST /api/v1/admin/search` with its rate limiter; - the admin-front command palette (`Ctrl+K` / `Cmd+K`), local page/guide search, recent queries and the client-side target registry; - the `useOpenQuery` deep-link composable that opens a record from a query parameter. It does not own domain authorization policy (the providers consume authority helpers but `core-back` remains the enforcement point), the underlying record APIs, or the guide content itself. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The historical deep-search design defines a federated, plugin-based search: - the server exposes a fixed set of 20 record groups, each with an explicit authority predicate; - providers fetch candidates independently and decide whether to appear based on the actor's authorities; - a shared parser understands free text, UUID/reference, email, phone variants and scoped tokens such as `type:merchant` and `status:ACTIVE`; - ranking is deterministic: exact field matches rank above prefix matches, which rank above substring matches, with recency as a tie-breaker; - sensitive fields are never returned in results; audit/AML data is filtered by confidentiality rules; - the admin BFF rate-limits search per session; - the frontend registry maps each server group to a route/drawer target and enforces the same route visibility on the client; - `useOpenQuery` turns a search result into a one-shot deep link (`?open=`) that the destination page opens and then clears. The design's "20 groups" is implemented. Its stronger claims are not: - the search is not full-text and does not use PostgreSQL ranking; it is a set of `contains` filters plus in-memory scoring over a small candidate window; - the token-kind hook is present but unused by every built-in provider; - the rate limiter is in memory in one admin-back process, not a shared Redis limiter; - there is no scale, latency or concurrency benchmark for deep search. ## 3. providers by type, preserves aliases/order/access/token hooks, and: - `getAllOrdered()` sorts by `order` then type; - `resolveAliasToTypes()` maps a scoped alias to one or more types; - `unregister()` supports tests and future plugins; - `registerSearchProvider()` registers against the default registry. `executeGlobalSearch` (`globalSearch.ts:1679-1814`): 1. Validates the body with a strict Zod schema: trimmed query length 2–120, optional `types` array, limit 1–10 default 5. 2. Rejects unknown requested types with `SEARCH_TYPE_UNSUPPORTED`. 3. Parses the query and applies alias scoping. 4. Filters providers by explicit type filter, `canAccess`, and optional `supportsTokenKind`. 5. Runs all authorized providers concurrently with `Promise.allSettled`, `take = limit * 3`. 6. Ranks each provider's candidates and slices to `limit`. 7. Aggregates non-empty groups, counts returned items and sets `partial = true` when any provider rejects. 8. Logs a warning when elapsed time exceeds 750 ms (`globalSearch.ts:1796-1807`). 9. Returns `{ query, groups, total, tookMs, partial }`. A provider rejection does not fail the request; it removes that group and marks the response partial. ### 3.3 Parser and token kinds `parseSearchQuery` (`core-back/lib/search/engine.ts:80-137`): - trims and caps raw input at 120 characters; - recognizes `type:`, `is:` and `kind:` aliases for scoped types; - recognizes `status:` and `merchant:`; - keeps the remaining tokens as the term; - builds Libyan phone variants for `+218`, `00218`, leading-zero national numbers and nine-digit local numbers; - classifies the term as `SHA256_HEX`, `EMAIL`, `PHONE`, `ID_OR_REF` or `FREE_TEXT`. The classification is reported in `ParsedSearchQuery.tokenKind`, but no built-in provider supplies `supportsTokenKind`, so classification currently does not narrow the provider set. It is used indirectly by phone-variant generation and by the audit/ID filters. ### 3.4 Ranking and sanitization `computeMatchScore` (`engine.ts:146-197`) scores every candidate from three signal classes: | Signal class | Exact | Prefix | Substring | | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | `exactFields` | 1000 | 750 | 450 | | `primaryTextFields` | 900 | 650 | 350 | | `secondaryTextFields` | 250 | 200 | 150 | An unmatched candidate still gets 100, so a provider can return a record whose searchable fields are related to the row (for example a nested merchant) even when the direct term does not match. `rankAndSliceCandidates` (`engine.ts:333-389`) deduplicates by result id, sorts by score descending, then timestamp descending, then id ascending, and slices to the limit. It also reports `truncated` when more than the limit survived. `sanitizeResultItem` (`engine.ts:254-300`) keeps only `id`, `title`, `subtitle`, `reference`, `status`, `merchantId`, `operatorCaseId` and scalar `meta` values. It drops any key matching a forbidden name or fragment: - ciphertext, secret, password, payout, bank, match list, `beforeJson`, `afterJson`, `rawPayload`, tax id, tax number, registration number, commercial registry. This is a defensive allow-list plus deny-list; it does not redact text inside allowed fields. ### 3.5 Provider query pattern Every provider uses Prisma `findMany` with a status scoping helper and an `OR` array of `contains` filters, `mode: "insensitive"`, plus exact UUID filters from `idSearchFilter`. Nested relations are searched through `is` filters. Each provider selects a narrow projection, orders by its domain timestamp, and takes `limit * 3` rows. Examples: - `merchant` searches id, legal/trade/display name, contact email/phone and (conditionally) tax/registration, plus phone variants. - `payment_attempt` searches id, reference, provider/gateway/network reference, idempotency key and nested merchant trade/legal name. - `operator_case` and `gateway_inquiry` search attempt references and nested merchant names. - `join_request`, `kyb_document`, `dispute`, `adjustment` and `cashout` search the relevant references and nested merchant names. - `reconciliation_run` searches run references and file names. - `approval` searches subject type/id and related references. - `gateway`, `rail` and `route` search codes/names/operator, with nested rail/gateway names for routes. - `user` searches id, email, phone and phone variants. - `audit_log` uses `AuditStorePort.queryAuditLogs` when a dedicated audit store is configured, otherwise the compatibility `audit_log` table. ### 3.6 Core route and BFF Core route: `POST /internal/admin/search` (`core-back/api/internal/admin.ts:682-709`). It reads the `x-pg-min-lsn` header, runs through `readThroughReplicaOrPrimary`, passes the actor derived from the internal principal, and sets `Cache-Control: no-store`. Admin BFF: `admin-back/api/protected/search.ts`: - strict Zod schema mirrors core (query 2–120, `types` max 30, limit 1–10); - `noStore` middleware; - per-process rate limiter with a 60,000 ms window and 120 requests per key; - key is a SHA-256 of the bearer token (or IP, or `anonymous`) truncated to 32 hex characters; - expired buckets are swept when the map exceeds 2,000 entries; - `429 SEARCH_RATE_LIMITED` with `Retry-After`; - forwards to `/internal/admin/search` with the validated body. Mounted at `/search` under the protected admin router (`admin-back/api/protected/index.ts:44`), so the public portal path is `/api/v1/admin/search`. ### 3.7 Admin palette and local commands `admin-front/src/components/search/GlobalSearchPalette.tsx` implements: - a `VDialog` palette opened by the app bar trigger and the global `Ctrl+K`/`Cmd+K` shortcut; - a 250 ms debounce before the server call; - a minimum of two characters for record search, while page and guide search can run on shorter input; - cancellation of the previous request through `AbortController` and a sequence guard; - a 60-second in-memory session cache for non-partial responses (`api.ts:14-18`, `api.ts:53-90`); - an 8-entry recent-query store in `localStorage` (`recents.ts:2`, `recents.ts:34-55`); - tabs for All, Records, Pages and Guide; - local page search over navigation items and local guide search via `searchGuideFn`; - partial/error banners and keyboard navigation; - result rendering through `SearchResultRow` with safe highlighting. `localCommands.ts` searches the navigation catalogue and guide entries. It does not query the server. ### 3.8 Client target registry and access checks `admin-front/src/components/search/targets.ts` registers 20 target plugins, one per server type, with icon, bilingual group/kind labels, a primary route name, optional additional route names and a `resolveTarget` function. Target shapes include: - route-param targets such as `MerchantDetail`, `OperatorCaseDetail`, `JoinRequestDetail`, `KybReviewDetail`, `GatewayWizard` and `AdminUserDetail`; - drawer targets with `?open=` for approvals, disputes, adjustments, cashouts, reconciliations, AML cases/screenings/rules/reports, rails, routes and audit logs; - a search-prefill fallback for gateway inquiries when no operator case is linked. `filterAndNormalizeServerGroups` (`targets.ts:387-435`) drops any group without a registered plugin, drops groups whose primary/additional route is not visible to the user, resolves each item to a target, validates the target and re-checks the target route. Route visibility checks authorities, roles and the visible route-name set (with parent lineage). This is advisory UI filtering; core remains the authority. ### 3.9 `useOpenQuery` `admin-front/src/composables/useOpenQuery.ts`: - watches a query parameter (default `open`); - normalizes string or array values; - uses loaded rows first unless `alwaysFetchDetail` is set; - otherwise calls the page's `fetchById`; - invokes `onOpenRecord` once per id and guards against reactive re-opens; - calls `onNotFound` on null or failure; - exposes `clearOpenQueryParam()` and `isResolvingOpenQuery`. It is used by approvals, AML cases/screenings/rules/reports, disputes, adjustments, cashouts, reconciliation, rails, routes and audit logs. The one-shot guard means a page must clear or change the query parameter to re-open the same record. ## 4. Contracts and invariants - Request body is strict: no unknown keys. Query is trimmed, 2–120 characters. Limit is 1–10 and defaults to 5. BFF `types` is capped at 30 entries. - A response group only contains authorized providers. `partial = true` when at least one authorized provider fails. - Unknown requested types are rejected in core before any provider runs. - Scoped type aliases narrow the requested set only when at least one alias resolves; an unknown alias does not silently disable all search. - Result items never include ciphertext, secrets, payout/bank details, AML match-list data, audit before/after JSON, raw payloads or tax/registration fields. The sanitizer is the last line of defence; providers should not select forbidden fields in the first place. - `id`, `title` and all returned scalar fields are coerced to strings; empty optional fields are omitted. - The frontend must not render a result whose target route is not visible to the user. - `useOpenQuery` opens a record once per id per mount; destinations must fetch the record when it is not in the loaded page. - BFF search responses are non-cacheable (`no-store`). The client cache is memory-only and only stores non-partial responses. - The BFF limiter is advisory abuse control, not an authority boundary. Core applies its own authentication and provider predicates. - Search reads may be served by a replica. The `x-pg-min-lsn` header provides read-after-write consistency when the admin BFF forwards it; the palette does not currently set it. ## 5.
