Operational usage - Use `Ctrl+K`/`Cmd+K` in the admin portal to open the record palette. `?` opens the shortcut help. - Type at least two characters for record search. Page and guide results can appear earlier. - Use the filter tabs to switch between all results, records, pages and guide entries. Tabs are applied client-side over the returned groups. - Use `type:merchant`, `status:ACTIVE` or `merchant:` tokens inside the query to scope server-side. The type/status aliases are server-side; the UI does not expose a separate type picker. - Results open the canonical detail page or a drawer with the record id. The destination page uses `useOpenQuery` to load the record if it is not in the current page data. - If a group is missing from the response, check the actor's authorities and the core log for a provider failure. A `partial: true` response means another group may still be usable. - If search returns 429, wait for `Retry-After`. The limiter is per admin-back process; a multi-node deployment can produce inconsistent limits until a shared limiter is introduced. - Search reads can hit a replica. If a just-written record is missing, retry from a route that sends the `x-pg-min-lsn` watermark or read the canonical detail endpoint on the primary. ## 7. Status and deviations ### Implemented - The 20-group server registry with aliases, order and authority predicates. - Strict request validation, scoped type/status/merchant tokens and Libyan phone variants. - Deterministic in-memory ranking with exact/prefix/substring weights and recency tie-break. - Sensitive-field sanitization and per-provider narrow projections. - Concurrent provider execution with partial-result semantics. - Replica-aware core search route and `x-pg-min-lsn` support. - Admin BFF proxy with per-process hashed-key rate limiting and no-store headers. - Frontend palette with debounce, abort, sequence guard, session cache, recents, local pages/guides, keyboard navigation, RTL support and partial/error states. - Client target registry for all 20 types and route/drawer deep links. - `useOpenQuery` one-shot deep links across the wired pages. - Unit and E2E coverage for parser/ranking/sanitization, client registry, recents, palette behavior and deep links. ### Partial - Token-kind routing: `supportsTokenKind` exists and is invoked, but every built-in provider omits it. The feature is effectively dormant. - Ranking: scoring happens in Node over at most `limit * 3` rows per provider, not in PostgreSQL. A broad query can truncate candidates before the best match is seen. - Missing fields: several schema columns are not in any provider WHERE clause. Examples: merchant `supportEmail`, `supportPhone`, `businessCategory` and `country`; payment attempt link key and attempt-group fingerprint; audit `requestId` and `clientIp`; KYB `docType` (used for scoring, not filtering) and `storageKey`. - Audit search: the dedicated audit adapter searches action, entity type, entity id and actor email through `ILIKE`; it does not search request id, client IP or before/after JSON, and it has no relevance ranking. - Frontend types filter: the palette sends only `query` and `limit`. The All/Records/Pages/Guide tabs do not send a `types` array, so server work is not narrowed by tab. - Rate limiting: in-memory per process, not shared across admin-back nodes; bucket sweeping is approximate and the key falls back to IP for unauthenticated requests. ### Missing / deferred - PostgreSQL full-text search (`tsvector`, `websearch_to_tsquery`, `ts_rank`) and SQL-side ranking. - Cursor pagination or "show all" for a group. Each group is capped at 10 and the palette displays at most that slice. - Typo tolerance/fuzzy matching beyond trigram-backed substring filters, prefix expansion or synonyms. - Cross-group deduplication (the same attempt can appear under multiple groups). - A shared/distributed rate limiter. - A deep-search scale benchmark with realistic record counts, broad queries, 20 concurrent providers and p95 latency. - Search analytics (zero-result queries, slow providers) beyond the 750 ms warning log. - Saved searches or per-user search history on the server. - Server-side `types` filtering from the UI tabs. ### Known bugs / risks - `supportsTokenKind` is dead configuration from the product's point of view. A future provider can use it, but no current provider narrows on token kind, so a SHA256 query still fans out to all authorized providers. Code gap. - Candidate truncation: `take = limit * 3` before ranking means a provider with many substring matches can return three mediocre rows and miss the exact match. Code risk. - `computeMatchScore` returns 100 for a row with no matching signals; if a provider's fetch filter is broader than its signals (nested relation matches), unrelated-looking rows can survive. Code risk. - Merchant tax/registration fields are searchable only for sensitive-access actors, but the fields are also included in the provider's selected projection only for those actors. A non-sensitive actor searching a tax id gets no match rather than a redacted result. Product decision, not a bug. - The audit fallback path does not search `requestId` or `clientIp`; dedicated audit search also omits them. Operators must use the audit list endpoint for those fields. Feature gap. - The BFF rate limiter keys on the full authorization header hash, so token rotation creates a new bucket. It also uses `request.ip`, which is proxy-dependent. Operational risk. - The BFF `types` schema allows up to 30 entries while the server registry has 20. Unknown types are rejected by core, so a stale client list can fail the whole request rather than ignore the unknown entry. Code risk. - The palette client cache does not include the actor/authority set in its key. After a role change in the same tab session, a cached group can remain visible until the 60-second TTL expires; the target-route filter still applies. Code risk. - `filterAndNormalizeServerGroups` silently drops a group if the client target registry lacks its type, so a server/client version skew hides results without an error. Code risk. - `useOpenQuery` marks an id handled before the fetch completes. If the fetch fails transiently, the same id will not retry until the query parameter changes or the component remounts. Code risk. - The `route` target uses `?open=` but the routes page must implement the drawer lookup; the target registry alone does not guarantee the page supports it. Test coverage is the guard. - No test asserts multi-node rate-limit behavior or shared-cache behavior, because neither exists. ## 8. Purpose and scope Backup control is the administrator-facing plane for PostgreSQL point-in-time recovery, the dedicated audit database, and optional Redis snapshots. It spans three layers: - `core-back` internal APIs and `BackupControlClient`; - the standalone `pg-backup-daemon` in `deploy/backup-daemon`, which wraps WAL-G or Barman and owns the schedule, catalog and restore drill; - the admin BFF and the admin portal backup page. This part owns: - the backup daemon contract (`/health`, `/v1/overview`, `/v1/backups/trigger`, `/v1/policy`, `/v1/runs`, `/v1/drills/run`, `/v1/drills`); - target selection (`all`, `postgres_core`, `audit_db`, `redis`); - full and delta backup execution; - the in-process full/delta/drill scheduler and UTC cron parser; - the JSON catalog of runs, drills and policy; - the maker-checker policy update workflow; - the scratch-restore and invariant drill; - catalog synchronization into `backup_catalog_runs` and `backup_restore_drills`; - the admin UI overview, trigger, drill and policy forms. It does not own the core database schema, storage-engine read path, or the deployment certificate PKI. Those are documented in `core.data`, `core.storage` and `07-deploy`. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The historical storage blueprint defines an admin-managed backup orchestrator: - a dedicated daemon wraps WAL-G and Barman, so operators do not run ad-hoc commands; - the daemon is reached over mTLS from core, and core is the only service allowed to call it; - administrators can trigger full/delta backups, run restore drills and change the schedule/retention policy; - policy changes require maker-checker approval; - backups cover the core database, the dedicated audit database and Redis; - the daemon writes to a primary S3/MinIO/R2 bucket and optionally mirrors to a secondary SSH/S3 vault; - a restore drill restores the latest base backup plus WAL to a scratch PostgreSQL instance, then verifies double-entry zero drift, sharded balance parity and audit hash-chain integrity; - the drill report is signed and stored; - the scheduler runs weekly full, weekday delta and weekly drill jobs. The design's false or outdated claims are corrected here: - the scheduler does not run at Tripoli 03:00; it evaluates five-field cron expressions in UTC; - there is no hourly Redis BGSAVE schedule; Redis is snapshotted only when a triggered or scheduled `target=all` backup includes it; - the audit shipper does not delete rows (this is a storage-engine behavior, but it affects backup scope); - the backup certificates are generated and distributed but are not proven ready-to-run for the `pgbackup` daemon user; ownership is not fixed; - the daemon policy retention fields are not the values WAL-G/Barman actually apply; - Barman mode does not mirror to the secondary target and its health still uses WAL-G commands; - the restore drill has a role mismatch for the audit database. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 Core internal API `core-back/api/internal/backups.ts` mounts under `/internal/admin/system/backups` and requires internal mTLS identity plus authorities: | Route | Authorities | Behavior | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `GET /overview` | `security:read` and `gateway:read` | Reads local catalog runs/drills, optionally fetches the daemon overview, syncs the daemon catalog into local tables, returns a merged payload | | `POST /trigger` | `security:write` | Validates `{ target, kind }`, requires a configured daemon, calls the daemon, inserts a local `QUEUED` run | | `POST /drill` | `security:write` | Requires a configured daemon, calls the daemon, inserts a local `QUEUED` drill with target time now minus 5 minutes | | `PUT /policy` | `security:write` | Creates or executes a maker-checker approval, then updates the daemon policy | | `GET /catalog` | `security:read` and `gateway:read` | Returns only the local `backup_catalog_runs` and `backup_restore_drills` | The policy schema is strict: three five-field cron expressions, `fullRetentionDays`, `walRetentionDays`, `alertLagSeconds` and an optional `approvalRequestId`. Defaults exposed when the daemon is absent are: - full: `0 2 * * 0`; - delta: `0 2 * * 1-6`; - drill: `0 4 * * 0`; - full retention: 56 days; - WAL retention: 14 days; - alert lag: 60 seconds. The trigger schema defaults `target` to `all` and `kind` to `full`. ### 3.2 Core policy maker-checker `PUT /policy` without `approvalRequestId` creates an `ApprovalRequest`: - `subjectType = "BACKUP_POLICY"`; - `subjectId = "backup-policy"`; - `payloadDiffJson` = the validated policy; - `mode = "STANDARD"`; - `makerUserId` = the current actor; - `state = "PENDING_REVIEW"`; - expiry 7 days. It returns HTTP 202 with `checkerRequired: true` and the approval id. With `approvalRequestId`, core: 1. loads the approval and requires `subjectType = "BACKUP_POLICY"`; 2. requires state `PENDING_REVIEW` or `APPROVED`; 3. rejects when `approval.makerUserId === actor.userId` with `MAKER_CHECKER_VIOLATION`; 4. requires the daemon to be configured; 5. applies `approval.payloadDiffJson` to the daemon (not the current request body); 6. marks the approval `EXECUTED`, records `checkerUserId` and increments `baseVersion`; 7. writes a `BACKUP_POLICY_UPDATED` audit row with before/after JSON and a stable-JSON checksum prefix. There is no maker-checker on `POST /trigger` or `POST /drill`; both are direct `security:write` actions. ### 3.3 Catalog synchronization `GET /overview` reads local runs and drills first, then checks whether the daemon is configured. If configured, it calls `GET /v1/overview`; on success it calls `syncDaemonCatalog`: - every daemon backup run is upserted into `backup_catalog_runs` by id; - every daemon drill is upserted into `backup_restore_drills` by id; - `sizeBytes` is converted to `BigInt`; - `storageTargets` and drill checks are stored as JSON; - errors are swallowed per write with `Promise.allSettled`, so a partial sync does not fail the overview. The response includes both the daemon view and `localCatalog: { backups, drills }`. If the daemon is unreachable, the response returns local rows and `daemonReachable: false` with `daemonError`. `GET /catalog` never calls the daemon. The admin BFF does not proxy it, so the portal cannot use it directly. ### 3.4 Backup control client `core-back/lib/storageEngine/backupControlClient.ts`: - reads `BACKUP_DAEMON_URL`, `BACKUP_DAEMON_TIMEOUT_MS`, and optional CA/client cert/key paths; - uses `http.Agent` for plain HTTP and `https.Agent` with `minVersion: "TLSv1.3"`, CA and client certificate for HTTPS; - serializes JSON manually, sets content length, parses JSON responses and maps daemon error envelopes to `BackupDaemonError` with code/status/details; - maps unreachable errors to 502 and timeouts to 504; - throws `BackupDaemonNotConfiguredError` (503) when no URL is configured; - exposes a singleton and `resetBackupControlClient()` for tests. The client has no retries, backoff or circuit breaker. A transient daemon failure is surfaced to the operator. ### 3.5 Daemon HTTP API `deploy/backup-daemon/src/server.ts` serves an mTLS HTTP API (plain HTTP only with `BACKUP_ALLOW_INSECURE_HTTP=true`): | Method | Path | Behavior | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `GET` | `/health` | `{ status: "ok", engineMode, version }` | | `GET` | `/v1/overview` | Engine health, WAL health, storage targets, schedule, policy, recent runs, latest/recent drills | | `POST` | `/v1/backups/trigger` | Validates target/kind, allocates an id, queues a background run, returns 202 | | `PUT` | `/v1/policy` | Validates and persists cron/retention/alert policy, returns the updated policy | | `GET` | `/v1/runs?limit=` | Recent catalog runs | | `POST` | `/v1/drills/run` | Queues a restore drill, returns 202 | | `GET` | `/v1/drills?limit=` | Recent drill reports | The server: - caps request bodies at 256 KiB; - validates with Zod and returns structured `{ error: { code, message, details } }` envelopes; - adds a request id and `cache-control: no-store`; - redacts configured secret values and credential-shaped keys from responses and logs; - tracks background tasks for graceful shutdown; - assigns unique ids and refuses conflicts with existing catalog ids. ### 3.6 Engines: WAL-G and Barman `deploy/backup-daemon/src/backupEngine.ts` defines `BACKUP_TARGETS = ["all", "postgres_core", "audit_db", "redis"]`, `BACKUP_KINDS = ["full", "delta"]`, and `RECOVERY_TARGETS = ["postgres_core", "audit_db"]`. WAL-G mode: - base backup: `wal-g backup-push `; - delta: `wal-g backup-push --delta `; - verify: `wal-g st ls `; - mirror: `rclone sync` for S3/rclone destinations, otherwise `rsync -a --delete` to the secondary target; - list: `wal-g backup-list --json`; - prune: `wal-g delete retain FULL --confirm`; - recover: `wal-g backup-fetch LATEST` plus a generated `recovery_target_time` and `recovery_target_action = 'promote'` config; - Redis: `redis-cli -u BGSAVE`, `redis-cli --rdb `, then `rclone copyto /redis/dump.rdb`. Barman mode: - `barman check ` for core and audit; - `barman backup ` or `barman backup --incremental `; - `barman-cloud-backup` to the primary S3 target; - `barman list-backup ` for listing; - `barman recover --target-time ... ` for recovery; - no daemon-side prune; the comment says Barman applies its own `retention_policy`. `backupDataDir` refuses the audit target when `PG_AUDIT_DATA_DIR` is absent, so `target=all` fails rather than silently backing up the core data directory under the audit prefix. ### 3.7 Scheduler `deploy/backup-daemon/src/scheduler.ts` implements an in-process scheduler: - `SCHEDULED_JOBS = ["full", "delta", "drill"]`; - policy changes are re-read every tick, so `PUT /v1/policy` takes effect without restart; - the next run is computed with `nextCronRun` from `cron.ts`; - a tick skips a due job if another backup/drill is still running and logs a warning; - full/delta run `engine.triggerBackup("all", kind)`; - after a successful full run, the scheduler calls `engine.prune("all", "full")`; - drill runs `RestoreDrillRunner.run({ requestedBy: "scheduler" })` and adds the report to the catalog; - failed jobs produce `FAILED` catalog entries; a failed drill gets a signed failed report. Defaults: full Sunday 02:00, delta Monday–Saturday 02:00, drill Sunday 04:00, tick every 30 seconds. All cron evaluation is UTC (`cron.ts` uses `getUTC*` and `setUTC*`), with no timezone or DST configuration. When `SCHEDULER_ENABLED=false`, the deploy provisioner writes a `/etc/cron.d/pg-backup` file with the same three jobs, invoking the trigger script or the legacy restore-drill script. The production default is the in-process scheduler with an explanatory cron file. The system-cron fallback uses the host time zone, so it is not equivalent to the UTC scheduler. ### 3.8 Catalog `deploy/backup-daemon/src/catalogStore.ts` is a JSON catalog at `BACKUP_CATALOG_PATH`: - `BackupCatalog = { runs, drills, policy }`; - atomic write-through temp file plus rename; - load-time Zod validation with a warning and fallback when the file is corrupt; - in-memory operation continues when persistence fails, with `isPersistent()` and `getPersistenceError()`; - default policy `fullRetentionDays: 56`, `walRetentionDays: 14`, `alertLagSeconds: 300`; - in-memory cap of 500 runs and 100 drills, independent of the policy retention fields. The catalog is daemon-local. Core synchronizes it into PostgreSQL only when `/overview` is fetched successfully. There is no reverse synchronization from core to the daemon. ### 3.9 Restore drill `deploy/backup-daemon/src/restoreDrillRunner.ts`: 1. computes `targetTime = now - 5 minutes`; 2. stops and removes both scratch directories (`BACKUP_SCRATCH_DIR`, `BACKUP_SCRATCH_AUDIT_DIR`); 3. recovers the core and audit clusters through `engine.recover`; 4. if the restore did not produce a `PG_VERSION`, runs `initdb -U PG_PRIMARY_USER --auth=trust` (core and audit); 5. appends recovery settings and creates `recovery.signal`; 6. starts both scratch clusters on `127.0.0.1` at their configured ports; 7. verifies double-entry drift is zero; 8. counts journal lines; 9. verifies sharded balance parity against `gl_accounts`/`gl_account_shards`; 10. verifies the audit hash chain; 11. stops and removes the scratch directories in `finally`; 12. returns a report with checks, counts, drift, replayed LSN, error and an HMAC-SHA256 signature over stable JSON using `BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX`. The scratch clusters use `--auth=trust` and listen only on loopback. The drill does not restore Redis and does not validate Redis contents. ### 3.10 Admin BFF and UI `admin-back/api/protected/backups.ts` proxies overview/trigger/drill/policy under `/api/v1/admin/system/backups` with the same authority split as core. It does not expose `/catalog`. `admin-front/src/pages/system/backups/index.tsx`: - loads the overview on mount and polls it on the page's refresh cycle; - shows daemon reachability, engine mode, WAL health, target health, schedule, policy, recent backups and latest drill; - displays double-entry, parity and audit-chain checks from the drill report; - opens a trigger dialog with target and kind; - runs a drill with a confirmation dialog; - opens a policy dialog and submits `PUT /policy`; because the first call returns `PENDING_REVIEW`, the page surfaces the approval id rather than pretending the policy changed; - disables actions when the daemon is not configured or unreachable. ## 4. Contracts and invariants - Only core may call the daemon in a deployment; the listener is private and requires mTLS by default. - The daemon must be configured before trigger/drill/policy; without `BACKUP_DAEMON_URL` the result is 503, never a silent no-op. - `target` is one of `all`, `postgres_core`, `audit_db`, `redis`; `kind` is `full` or `delta`. - `target=all` includes core, audit and Redis when configured. If `PG_AUDIT_DATA_DIR` is missing the whole trigger fails; the core data directory is never used for the audit prefix. - Policy changes require a different maker and checker; the approved payload, not the current request body, is applied. - The in-process scheduler uses five-field cron expressions evaluated in UTC. The fallback `/etc/cron.d` file is interpreted by host cron in its local time zone. A full scheduled backup prunes full backups in WAL-G mode; delta does not prune. - Restore drills target now minus five minutes, are destructive only to scratch directories, run loopback-only and are cleaned up before the report returns. - Drill reports are signed and stored; core copies the signature when it syncs. - Catalog writes are atomic at the file level; a failed write is surfaced but does not stop the daemon. - The daemon must never return or log encryption keys, S3 credentials, database passwords or private key material. ## 5. Operational usage - Set `BACKUP_DAEMON_URL` and client CA/cert/key paths in core. Use HTTPS in production; plain HTTP is local only. - Ensure the daemon has a primary S3 bucket and an encryption key. A typo fails at boot, not during a restore. - For a manual backup, call the admin page or `POST /trigger`; poll `/overview` or `/runs` for completion. - For `target=all`, confirm `PG_AUDIT_DATA_DIR` is set and the audit database is reachable. - For a policy change, submit without an approval id, then have a different `security:write` user submit with the returned id. - Watch `archiveLagSeconds` against `BACKUP_ALERT_LAG_SECONDS`. A non-zero lag with a healthy bucket usually means archive_command, credentials or the archive process is failing. - Inspect `backup_catalog_runs` and `backup_restore_drills` for the local copy and the daemon catalog for the in-process view. A failed drill's three checks identify double-entry, parity or audit-chain failure. - After a real restore, verify schema version 8, the ledger invariant, shard parity and audit chain. - Do not rely on policy `fullRetentionDays` for WAL-G pruning; WAL-G uses `BACKUP_RETENTION_FULL_COUNT` and Barman uses its server-side policy. ## 7. Status and deviations ### Implemented - Core backup internal routes and authority checks. - mTLS backup control client with typed errors and timeouts. - Daemon `/health`, overview, trigger, policy, runs and drills routes. - WAL-G base/delta backup, verify, list, mirror, prune and recover command builders. - Barman check/backup/list/recover paths; Redis BGSAVE/RDB/upload when configured. - In-process UTC cron scheduler with policy hot-reload and skip-on-overlap. - JSON catalog with atomic writes, validation, in-memory fallback and caps. - Policy maker-checker through `ApprovalRequest`, with maker ≠ checker enforcement. - Restore drill with double-entry, parity and audit-chain checks, signed reports and scratch cleanup. - Catalog synchronization from daemon overview into core tables. - Admin BFF proxy and admin backup page with trigger/drill/policy flows. - Unit tests for the daemon, core client/routes and the Playwright backup page. ### Partial - Target-aware backups: `all` works, but Redis is coupled to `all` and has no independent schedule. - Secondary vault: WAL-G core/audit backups mirror; Barman and Redis do not. - Retention: the policy is stored and displayed, but effective WAL-G/Barman behavior is driven by other settings. - Health: WAL health uses archive/replay queries and can be degraded by an empty archive; Barman mode still uses WAL-G commands. - Drill: core and audit are tested with fake command runners; no live end-to-end restore is in the default suite. - Policy: only policy updates are maker-checker protected; trigger and drill are single-actor actions. ### Missing / deferred - Certificate ownership fix: files under `BACKUP_DAEMON_CERT_DIR` are uploaded as root with mode 0600 and no `chown pgbackup`, so the daemon cannot read them. - Audit drill role mapping: the restored audit cluster is queried with `PG_PRIMARY_USER`, while the audit database uses `AUDIT_DB_USER`. - Barman audit slot: `barmanConfig` declares `slot_name = barman_audit`, but `barmanStreamingSql()` only creates the `barman` slot. - WAL archive lag correctness: `WAL_ARCHIVE_STATUS_QUERY` passes `COALESCE(last_archived_wal, '')` to `pg_wal_lsn_diff`, and an empty string is not a valid `pg_lsn`. - WAL replay lag semantics: `WAL_LAG_QUERY` uses replay/receive LSN on the first replica (or primary) and is labeled `lastArchivedLsn`; it is not the archive lag. - Retention enforcement: WAL-G prune uses the environment full count; catalog policy days are not applied. Barman uses a static server policy. - Secondary mirroring for Barman/Redis: Barman returns only `primary-s3`; Redis writes only to the core prefix. - Redis schedule: no `redis` cron; scheduled full/delta jobs use `target=all`, and a `delta` Redis run still performs a full BGSAVE/RDB copy. - UTC cron: the in-process scheduler has no timezone field and evaluates UTC; the system-cron fallback uses host local time, so the historical Tripoli schedule is not honored consistently. - Barman health: `BarmanEngine.overviewHealth` still calls WAL-G bucket/WAL commands. - Catalog exposure and destructive-action controls: admin-back does not proxy `/catalog`; trigger/drill are not maker-checker protected. - Restore drill target selection: the drill always uses now minus 5 minutes. ### Known bugs / risks - The certificate ownership gap blocks the intended mTLS daemon path; code/deploy gap. - The audit role mismatch can produce a false `FAILED` drill on a correctly restored audit database; code gap. - The `barman_audit` slot mismatch can break audit streaming while core works; code gap. - An empty `last_archived_wal` can make health report zero lag instead of "no archive yet"; code gap. - The scheduler advances `next` before skip-on-overlap, so a long-running job can silently miss a slot; code risk. - A failed prune is only logged, while the backup remains `PASSED`; operational risk. - The daemon catalog cap diverges from the unbounded PostgreSQL history; design gap. - The first policy submission returns `PENDING_REVIEW`; an operator who skips the checker step may believe the schedule changed; UX risk. - Scratch port collisions fail the drill; operational risk. - `target=all` fails when audit is not configured; select `postgres_core` explicitly for core-only backups. ## 8. Purpose and scope The synthetic seeder builds a deterministic, multi-year operational history for a designated test/sandbox deployment that is wired to the Fake Payment Rails emulator. It exists so the portals, lists, filters, reconciliation, AML, operator cases, ledger checkpoints and dashboard-style views have realistic data without copying production records. It owns: - the five-layer safety gate; - the scale profiles and environment parsing; - the chronological simulation clock and Libyan market seasonality; - the nine domain generators; - the in-memory 55-collection dataset; - the topological, chunked bulk writer; - Fake Rails transaction/event synchronization; - KYB document enrichment through the Vault; - the completed-run registry in `platform_settings`; - the in-memory and post-seed invariant audit. It does not own the baseline seed (gateways, rails, flows, GL accounts and credential sets) or the Fake Rails emulator implementation. It depends on both. The seed is optional and must never run against a production or non-Fake-Rails environment. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The historical seeder specification describes: - a test-server-only seeder guarded by an explicit environment declaration and a live Fake Rails handshake; - three scale profiles (COMPACT, STANDARD, STRESS) with a multi-year span; - realistic Libyan market seasonality: weekday/weekend rhythm, Ramadan/Eid peaks, salary-day spikes and historical outages; - coverage of the entire schema, including every attempt state, ledger templates, checkpoints, reconciliation, disputes, AML and maker-checker queues; - a two-phase design: build an in-memory chronological graph, then bulk-write it in foreign-key order; - Fake Rails bulk synchronization so inquiries, refunds and statement reconciliation hit the emulator coherently; - encrypted KYB document payloads, not fake plaintext; - a post-seed audit that proves zero ledger drift and balanced entries. The actual implementation keeps the two-phase design, the safety gate and the audit, but its coverage is narrower than the specification: - it writes 49 model collections out of 55 in-memory collections; - seven profile volume fields are not used, so join requests, KYB documents, owners, users, wallets, applications and AML cases are derived rather than controlled; - several ciphertext fields are plain base64 rather than Vault ciphertext; - the seeded staff authority map does not match the auth parser; - the deployed years-span key does not match the key the seeder reads; - the safety gate checks the declared test flag and Fake Rails hosts but not the database host. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 Safety gate `core-back/prisma/syntheticSeeder/SeederSafetyGate.ts` implements five checks before any context is created: 1. `IS_TEST_SERVER === "true"` — otherwise `SEEDER_BLOCKED_NOT_TEST_SERVER`. 2. `FAKE_RAILS_ENABLED === "true"` and `FAKE_RAILS_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` is set — otherwise `SEEDER_BLOCKED_FAKE_RAILS_DISABLED`. 3. When `NODE_ENV === "production"`, `FAKE_RAILS_ALLOW_IN_PRODUCTION === "true"` is required. 4. `FAKE_RAILS_ALLOWED_HOSTS` is non-empty and every configured `gateway_environments.baseUrls` host is in that set. Invalid URLs, empty gateway sets and external hosts fail closed. 5. A live `POST /portal-api/internal/seeder-handshake` with `x-fake-rails-seeder-token` must succeed within 10 seconds. The gate does not inspect `DATABASE_URL`, the host name of the core database, or the presence of production data. It trusts `IS_TEST_SERVER` and the gateway host allowlist. A mis-pointed test flag against a production database is not blocked by code. ### 3.2 Configuration and profiles `core-back/prisma/syntheticSeeder/config.ts` defines: - `SeederProfile = "COMPACT" | "STANDARD" | "STRESS"`; - 19 `ProfileVolumes` fields; - `PROFILES` with the three volume sets; - `loadSeederConfig()` reading `SYNTHETIC_SEED_PROFILE` (or `SYNTHETIC_DATA_PROFILE`), `SYNTHETIC_SEED_KEY` (or `SYNTHETIC_DATA_SEED`), `SYNTHETIC_DATA_NAMESPACE` and `SYNTHETIC_YEARS_SPAN` (or `SYNTHETIC_DATA_YEARS`). | Profile | Merchants | Payment links | Attempts | Recon items | Operator cases | Years | | :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | COMPACT | 65 | 8,500 | 15,000 | 12,000 | 450 | 3.5 | | STANDARD | 250 | 65,000 | 120,000 | 95,000 | 2,900 | 3.5 | | STRESS | 1,200 | 280,000 | 500,000 | 400,000 | 11,500 | 4.0 | The seven volume fields not referenced by any generator are `joinRequests`, `kybDocuments`, `beneficialOwners`, `users`, `wallets`, `applications` and `amlCases`. Their collections are produced as a function of merchants: join requests per merchant lifecycle, one or more wallets and GL accounts per merchant, 1–3 applications, 1–4 users per merchant, KYB documents per business category, owners per ownership threshold, and AML cases from a sample of non-clear screenings. `yearsSpan` is used by the timeline. `SYNTHETIC_YEARS_SPAN` is parsed as a positive number and overrides the profile value. ### 3.3 Context and ID factory `createContext` loads existing references (`gateways`, versions, rails, routes, credentials, GL accounts, admin users, statement sources), builds a seeded PRNG from `seedKey`, builds the timeline, creates an empty dataset, and creates `nextId`. `nextId` ignores its `entity` argument and returns: ```text 00000000-0000-7000-8000- ``` This is a UUIDv7-shaped, visually distinct synthetic id. It is stable within a run. Because the counter resets for every run and the namespace is not included, two different seed keys generate the same ids; `skipDuplicates` then drops the second dataset instead of creating a parallel history. ### 3.4 Timeline `core-back/prisma/syntheticSeeder/timelineClock.ts`: - `buildTimeline(now, yearsSpan)` sets `start = now - round(yearsSpan * 12) months` at 08:00 UTC and `end = now`; - `adoptionMultiplier` grows from 1.0 to 8.0 over the span; - `dayVolumeMultiplier` applies Friday 0.72, Saturday 1.05, salary window 1.35, Ramadan 1.8 and Eid 1.5; - `businessHour` returns a Tripoli-style hour distribution; - `dateAt` writes the chosen hour with `setUTCHours`. There is no +2 offset or timezone database conversion. The simulated "Tripoli hour" is stored as a UTC hour. This is a modeling simplification, not a production behavior. ### 3.5 The nine generators | Generator | Main outputs | | :--- | :--- | | `01_adminAndStaffGenerator` | 12 platform users across `GATEWAY_ADMIN`, `SECURITY_ADMIN`, `FINANCE`, `OPERATOR`, `COMPLIANCE`, `MLRO`, `SUPPORT`; maker/checker flags; user identities; 10 notification templates; velocity, AML and reporting rules | | `02_merchantCohortGenerator` | Merchant lifecycle states; wallets and GL accounts; 1–3 applications; merchant users; join requests and status transitions; KYB documents; beneficial owners; duplicate-document showcase | | `03_gatewayLifecycleGenerator` | Version history (`SUPERSEDED`, `LIVE`, and up to two `PENDING_APPROVAL`); environments; auth rows; settings; confirmation channels; go-live evidence; statement sources; 30 days of hourly route health samples | | `04_linksAndAttemptsGenerator` | Payment links across states; attempt groups; attempts across all 14 statuses; masked customer fields; step logs; inbound events; OTP/failure/conflict/late-success/manual-review substatuses | | `05_ledgerAndCheckpoints` | Balanced journal entries for succeeded/refunded/partially refunded/disputed attempts; refund, partial-refund and chargeback entries; monthly GL checkpoints except the current month | | `06_reconAndStatements` | Reconciliation runs across the span; statement items with matched and exception results; stats JSON; exception budget derived from operator-case volume | | `07_disputesCashoutsAdjustments` | Disputes across seven statuses; chargeback/refund adjustments; cash-out requests; negative-balance wallets after post-cashout chargebacks | | `08_amlAndGovernanceQueues` | Screenings and matches across the seven-layer history; AML cases; regulatory reports; approvals; notifications; audit logs; detail change logs | | `09_operatorCasesGenerator` | Operator cases for UNKNOWN, HELD, CONFLICT, MISMATCH, LATE_SUCCESS, MANUAL_REVIEW and UNMATCHED_STATEMENT; SLA/priority; evidence links; maker-checker resolutions | ### 3.6 The 55 in-memory collections `core-back/prisma/syntheticSeeder/dataset.ts` defines 55 arrays: - Identity and onboarding: `users`, `userIdentities`, `merchants`, `joinRequests`, `kybDocuments`, `beneficialOwners`, `wallets`, `glAccounts`, `applications`, `accessTokens`, `accessTokenIps`, `posTerminals`, `posScreens`, `commissionProfiles`. - Catalogue and credentials: `credentialSets`, `gatewayVersions`, `gatewayVersionEvidence`, `gatewayEnvironments`, `gatewayAuths`, `gatewaySettings`, `confirmationChannels`, `statementSources`. - Reference collections loaded from the baseline: `rails`, `railFields`, `railRoutes`, `widgets`, `redirects`, `pollPolicies`. - Collection flow: `paymentLinks`, `attemptGroups`, `paymentAttempts`, `attemptStepLogs`, `inboundEvents`, `journalEntries`, `journalLines`, `gatewayHealthSamples`. - Reconciliation: `reconciliationRuns`, `reconciliationItems`, `disputes`, `adjustments`, `cashoutRequests`. - Risk and governance: `amlScreenings`, `amlScreeningMatches`, `amlCases`, `regulatoryReports`, `operatorCases`, `approvalRequests`, `notifications`, `auditLogs`, `detailChangeLogs`, `velocityRules`, `amlRules`, `reportingRules`, `platformSettings`. ### 3.7 Bulk writer `core-back/prisma/syntheticSeeder/sync/bulkDataWriter.ts` writes **49 models** in topological FK order: - merchants before users, because users carry `merchant_id`; - GL accounts before wallets; - journal entries before attempts, because attempts carry `ledger_entry_id`; - journal lines after attempts and inbound events; - disputes and adjustments initially strip their circular references, then link them in a second pass; - monthly GL checkpoints are applied last with per-account `update` calls. Each model is written in 2,500-row `createMany` chunks with `skipDuplicates: true`. The writer skips any empty collection. The six in-memory collections not written are `rails`, `railFields`, `railRoutes`, `widgets`, `redirects` and `pollPolicies`; these are expected to exist from the baseline blueprint seed and are only used as read-only references. The writer is not a transaction. A failure partway through leaves the previous chunks committed; re-running with the same seed key is not automatic because the completed-run marker is written only at the end. A failed run can be retried, but duplicate ids are skipped and a partial dataset may remain. ### 3.8 Fake Rails synchronization `core-back/prisma/syntheticSeeder/sync/fakeRailsBulkSyncClient.ts` maps attempts and step logs to the Fake Rails SQLite schema and posts them in batches of 5,000: - `POST /portal-api/internal/bulk-seed` with `x-fake-rails-seeder-token`; - transactions first, then events; - status mapping from core statuses to Fake Rails statuses (`SUCCEEDED` → `PAID`, in-flight → `INITIATED`/`AWAITING_ACTION`, `UNKNOWN` → `UNKNOWN_SIMULATED`); - provider references, OTP code selection, amounts, timestamps and gateway/rail codes. Fake Rails stores the history so "Inquire now" on a seeded UNKNOWN attempt, refunds on seeded successes and statement reconciliation return coherent answers. The sync does not create refunds, disputes or cash-out records in Fake Rails; those remain core-side histories. ### 3.9 KYB enrichment `core-back/prisma/syntheticSeeder/sync/enrichKybDocuments.ts` runs after the bulk write and adds data that the synchronous generators cannot produce: - generates a tiny valid PDF preview per KYB document; - encrypts it with `Vault.encryptSecret(..., "kyb-document")`; - sets `originalFileName` and `uploadedById` where missing; - creates missing required documents for ACTIVE merchants according to `readRequiredDocuments`; - creates owner `OWNER_ID` documents for up to 24 active beneficial owners; - sets `nextKybReviewAt` for ACTIVE merchants that lack one; - creates up to 12 periodic revalidation requests and sets those merchants to `KYB PENDING`. Unlike the base generators, this enrichment uses the real Vault. ### 3.10 Completed-run registry `core-back/prisma/syntheticSeeder/seedRunRegistry.ts` stores a `PlatformSetting`: - scope `SYNTHETIC_SEED`; - key `synthetic.seed.completed:`; - value includes seed key, namespace, profile, years span, completion time and optional attempt/journal/drift counts. `runSyntheticSeeder` checks `findCompletedSeedRun` before the safety gate. A completed key is skipped with a message. A failed or interrupted run never writes the marker. `recordCompletedSeedRun` upserts version 1. ### 3.11 Post-seed audit `verify/postSeedAudit.ts` runs an in-memory audit before writing and again after: - computes debit and credit totals and per-entry balance; - counts succeeded attempts without a ledger entry; - verifies `active_locked_count` matches in-flight attempts per link; - audits operator cases for missing/wrong evidence, maker-checker violations, invalid resolution actions, duplicate open cases, timestamp violations, item backlinks, missing cases for non-MATCHED items and inbound-event integrity; - returns `ok`, drift, unbalanced entries, counts by collection and an operator-case summary. The post-seed version adds database counts for attempts, journal entries and links. It does not assert that the database counts equal the in-memory dataset counts; it only reports both. ### 3.12 Execution flow `core-back/prisma/syntheticSeeder/index.ts`: 1. load config; 2. `ensureSchemaVersion()`; 3. skip when the seed key is already complete; 4. run the safety gate and print Fake Rails health; 5. load references and reject empty gateways/rails; 6. run the nine generators in order; 7. run the in-memory audit and fail on any violation; 8. bulk-write 49 models; 9. enrich KYB documents; 10. sync transactions/events to Fake Rails; 11. run the post-seed audit and fail on any violation; 12. record the completed run. The console summary reports profile, span, phase timings, rows written, KYB enrichment counts, Fake Rails sync counts and final attempts/journal lines/drift. ## 4. Contracts and invariants - The seeder must never run unless `IS_TEST_SERVER=true`, Fake Rails is enabled with a public URL, the production guard is satisfied when applicable, every gateway host is allowed and the live handshake succeeds. - The seeder requires the baseline seed (gateways, rails, routes, credential sets, GL accounts, statement sources) and Fake Rails blueprints. Empty gateways or rails abort. - The dataset must be deterministic for a given `seedKey`, profile and current time. The PRNG and the chronological clock are seeded from the key. - The generated ledger must satisfy `SUM(DEBIT) = SUM(CREDIT)` per entry and system-wide within 0.00005 LYD. - Every SUCCEEDED attempt must have a journal entry; attempts in flight must match each link's `active_locked_count`. - Every non-MATCHED reconciliation item must have a candidate operator case; the operator-case generator uses the same exception budget. - Maker-checker seeded approvals must have `makerUserId <> checkerUserId`; resolved cases must have notes and an executed approval. - All linked evidence (attempt, reconciliation item, confirmation channel, inbound event) must exist and be consistent. - The completed-run marker is written only after the post-seed audit passes. - Re-running the same seed key is a no-op. A new seed key must not assume a clean database; `skipDuplicates` can mask id collisions. ## 5. Data / API / config / deployment surface ### Collections and models The seeder writes 49 Prisma models through `createMany`, including merchant/user/KYB/owner, wallet/application/token, gateway/version/environment/auth/setting/channel/evidence/health, statement source, link/attempt/step/inbound, journal/line, reconciliation, dispute/adjustment/cashout, AML screening/match/case/report, approval, operator case, notification/template/audit/change-log, velocity/AML/reporting rule and platform setting. ### Environment | Key | Purpose | | :--- | :--- | | `IS_TEST_SERVER` | Must be `true` | | `FAKE_RAILS_ENABLED` | Must be `true` | | `FAKE_RAILS_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` | Public emulator base URL | | `FAKE_RAILS_ALLOW_IN_PRODUCTION` | Required when `NODE_ENV=production` | | `FAKE_RAILS_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | Comma-separated allowed emulator hosts | | `FAKE_RAILS_SEEDER_TOKEN` | Shared handshake/bulk-seed token | | `SYNTHETIC_SEED_PROFILE` | `COMPACT`, `STANDARD`, `STRESS` (default `STANDARD` in the seeder; deploy default `COMPACT`) | | `SYNTHETIC_SEED_KEY` | Completed-run key and PRNG seed | | `SYNTHETIC_DATA_NAMESPACE` | Namespace used in emails/references (default `synthv1`) | | `SYNTHETIC_YEARS_SPAN` | Timeline span in years | | `SYNTHETIC_SEED_VERBOSE` | Prints per-model written counts | ### Deploy surface `deploy/lib/configSchema.ts` defines `RUN_SYNTHETIC_HISTORY_SEED`, `SYNTHETIC_SEED_PROFILE`, `SYNTHETIC_SEED_KEY` and `SYNTHETIC_YEARS_SPAN`, with validation that the run requires `IS_TEST_SERVER=true`, Fake Rails enabled and (in production) the production override. `deploy/lib/hostPlanner.ts:309-313` injects the synthetic environment into the core host. It writes **`SYNTHETIC_SEED_YEARS_SPAN`**, while `core-back/prisma/syntheticSeeder/config.ts` reads **`SYNTHETIC_YEARS_SPAN`**. The configured years span is therefore ignored by the seeder, which falls back to the profile's `yearsSpan`. `deploy/deploy.ts:797-807` runs `bun run seed-synthetic-history` on the core host when `RUN_SYNTHETIC_HISTORY_SEED` is true, with a one-hour timeout, and logs the last lines. `deploy/deploy.env` enables the seed with the STANDARD profile and seed key `libya-pg-2023-2026_2`. ### Fake Rails endpoints - `POST /portal-api/internal/seeder-handshake` - `POST /portal-api/internal/bulk-seed` Both require the seeder token and are implemented in `fake-rails-back/api/portal/seederSync.ts`. ## 6. Operational usage - Provision a test server, install Fake Rails, run `bun run db-seed` and `bun run seed-fake-rails` first. - Set `IS_TEST_SERVER=true`, `FAKE_RAILS_ENABLED=true`, `FAKE_RAILS_PUBLIC_BASE_URL`, `FAKE_RAILS_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, a strong `FAKE_RAILS_SEEDER_TOKEN` and the `SYNTHETIC_*` controls. - Choose `COMPACT` for a laptop, `STANDARD` for a shared test host and `STRESS` only with enough disk, memory and time. The STANDARD profile writes roughly 280k rows and syncs 120k attempts; the deploy step allows up to one hour. - Use a new `SYNTHETIC_SEED_KEY` for every intentionally distinct history. Reusing a key is a no-op; changing the key does not clean the previous synthetic rows. - Run `cd core-back && bun run seed-synthetic-history`. - Watch the phase timings and the final audit line. A nonzero drift, unbalanced entries, succeeded-without-ledger count or slot violation aborts before the completion marker. - If Fake Rails sync fails after the database write, fix the emulator and rerun with the same key. The run marker is absent, so the seeder retries; existing ids are skipped. - To rebuild cleanly, recreate the database and rerun the baseline seed, Fake Rails bridge and synthetic seeder. Deleting only the marker is not a clean rebuild because the old synthetic rows remain. - Do not run the seeder against a production database or a non-Fake-Rails gateway set. ## 7. Status and deviations ### Implemented - Five-layer safety gate with live Fake Rails handshake. - Three profiles, a deterministic PRNG and a multi-year timeline. - Nine generators covering merchant/onboarding, gateway lifecycle, links/attempts, ledger/checkpoints, reconciliation, disputes/cash-outs/adjustments, AML/governance, operator cases and admin/staff. - 55 in-memory collections and a 49-model topological bulk writer with 2,500-row chunks. - Fake Rails transaction/event synchronization in 5,000-row batches. - Vault-backed KYB document enrichment. - Completed-run registry in `platform_settings`. - In-memory and post-seed invariant audits. - Deploy integration and safety validation. ### Partial - Volume control: seven `ProfileVolumes` fields are unused; the counts of join requests, KYB documents, owners, users, wallets, applications and AML cases are derived from merchant volume and randomness. - Collection coverage: 49 of 55 collections are written; the six reference collections are assumed to come from the baseline. - Template coverage: 10 notification templates are seeded, and generated notifications use only `PAYMENT_SUCCEEDED`, `PAYMENT_FAILED`, `KYB_DOC_EXPIRING` and `CASHOUT_COMPLETE`. There is no complete bilingual catalogue for every event. - Ciphertext realism: KYB content uses the Vault; merchant national ids, attempt context, AML report payloads and notification addresses use plain base64. - Authority realism: seeded staff have a nested authority map that the auth parser does not understand. - Temporal realism: the Tripoli hour distribution is written as UTC without an offset. - Safety: the gate checks the declared test flag and gateway hosts, not the database host or existing data. ### Missing / deferred - A generator that uses `joinRequests`, `kybDocuments`, `beneficialOwners`, `users`, `wallets`, `applications` and `amlCases` volumes directly. - Writing for the six reference collections. - A full notification template catalogue with both languages for every code. - Vault encryption for the remaining synthetic ciphertext fields. - A flat or boolean authority map compatible with `parseAuthorities`. - Correct deploy propagation of the years-span key. - Database-host and data-presence checks in the safety gate. - Namespace-aware id generation. - An exact database-versus-dataset count assertion in the post-seed audit. - A transactional or resumable bulk writer. ### Known bugs / risks - `nextId` ignores its entity argument and namespace. Two seed keys produce the same ids; `skipDuplicates` silently keeps the first history and drops the second. Code gap. - `hostPlanner` writes `SYNTHETIC_SEED_YEARS_SPAN` while the seeder reads `SYNTHETIC_YEARS_SPAN`, so deployed years span is ignored. Code gap. - The seeded `authoritiesMap` is `{ gateway: ["read", ...] }`; `parseAuthorities` accepts arrays or flat boolean maps, so seeded platform users resolve to no authorities. They can authenticate but fail authority checks. Code gap. - `nationalIdCiphertext`, `contextCiphertext`, `payloadCiphertext`, `addressCiphertext` and similar fields are base64, not encrypted. Any code that tries to decrypt them with the Vault will fail or produce garbage. Code gap. - The bulk writer is not transactional. An interrupted run leaves partial rows and the next retry skips duplicates rather than repairing missing links. Operational risk. - The completion marker is per key only. A new key over a dirty database can duplicate semantic histories while id collisions drop rows. Operational risk. - The seeder does not clear previously seeded rows. A rebuild requires a database reset. - The safety gate assumes all gateway environments point at Fake Rails. A stray live gateway host blocks the seed, which is safe but can be confusing after a partial blueprint seed. Operational risk. - `FAKE_RAILS_SEEDER_TOKEN` may be empty in the handshake if the environment is misconfigured; the Fake Rails side decides whether to reject. Code/configuration risk. - The timeline's adoption/seasonality is applied to link/attempt generation but not to every collection, so some histories are not volume-curved. Modeling limitation. - The post-seed audit reports database counts but does not fail on a dataset/database mismatch, so a partially skipped bulk write can pass the audit. Code gap. ## 8. Contracts and invariants - A test that requires PostgreSQL 18 or Redis must skip explicitly when the service is absent. It must not silently pass a mock that claims to prove live behavior. - The exhaustive runner's success means only that executed tests passed. Purpose and scope This part documents the edge-to-core transport used by `admin-back`, `merchant-back` and `checkout-back`. It owns the mTLS agent, the `CORE_BACK_URLS` node pool, node selection, passive failure detection, retries, request identity headers, the `x-pg-min-lsn` consistency hint, path/channel confinement, core error mapping and the SSE stream proxy. It does not own authorization or business validation. `core-back` remains authoritative for token verification, authorities, maker-checker, amount resolution, idempotency and channel-bound client-certificate checks. The client only guarantees that a request reaches an allowed core channel over an authenticated TLS 1.3 connection. The implementation exists as three near-identical copies: - `admin-back/lib/coreInternalClient.ts` - `merchant-back/lib/coreInternalClient.ts` - `checkout-back/lib/coreInternalClient.ts` Each copy is 761 lines and differs only in `CORE_SERVICE_NAME` and `CORE_CHANNEL_PREFIX`. There is no workspace package, no generated shared module and no single build artifact for the pool. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The historical design requires every edge request to cross a private LAN boundary over mutual TLS 1.3. The edge authenticates with a dedicated client certificate whose CN names the service, and `core-back` binds each internal namespace to that CN. Edge services never receive `DATABASE_URL`, `KMS_MASTER_KEY` or another host's client key. When `core-back` scales horizontally, each edge receives `CORE_BACK_URLS`. The intended behavior is: - persistent keep-alive connections to every core node; - least-in-flight selection with round-robin tie-breaking; - passive removal of a failed node, a cooldown, and a half-open probe after the cooldown; - retry of idempotent requests on a different node; - propagation of `x-pg-min-lsn` so LSN-aware reads can wait for a replica that has replayed the caller's write; - no loss of the edge's identity headers (`x-request-id`, `x-real-client-ip`, `x-client-user-agent`, `x-edge-service`). The design describes this as enabling rolling core restarts without dropping edge traffic. The implementation provides that only for requests that can be retried and only while at least one other eligible node exists; it does not make an individual single-node core restart seamless. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 Agent and TLS material `createCoreAgent()` in each copy builds one `https.Agent` per configured node: - client certificate from `MTLS_CLIENT_CERT_PATH`; - client private key from `MTLS_CLIENT_KEY_PATH`; - CA from `MTLS_CA_CERT_PATH`; - `minVersion` and `maxVersion` fixed to `TLSv1.3`; - `rejectUnauthorized: true`; - keep-alive enabled with 30-second keep-alive delay and `maxSockets: 64`; - the agent-level timeout is `CORE_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`. Material is loaded synchronously with `fs.readFileSync` when the agent is created. A missing file becomes `MTLS_MATERIAL_UNAVAILABLE` (HTTP 500) rather than a process crash. Because the agent is cached, replacing certificate files on disk does not affect a running process until the pool is rebuilt. The pool is rebuilt when the configured URL signature changes or when `resetCoreAgent()`/`resetCorePool()` is called by tests. ### 3.2 Pool lifecycle and selection `ensureNodes()` parses `CORE_BACK_URLS` or falls back to `CORE_BACK_URL`. `parseCoreBackUrls()`: - splits on commas; - rejects empty entries; - requires absolute `https:` URLs; - de-duplicates by normalized `URL.toString()`; - preserves the original trimmed strings for requests. Each node state tracks `url`, `agent`, `healthy`, `inFlight`, `failures`, `lastFailureAt` and `cooldownUntil`. `eligiblePool(excluded)` implements the cooldown/half-open state: 1. If any excluded node is unhealthy, has zero in-flight requests and its cooldown has elapsed, return only those half-open nodes. This lets one request probe recovery before the node rejoins the general pool. 2. Otherwise return every healthy, non-excluded node. 3. If neither set is non-empty the request fails with `503 CORE_UNAVAILABLE`. `selectNode()` picks the minimum in-flight count and uses a monotonic round-robin cursor to break ties. The cursor advances on every selection and is reduced modulo the tied set size. A node selected for an attempt is added to the request-local `attempted` set, so a retry never targets the same URL within one logical call. ### 3.3 Failure marking and retries `markNodeFailure()` sets `healthy=false`, increments `failures`, records `lastFailureAt` and sets `cooldownUntil = now + CORE_FAILURE_COOLDOWN_MS` (5 seconds). `markNodeHealthy()` clears all failure state. Retry eligibility is controlled by `retryAttemptsFor()`: - idempotent methods default to retrying: `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`; - `POST` and `PATCH` do not retry by default; - `retryIdempotent: true` forces retries; `retryIfUnavailable: true` allows a non-idempotent call to retry; - `maxAttempts` defaults to 2 and is floored to at least 1; there is no upper cap. `request()` marks a node failed and retries when the node returns HTTP `502` or `503`, or when the request throws a connection/TLS error. Any other status, including other `5xx` responses, marks the node healthy and is returned to the caller. If every attempt ends in a `502`/`503`, the last response body is returned rather than converted to a local error. If every node has already been attempted and no eligible node remains, the call fails with `CORE_UNAVAILABLE`. `mapCoreTransportError()` maps transport failures to stable edge errors: | Transport condition | Edge error | | :--- | :--- | | `ETIMEDOUT`, `ESOCKETTIMEDOUT` | `504 CORE_TIMEOUT` | | `ECONNREFUSED`, `ECONNRESET`, `EPIPE`, `EHOSTUNREACH` | `502 CORE_UNREACHABLE` | | `ENOTFOUND`, `EAI_AGAIN` | `502 CORE_DNS_FAILURE` | | TLS error codes | `502 CORE_TLS_ERROR` | | other failures | `502 CORE_CONNECTION_ERROR` | ### 3.4 Headers and consistency `buildCoreHeaders()` emits: - `x-request-id`: the resolved edge request id; - `x-real-client-ip`: the client IP resolved from the trusted proxy; - `x-client-user-agent`: the caller's user agent, possibly empty; - `x-edge-service`: `admin-back`, `merchant-back` or `checkout-back`; - `accept: application/json`; - `content-type: application/json` when a JSON body exists, or the supplied raw content type; - `authorization` when present; - every caller-supplied header, lowercased; - `x-pg-min-lsn` when `minLsn` or `consistencyLsn` is non-empty. `consistencyHeader(lsn)` is a helper that returns the same header or an empty object. The client does not generate an LSN. Callers must obtain one from a write response or another trusted source. `x-pg-min-lsn` is passed through to `core-back`, where `lib/storageEngine` converts it into an `atLeastLsn` read constraint with a 250 ms wait. ### 3.5 Path and channel confinement `assertCorePath()` rejects: - empty paths and non-rooted paths; - protocol-relative paths (`//...`), embedded `://` and backslashes; - invalid percent escaping; - decoded `.` or `..` segments; - any path outside the service's channel prefix. The prefixes are: | Service | Prefix | | :--- | :--- | | `admin-back` | `/internal/admin` | | `merchant-back` | `/internal/merchant` | | `checkout-back` | `/internal/checkout` | `resolveCoreUrlAgainst()` pins the result to the configured base origin and appends the path to the base pathname. `resolveCoreUrl()` exposes the same behavior for callers and tests. This is a client-side guard only; `core-back` independently enforces the certificate CN with `requireEdgeIdentity()` in `core-back/api/middleware/mtlsGuard.ts`. ### 3.6 SSE streams and fallback behavior `openCoreStream()` is the streaming counterpart of `request()`: - sets `accept: text/event-stream` and `cache-control: no-cache`; - uses the same node selection, retry count, cooldown and attempted-node set; - increments `inFlight` until the stream ends, closes or errors; - if a node answers `502`/`503` and another attempt is possible, drains that response into a buffer, records it as `lastStream`, and tries the next node; - if retries are exhausted, returns `lastStream` or maps the transport error. `proxyCoreStream()` converts a non-2xx upstream into the normal core HTTP error, then copies the stream to the express response with `cache-control: no-cache, no-transform`, `connection: keep-alive` and `x-accel-buffering: no`. On client disconnect it aborts the upstream request. There is no true fallback to polling at the edge. Checkout and POS SSE are implemented by the core endpoint polling PostgreSQL on a timer; an established edge stream that breaks is ended, not resumed. The buffered `lastStream` fallback only preserves a failed handshake response body for retry purposes. ## 4. Contracts and invariants - Every core URL must be an absolute `https:` URL. Plain HTTP is not accepted by the edge configuration schema. - TLS 1.3 is the only accepted protocol version. - The client cert CN must match the channel; the client path guard prevents accidental cross-channel calls, and `core-back` prevents forged ones. - A call never retries against the same URL twice. - A default retry only applies to idempotent methods. - A `502`/`503` from any node is interpreted as node unavailability even if generated by application code. - Request identity headers and `authorization` are forwarded verbatim; the edge does not mint or re-sign tokens. - The pool does not load-balance SSE streams after establishment; selection happens once per stream open. - LSN hints are propagated, not validated. A malformed value is passed to core, where the storage layer decides how to handle it. - The client never receives or uses `DATABASE_URL`, `KMS_MASTER_KEY`, or another service's certificate. ## 5. Operational usage - When adding a core node, add it to `CORE_NODES` or set `CORE_BACK_URLS`; re-deploy the edge tiers so their process environment changes. The pool itself would notice a changed environment only if the process configuration changes, which requires a restart in a deployed environment. - When rotating certificates, restart or redeploy the edge processes. Replacing files in place is not sufficient for a running pool. - Check `/health` on the edge only for process liveness; it does not probe core. Use `deploy/lib/healthVerifier.ts` or a manual mTLS request to check the upstream. - Use `x-request-id` to correlate an edge failure with core logs. The edge maps core envelopes and preserves `code`, `message`, `details` and `reference`. - To debug node selection, inspect `CORE_BACK_URLS` in the generated `.env`, the edge logs and the core health endpoint. There are no exported pool metrics or a status endpoint. ## 7. Status and deviations ### Implemented - Per-node keep-alive TLS 1.3 agents with client certificates and CA verification. - Least-in-flight selection with round-robin tie-breaking. - Passive failure marking with a 5-second cooldown. - Half-open selection: one zero-in-flight request probes an unhealthy node after cooldown. - Idempotent retries and explicit non-idempotent retry opt-in. - `x-pg-min-lsn` propagation and header helper. - Channel path confinement and URL origin pinning. - Core envelope and transport error mapping. - SSE stream proxying with pre-establishment retry and buffering of failed handshake responses. ### Partial - The "shared" client is a copy-paste implementation. Behavior is consistent today, but a change must be applied three times. - Certificate rotation requires a restart; there is no file watcher or hot reload. - The SSE fallback preserves a failed response but does not resume an interrupted stream. ### Missing / deferred - No circuit-breaker metrics, pool introspection, or administrative pool status endpoint. - No request hedging or per-attempt deadline separate from the overall timeout. - No automatic retry for `POST`/`PATCH` unless a caller opts in. - No jitter on cooldown or randomized selection. ### Known bugs / risks - Treating every upstream `502`/`503` as a node failure can evict a healthy core node that legitimately returned a gateway-style `502`/`503`. - A half-open node is preferred over healthy nodes while any half-open candidate exists. With several recovering nodes this can concentrate probe traffic rather than spread it. - `maxAttempts` can exceed the number of nodes; the attempted set then stops the loop early. - A pool with an empty URL list throws `CORE_UNAVAILABLE`; there is no startup-time rejection of an empty `CORE_BACK_URLS` beyond the fallback to `CORE_BACK_URL`. - The stream path does not retry after response headers are delivered; a mid-stream core restart is visible to the browser. ### Code gap versus documentation The historical design describes zero-downtime rolling core restarts. The client enables retry-based continuity for idempotent one-shot calls and for stream establishment, but it does not guarantee zero downtime for non-idempotent calls, established SSE streams, or a single core node. This document records the as-built behavior. ## 8. Purpose and scope `admin-back` is the private-LAN API edge for the back office. It terminates browser requests from `admin-front`, enforces the LAN boundary and coarse-grained authority hints, validates and translates the public admin vocabulary into the canonical `core-back` contract, and forwards every operation over mTLS to `/internal/admin/*`. It owns no database connection, no Prisma client, no `DATABASE_URL`, no `KMS_MASTER_KEY` and no business authority. The service is a stateless Express 5 application built for Bun. Scope boundaries: - Owns the admin LAN ingress, LAN CIDR check, rate limiting, request logging, upload buffering, schema validation and body mapping. - Does not own JWT signature verification, session revocation, MFA state, IP allowlists for individual users, maker-checker enforcement or money movement. - Does not own the backup daemon; it proxies backup control routes to `core-back`, which talks to `pg-backup-daemon` over mTLS. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The historical design places the admin portal on a private LAN, behind a non-forwarded reverse proxy on port 8443. The admin backend binds to loopback. Every request is forwarded to `core-back` over TLS 1.3 using a client certificate with `CN=admin-back`; the core rejects that certificate on the merchant or checkout channels. The design describes the edge as validating input with shared Zod schemas, enforcing LAN rate limits and admin session/MFA headers, and leaving session verification, revocation, MFA and authority checks to `core-back`. It also requires maker-checker for sensitive actions, with the checker different from the maker, enforced by the core. The admin surface is intentionally broad: users, join requests and KYB, merchants, approvals, AML, gateway catalog and wizard, rails/routes, operations, reconciliation, finance, settings, audit logs and backup controls. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 Process and listener `admin-back/index.ts` creates an Express app with: - `x-powered-by` disabled; - `trust proxy` disabled at the Express layer (`app.set("trust proxy", false)`); - CORS with `origin: true` and `credentials: false`; - request logging middleware; - an unauthenticated `GET /health` returning `{ status: "ok", service: "admin-back", uptime }`; - JSON and URL-encoded body parsers limited by `MAX_JSON_BODY_BYTES`; - the admin router mounted at `/api/v1/admin`, wrapped by `enforceLanAccess`; - a JSON 404 handler and the shared error handler. The listener binds to `ADMIN_BIND_HOST` (default `127.0.0.1`). The deploy engine writes `ADMIN_BIND_HOST=127.0.0.1`, so only the co-located Nginx vhost reaches the process. The admin Nginx vhost is exposed on `ADMIN_NGINX_LAN_PORT` (default 8443) and restricted to `LAN_ALLOWED_CIDRS`. ### 3.2 Middleware and guards | Layer | Behavior | | :--- | :--- | | `enforceLanAccess` | Resolves the client IP from `x-real-ip`/`x-real-client-ip` only when the immediate peer is loopback or in `TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`, then requires the result to be inside `ADMIN_LAN_CIDRS`. Failure is `403 ADMIN_LAN_ONLY`. Applied to the entire `/api/v1/admin` router, including `/auth`. | | `adminLimiter` | 600 requests per 60 seconds by default (`ADMIN_RATE_LIMIT_MAX`), applied to the protected router. It does not parse or verify the header. | | `requireAuthorities` | Reads `role`, `roles`, `authorities` and `authorities_map` from the base64url JWT payload, then checks that at least one requested authority or role is present. `COMPLIANCE` and `MLRO` are aliases for `aml:read`/`aml:write`. | | Search limiter | `POST /search` has its own 120-requests-per-minute limiter keyed by a SHA-256 hash of the bearer token or IP. | | Upload middleware | Multer memory storage with `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`; the reconciliation route validates the detected MIME type and magic bytes through `assertAllowedUpload`, while the join-request KYB route forwards the raw file without that check. | `extractAuthorityHints()` does not verify the token signature and does not check `exp` or `nbf`. This is documented as advisory gating, not authentication. `ADMIN_AUTHORITY_HINTS` filters which requested authority strings the edge checks. Contracts and invariants - The admin API is reachable only from `ADMIN_LAN_CIDRS`; the deploy engine aligns the UFW admin rule with `LAN_ALLOWED_CIDRS`. - Every forwarded path must stay under `/internal/admin`; the shared client enforces this and core re-checks the client CN. - The edge never accepts a core path from the request; route modules construct the path. - The edge never performs money arithmetic; amount and currency fields are validated and forwarded for core to re-check. - Sensitive mutations are not approved at the edge. Maker-checker, base-version checks, state transitions and audit writes happen in `core-back`. - The backup policy route creates a maker-checker approval when `approvalRequestId` is absent; a checker must be a different user from the maker. - The admin edge never receives database credentials, the KMS key or another host's certificate. - Error envelopes from core (`code`, `message`, `details`, `reference`) are preserved by `mapCoreHttpError()`. ## 5. Purpose and scope `merchant-back` is the public merchant edge. One Bun/Express process serves two audiences: - the authenticated merchant portal under `/api/v1/merchant/*`; - the merchant server API under `/api/v1/external/*`, authenticated by a `pg_live_` bearer token and a core-side IP allowlist. It owns request validation, edge translation to the canonical core contract, upload verification, rate limiting, the public merchant API shape and mTLS forwarding to `/internal/merchant/*`. It owns no database connection, no Prisma client, no `DATABASE_URL`, no `KMS_MASTER_KEY` and no authority decisions. The merchant vhost serves the SPA through Nginx. The backend itself binds to loopback in deployment. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The design splits the merchant experience into a portal API and a server-to-server API. The portal covers registration, identity verification, login/MFA, KYB onboarding, wallets, applications, links, POS terminals and cashier screens, payments, disputes, cash-outs, API tokens, credential sets, team users and overview statistics. The external API covers link creation/inspection/cancellation and payment lookup using a long-lived merchant token. All operations are forwarded over mTLS 1.3 with `CN=merchant-back`. The edge validates multipart KYB documents for MIME type, magic bytes and size before forwarding raw bytes to core. The portal may accept amounts and currencies when the merchant owns link creation; the edge never performs money arithmetic and core re-validates every monetary field. The external API is meant to enforce a `pg_live_` bearer token and an IP allowlist, with core as the authority. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 Process, listener and middleware `merchant-back/index.ts`: - disables `x-powered-by`; - sets `trust proxy` to false; - enables CORS with any origin and no credentials; - installs request logging; - serves unauthenticated `GET /health`; - parses JSON and URL-encoded bodies with `MAX_JSON_BODY_BYTES`; - mounts `/api/v1`; - adds the shared 404 and error handlers. The listener binds to `BIND_HOST` (default `0.0.0.0` in the service schema). The deploy engine overrides this to `127.0.0.1`; direct exposure of port 4102 is a configuration error. Middleware layers: | Layer | Behavior | | :--- | :--- | | `authLimiter` | Fixed 15-minute window, `AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_MAX` (default 20), on `/api/v1/merchant/auth`. | | `onboardingLimiter` | 60-second window, `API_RATE_LIMIT_MAX` (default 300), on `/api/v1/merchant/onboarding`. | | `apiLimiter` | 60-second window, `API_RATE_LIMIT_MAX` (default 300), on the protected merchant router. | | `externalLimiter` | 60-second window, `EXTERNAL_RATE_LIMIT_MAX` (default 120), on `/api/v1/external`. | | `requirePgLiveToken` | Requires `Authorization: Bearer pg_live_...` by prefix only. Applied to the whole external router. | | `coreForward` `requireAuth` | Rejects a missing `Authorization` header for protected portal routes. Defaults to required; auth/onboarding routes opt out with `requireAuth: false`. | | `requireBearer` | Helper used by dispute evidence and merchant user routes to require a header before multipart work. | | `requireAuthHeader` | Exported from `api/public/auth.ts` but a no-op; it is not a security control. | There is no edge session parser, role guard or token verifier in `merchant-back`. An arbitrary non-empty bearer token reaches core for every protected portal route. ### 3.2 Forwarding behavior `merchant-back/api/forward.ts` implements a stricter forwarder than admin's: 1. Requires `Authorization` unless `requireAuth === false`. 2. Validates route params and query with Zod. 3. Validates the public body with `schema`. 4. Applies `bodyMapper()` to translate product vocabulary into the core body. 5. Applies `bodyFrom()` when the route replaces the body entirely. 6. Re-validates the translated body with `coreSchema` when configured, so a request that core would reject is stopped at the edge. 7. Calls `callCoreResponse()` with request id, resolved client IP, user agent and the bearer token. 8. Returns the core body with the declared status, or the core status when `relayStatus: true`. The external router also has its own PG-live prefix check. It does not hash or validate the token; core does the authoritative token lookup and IP check. ### 3.3 Uploads `merchant-back/api/upload.ts` uses Multer memory storage with `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`, one file and at most 32 fields. `forwardUpload()` and the dispute route call `assertAllowedUpload()`: - checks the declared MIME type against `UPLOAD_ALLOWED_MIME`; - checks magic bytes for PNG (`89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A`), JPEG (`FF D8 FF`) and PDF (`25 50 44 46 2D`); - enforces the size cap; - computes SHA-256; - forwards raw bytes with `x-upload-filename`, `x-upload-content-type`, `x-upload-sha256`, `x-upload-size` and base64url `x-upload-metadata`. Contracts and invariants - All portal business routes require an `Authorization` header at the edge; its validity is decided by core. - The external API requires a `pg_live_` prefix at the edge; access-token validity, revocation and source-IP allowlist are decided by core. - Every forwarded path stays under `/internal/merchant`; the shared client enforces this and core re-checks `CN=merchant-back`. - The edge never accepts arbitrary core paths. - Link creation accepts decimal-string amounts and ISO 4217 currencies; the edge does not do arithmetic and core re-validates amount, currency and fee model. - Checkout money semantics do not apply here: merchant link creation is an owning operation. - Uploaded KYB and dispute files are validated for MIME, magic bytes and size before the core call. - Team/user and credential-set operations are forwarded with the caller's bearer token; the core enforces merchant roles and maker-checker where applicable. - The POS SSE route requires a bearer header, then proxies the core stream. ## 5. Purpose and scope `checkout-back` is the public checkout and inbound-webhook edge. It serves anonymous payers and external payment gateways: - payer link resolution and attempt lifecycle under `/api/v1/pay/*`; - the checkout status SSE stream; - browser return handling under `/api/v1/return/*`; - raw inbound gateway webhooks under `/api/v1/inbound/:gateway/:env/:pathToken`.
