Purpose and scope This part documents the four modular storage provisioners invoked by the deployment pipeline: - `postgres18Provisioner.ts`: PostgreSQL 18 primary, replicas, replication slots, `pg_hba`, PgBouncer, tuning and journal partition cron; - `redisProvisioner.ts`: Redis cache/velocity nodes; - `auditAndLogDbProvisioner.ts`: append-only audit database and partitioned log database; - `backupEngineProvisioner.ts`: WAL-G/Barman archive engine, daemon environment/unit, schedules and S3/secondary target checks. It covers what is installed, what is written, what is not consumed (especially TLS/mTLS) and the operational consequences. It does not own the backup daemon runtime (`deploy.backup`), the host plan (`deploy.planner`), the firewall (`deploy.firewall`) or the pipeline ordering (`deploy.pipeline`). ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The storage plane is PostgreSQL 18 only. The design specifies: - a tuned primary with streaming replicas initialized by `pg_basebackup -R` and physical replication slots; - PgBouncer in transaction mode on the primary and replicas; - SCRAM authentication and TLS-only remote database connections; - Redis bound to the private LAN with a password and no public exposure; - an append-only audit database with a SHA-256 hash chain and immutable rows; - a monthly-partitioned log database with a retention function and cron; - WAL-G or Barman for continuous WAL archiving and full/delta backups, with an S3 primary and optional secondary vault; - journal-line partition maintenance on a daily cron; - storage client certificates for mTLS links. The code implements most of the topology, authentication and scheduling. The TLS/mTLS wiring is incomplete and is recorded explicitly below. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 PostgreSQL 18 -`bootstrapCommands()` installs `postgresql-${PG_VERSION}`, `postgresql-contrib-${PG_VERSION}` and `pgbouncer` with `apt-get`, enables PostgreSQL and PgBouncer (on the primary and on replicas that also run PgBouncer), and creates the data directory with owner `postgres`. +`bootstrapCommands()` installs `postgresql-${PG_VERSION}`, `postgresql-contrib-${PG_VERSION}` and `pgbouncer` with `apt-get`, ensures the Debian cluster (`main` on 5432, or a named cluster on another port) exists, starts it, enables `postgresql@18-` and PgBouncer where applicable, and creates the data directory with owner `postgres`. The version comes from `PG_VERSION` (default `18`). The schema allows any one- or two-digit major version; there is no runtime assertion that it is exactly 18. -`postgresConfigSnippet()` writes `/etc/postgresql//main/conf.d/zz-pg-switch.conf` with `listen_addresses='*'`, 300 connections, 8 GB shared buffers, 24 GB effective cache, 32 MB work memory, 1 GB maintenance memory, `io_method='io_uring'`, `synchronous_commit=on`, `wal_level=replica`, 16 WAL senders/slots, 16 GB max WAL, `pg_stat_statements` and `track_io_timing=on`. +`postgresConfigSnippet()` writes `/etc/postgresql///conf.d/zz-pg-switch.conf` (where `` is `main`, `replica_`, `audit` or `log`) with `listen_addresses='*'`, 300 connections, 8 GB shared buffers, 24 GB effective cache, 32 MB work memory, 1 GB maintenance memory, `io_method='io_uring'`, `synchronous_commit=on`, `wal_level=replica`, 16 WAL senders/slots, 16 GB max WAL, `pg_stat_statements` and `track_io_timing=on`. The file contains no `ssl`, `ssl_cert_file`, `ssl_key_file`, `ssl_ca_file` or `ssl_crl_file` settings. The database listens on all interfaces and relies on UFW plus `pg_hba`. `primaryBootstrapSql()`: - creates the application role if absent, otherwise resets its password; - creates the application database owned by that role if absent; - creates the replication role with `REPLICATION LOGIN`, or resets its password; - creates one physical replication slot per replica using a sanitized node id; - emits a comment listing the intended `pg_hba` sources. `pgHbaSnippet()` writes `local ... peer`, loopback `host ... scram-sha-256`, and `hostssl` all/replication lines with `scram-sha-256` for every allowed source. There is no `clientcert=verify-full` and no `cert` auth method, so the generated `pg-client` certificate is not part of database authentication. The primary source list includes the primary itself, every replica, every core private IP, and the backup/audit/log node private IPs. The replica source list includes the primary and the backup nodes. The provisioner writes `pg_hba.conf`, applies the bootstrap SQL through `su - postgres`, restarts PostgreSQL, and installs `/etc/cron.d/pg-journal-partitions`: ```text 30 1 * * * root su - postgres -c "psql -d -c 'SELECT ensure_journal_line_partitions(18)'" >/var/log/pg-journal-partitions.log 2>&1 ``` The function `ensure_journal_line_partitions` must already exist from the core migrations. The same cron file is also written by the backup provisioner; the last writer wins with identical content. ### 3.2 Replicas and slots For each replica, `replicaCommands()`: - creates `/var/lib/postgresql` and writes `/var/lib/postgresql/.pgpass` with the replication credentials; -- runs `pg_basebackup -h -p -U -D -Fp -Xs -P -R -S ` only when the data directory has no `PG_VERSION`; +- stops the empty cluster, replaces its data directory with `pg_basebackup -h -p -U -D -Fp -Xs -P -R -S `, writes the slot into `postgresql.auto.conf`, starts the cluster and enables its systemd unit; - ensures `primary_slot_name` in `postgresql.auto.conf`; - enables and starts PostgreSQL. The slots are created on the primary by `primaryBootstrapSql()`. Replication is asynchronous; `synchronous_commit=on` is local commit durability, not synchronous replication. There is no quorum or automatic failover. `pg_basebackup` and the replica `.pgpass` use the replication password. The `.pgpass` is created under `/var/lib/postgresql` with a restrictive umask. ### 3.3 PgBouncer When `PGBOUNCER_ENABLED=true`, PgBouncer is installed and configured on the primary and every replica. `/etc/pgbouncer/pgbouncer.ini` sets `listen_addr=0.0.0.0`, `listen_port=6432`, transaction pooling, `server_tls_sslmode=require`, 2000 client connections, pool size 50, reserve 10, 256 prepared statements, SCRAM auth and `/etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt`. The userlist contains the application and replication users with plaintext passwords, mode 0600. PgBouncer is restarted after writing it. Important as-built facts: - There is no `[databases]` section. PgBouncer has no mapping from a client database name to a PostgreSQL host/port/database. A client connecting to `:6432` cannot be routed to the application database by this configuration. - `server_tls_sslmode = require` encrypts the PgBouncer-to-PostgreSQL leg but does not verify the server certificate (`verify-full` would) and supplies no client certificate. - There is no `client_tls_sslmode`, `client_tls_cert_file` or `client_tls_key_file`; clients are not required to present a certificate. - `listen_addr = 0.0.0.0` is protected by UFW only; the plan opens 6432 to core sources. The core environment points `PG_PRIMARY_PORT` and `DATABASE_REPLICA_URLS` at `PGBOUNCER_PORT` when the pooler is enabled. Because the generated PgBouncer has no database mapping, this is a deployment-breaking gap until a `[databases]` entry (or wildcard) is supplied. ### 3.4 Redis `redisProvisioner.ts` installs `redis-server`, enables it, and writes both `/etc/redis/redis.conf.d/zz-pg-switch.conf` and `/etc/redis/redis.conf` with a private-IP + loopback bind, `protected-mode yes`, the node port, `requirepass `, `save 3600 1`, maxmemory/policy `allkeys-lru`, no append-only file and daemonize on. It runs `ufw allow` for core and backup sources and restarts Redis with `redis-cli PING`. There is no `tls-port`, `tls-cert-file`, `tls-key-file`, `tls-ca-cert-file` or `tls-auth-clients` setting. Redis traffic is plaintext inside the private network. The generated `redis-client` certificate is unused. ### 3.5 Audit database `auditAndLogDbProvisioner.ts` installs PostgreSQL on `AUDIT_DB_NODE` when `AUDIT_DB_MANAGE_VIA_SSH` is true, applies a minimal PostgreSQL config (`listen_addresses='*'`, `wal_level=replica`, senders/slots), writes a `pg_hba` restricted to core and backup sources, restarts PostgreSQL, creates the audit role/database, and applies: - `pg_trgm`; - `audit_records` with `seq_no` identity, UUID primary key, actor/action/entity fields, before/after JSON, `prev_hash`, `row_hash`; - entity, actor, BRIN and trigram GIN indexes; - `forbid_audit_mutation()` and `trg_audit_immutable` on UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE; - least-privilege grants: `SELECT, INSERT` only for the audit writer, plus sequence usage and default privileges. The audit DDL is applied to the audit database. The `pg_hba` has the same `hostssl`-without-client-cert pattern as the core database. ### 3.6 Log database The log provisioner installs PostgreSQL on `LOG_DB_NODE` when `LOG_DB_MANAGE_VIA_SSH` is true and applies: - `attempt_step_logs` with a `(id, created_at)` primary key, partitioned by `RANGE (created_at)`; - `http_access_logs` with a `(id, created_at)` primary key, partitioned by `RANGE (created_at)`; - attempt/created indexes and BRIN indexes; - `ensure_log_partitions(months_ahead, retention_months)`, which creates missing monthly partitions and drops partitions older than the retention cutoff; - initial partitions six months ahead; - `GRANT SELECT, INSERT` only for the log writer; - `/etc/cron.d/pg-log-partitions` at `15 1 * * *` calling `ensure_log_partitions(6, )`. The retention function only drops partitions whose names match the monthly suffix pattern; it never drops the default partition or non-monthly tables. The log database `pg_hba` is restricted to core and backup sources and has no client-certificate requirement. ### 3.7 Backup engine provisioner `provisionBackupEngine()` installs: - `barman`, `zstd`, `lz4`, `brotli`, `xz-utils`, `rclone`, `curl`, `ca-certificates`; - WAL-G when `BACKUP_ENGINE_MODE=wal-g`, by downloading `wal-g-pg-ubuntu-20.04-amd64` from the GitHub "latest" release and chmod +x; - the `pgbackup` system user and `/var/lib/pg-backup`, log and cert directories; - `/etc/pg-backup/backup.env` from `backupDaemonEnv()`; - `/etc/pg-backup/wal-g.env` for the core target; - the systemd unit and `/etc/cron.d/pg-backup`; - `/usr/local/bin/pg-backup-daemon-trigger` and `/usr/local/bin/pg-backup-restore-drill`; - Barman configuration and `.pgpass` in Barman mode; - target reachability checks. Archive configuration: - WAL-G: writes `/etc/pg-backup/wal-g-core.env` on the primary and sets `archive_mode=on`, `archive_command` to `wal-g wal-push %p` with the core prefix, `restore_command` to `wal-g wal-fetch`, and `archive_timeout=60s`; restarts PostgreSQL. - Barman: sets `wal_level=replica`, `archive_mode=off`, creates the `barman` slot and uses `barman-wal-archive %p` from `streaming_archiver=on`. It writes `/etc/barman.conf` with a server section using the replication user, a `slot_name`, and `backup_method=postgres`. The same archive configuration is applied to the audit database when `AUDIT_DB_MANAGE_VIA_SSH` is true, with `archive_command` targeting the audit prefix/server. The provisioner also runs `verifyBackupTargetCommands()`: -- `rclone lsd --max-depth 1`; +- `curl -fsS /minio/health/live`; - an SSH `true` to the secondary target when configured; - a non-empty encryption key check. -The `rclone` check assumes the bucket string is a configured rclone remote or a path rclone understands; an S3 URL with no rclone configuration fails the deploy. +The MinIO health check verifies the local S3-compatible endpoint without requiring an rclone remote configuration. The systemd unit runs `bun run src/index.ts` as `pgbackup` with `EnvironmentFile=/etc/pg-backup/backup.env`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, `NoNewPrivileges=true`, and `ReadWritePaths` for the backup, log, catalog, cert, scratch and pgpass directories. ## 4. Contracts and invariants - PostgreSQL 18 is the only runtime database; `DB_ENGINE` is restricted to `postgresql`. - Application and replication roles use SCRAM passwords; replication slots are physical. - Replicas are initialized only when the data directory is empty. - Remote database connections use `hostssl` rules; loopback uses SCRAM without TLS. - The audit table is append-only at the trigger and grant level. - Log partitions are monthly; retention only affects matching monthly partitions. - Redis is bound to the private IP plus loopback and requires a password. - No storage provisioner writes database credentials to an edge host. - The journal partition cron is installed on the primary and must call an existing database function. - Backup archiving is configured on the primary/audit database, not on replicas. ## 5. Purpose and scope `pg-backup-daemon` is the backup and point-in-time-recovery control plane for the storage tier. It wraps WAL-G or Barman, owns the full/delta/drill schedule, keeps a local catalog, exposes an mTLS HTTP API and runs scratch restore plus ledger/audit invariant drills. It owns engine selection, scheduling, the catalog, the HTTP API, target/WAL health and drills. It does not own the PostgreSQL cluster, archive configuration (the provisioner does), the admin approval workflow (core does) or the admin UI. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The design calls for a Bun service that supports WAL-G on the database host and Barman on a dedicated backup host, streams WAL with compression and client-side encryption, takes weekly full and daily delta backups for core and audit, snapshots Redis, mirrors to an optional secondary vault, and runs a weekly scratch restore that verifies double-entry zero drift, sharded balance parity and the audit hash chain before signing and cleaning up. It exposes overview, trigger, policy, run and drill endpoints over mTLS to core, which surfaces them to the admin portal. Policy changes require core-side maker-checker. The historical design's Tripoli 03:00 and hourly Redis claims are superseded; the code uses UTC cron expressions and triggered Redis snapshots. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 Process lifecycle `src/index.ts` loads and validates the environment, creates a `SpawnCommandRunner`, creates the WAL-G/Barman engine, loads the catalog (or falls back to memory), builds a default policy, creates the drill runner, scheduler and server, starts the scheduler when enabled, and logs the listener/engine/scheduler state. SIGTERM/SIGINT stops the scheduler and server, waits up to 15 seconds for in-flight work and exits. ### 3.2 HTTP server and mTLS `src/server.ts` uses `Bun.serve` with a JSON handler: | Method | Path | Purpose | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | GET | `/health` | Liveness, engine mode and version. Does not run engine health checks. | | GET | `/v1/overview` | Engine health, WAL lag, targets, schedule/policy, scheduler state, recent backups and drills. | | POST | `/v1/backups/trigger` | Validates `{ target, kind }`, queues a run and returns 202. | | PUT | `/v1/policy` | Persists cron/retention/lag and returns the policy. | | GET | `/v1/runs`, `/v1/drills` | Recent records with `limit` 1-500. | | POST | `/v1/drills/run` | Queues a drill and returns 202. | Bodies are capped at 256 KiB. Responses use `cache-control: no-store` and recursively redact credential-shaped keys/values. `HttpError` becomes a JSON envelope; unexpected errors become a generic 500 with a request id. `loadTlsOptions()` returns plain HTTP only when `BACKUP_ALLOW_INSECURE_HTTP=true`. Otherwise it requires the server certificate, key and CA and sets `requestCert: true`, `rejectUnauthorized: true`. The daemon verifies the client chain but does not inspect the client CN; any CA-signed client can call every route. Core presents `backup-client`. ### 3.3 Engines `createBackupEngine()` selects `WalGEngine` or `BarmanEngine`. **WAL-G**: - `triggerBackup("all", kind)` expands to `postgres_core`, `audit_db` and, when `REDIS_URL` is set, `redis`; - refuses `audit_db` when `PG_AUDIT_DATA_DIR` is empty; - runs `wal-g backup-push ` for full, `--delta` for delta; - verifies the bucket with `wal-g st ls `; - mirrors with `rclone sync` or `rsync -a --delete` when a secondary target exists; - `prune("all","full")` runs `wal-g delete retain FULL --confirm`; delta pruning is a no-op; - lists with `wal-g backup-list --json`; `recover()` fetches the latest base backup and returns a recovery fragment; - Redis backup runs `BGSAVE`, `redis-cli --rdb ` and `rclone copyto /redis/dump.rdb`, then removes the temp file. Health checks the S3 target with `wal-g st ls`, PostgreSQL with `psql SELECT 1`, optional secondary/Redis, WAL lag from the first replica or primary, and archive lag/bytes from `pg_stat_archiver`. It is healthy when every target passes and archive lag is within `BACKUP_ALERT_LAG_SECONDS`. **Barman**: - `triggerBackup` expands `all` the same way (including audit), runs `barman check`, `barman backup`/`--incremental`, then `barman-cloud-backup`; it reports only `primary-s3`, with no secondary mirror; - lists with `barman list-backup`; `recover()` picks the latest and runs `barman recover --target-time`; `prune()` is a no-op because Barman applies server-side retention. Barman health runs `barman check` for core and audit, checks S3 with the **WAL-G** `st ls` command, checks PostgreSQL, and adds optional secondary/Redis. Barman health therefore requires WAL-G and does not prove Barman's cloud/retention path. This document does not claim complete Barman health. ### 3.4 Scheduler `src/scheduler.ts` uses a strict five-field cron parser (no macros or seconds), computes the next full/delta/drill slots, ticks every `SCHEDULER_TICK_MS` (default 30 seconds), reloads policy from the catalog, skips a due job when another job is running, records runs as `QUEUED`/`RUNNING`/`PASSED`/`FAILED`, reserves unique ids, attempts a full prune after a successful full backup, and records signed drill reports. A policy update through `PUT /v1/policy` takes effect on the next tick without a restart. ### 3.5 Catalog `src/catalogStore.ts` stores runs, drills and policy in one JSON file (`BACKUP_CATALOG_PATH`), writes atomically via temp file + rename, serializes writes, keeps at most 500 runs and 100 drills, validates on load, falls back to in-memory operation when unwritable or corrupt, and reports the persistence error. The catalog is not encrypted and is not backed up by the daemon. ### 3.6 Restore drill `src/restoreDrillRunner.ts`: 1. Sets `targetTime = now - 5 minutes` and stops/removes prior scratch clusters. 2. Calls `engine.recover()` for `postgres_core` and `audit_db`. 3. Refuses `initdb` over a failed restore unless the engine explicitly reports an initialized empty directory. 4. Writes `recovery.conf` into `postgresql.auto.conf`, creates `recovery.signal`, and starts both clusters on the configured ports over loopback. 5. Runs the double-entry zero-drift query, the sharded-balance parity query and the audit hash-chain query. 6. Builds a report with status, duration, target time, replayed LSN, drift, mismatch counts, broken links and per-check details. 7. Signs it with HMAC-SHA256 using `BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX`. 8. Stops and removes both scratch clusters in `finally`. A failed restore, start or check still produces a signed `FAILED` report through the scheduler or HTTP path. The drill requires an audit recovery target; without an audit database or `PG_AUDIT_DATA_DIR`, the audit recovery fails and the drill fails. ### 3.7 Core and admin integration `core-back/lib/storageEngine/backupControlClient.ts` builds a TLS 1.3 keep-alive agent with the internal CA and `backup-client` cert/key and calls overview/health/trigger/drill/policy/runs/drills. `core-back/api/internal/backups.ts`: - `GET /overview` requires `security:read` or `gateway:read`, fetches daemon health and upserts runs/drills with `Promise.allSettled`; - `POST /trigger` and `POST /drill` require `security:write`, require a configured daemon, call it and insert a local queued row; - `PUT /policy` requires `security:write`; without `approvalRequestId` it creates a `BACKUP_POLICY` approval (`PENDING_REVIEW`, 7-day expiry) and returns 202; with an id it checks subject type, state and maker != checker, sends the **approved payload** to the daemon, marks the approval `EXECUTED`, bumps the base version and writes an audit record; - `GET /catalog` returns local runs/drills. `admin-back/api/protected/backups.ts` applies `security:read`/`security:write` at the edge, forwards overview/trigger/drill/policy and relays core status. The daemon's own `PUT /v1/policy` has no maker-checker, so a direct mTLS client can bypass the core approval workflow. ### 3.8 Systemd and source deployment `backupEngineProvisioner.ts` writes `/etc/systemd/system/pg-backup-daemon.service`: `User/Group=pgbackup`, `WorkingDirectory=/opt/pg-backup-daemon`, `EnvironmentFile=/etc/pg-backup/backup.env`, `ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/bun run src/index.ts`, `Restart=always`, `RestartSec=3`, `LimitNOFILE=65536`, `NoNewPrivileges=true`, `ProtectSystem=strict`, and `ReadWritePaths` for backup, log, catalog, cert, scratch and pgpass directories. `deploy.ts` copies `deploy/backup-daemon` to `/opt/pg-backup-daemon` with rsync `--delete`, excludes `node_modules`, `.git`, `dist`, `test`, `*.log` and `.env`, chowns to `pgbackup`, runs `bun install --frozen-lockfile` as `pgbackup`, and enables/restarts the unit. The provisioner writes `/etc/cron.d/pg-backup`: when the scheduler is enabled only a comment; otherwise full/delta trigger lines as `pgbackup` and the drill script as root. `/usr/local/bin/pg-backup-restore-drill` restores core and checks double-entry only; it is narrower than the in-process drill. ## 4. Contracts and invariants - The daemon listens over mTLS by default and refuses plain HTTP unless explicitly allowed for development. - Core presents a CA-signed `backup-client` certificate; the daemon does not authorize a CN per route. - Trigger and drill return 202 and complete asynchronously; the catalog is the state store. - Scheduled jobs do not overlap; HTTP triggers are not globally serialized. - Catalog writes are atomic; a failed write does not crash the daemon. - Secrets are redacted from responses and error messages. - Full backups are followed by a best-effort prune; delta pruning is non-destructive. - Audit backups require `PG_AUDIT_DATA_DIR`; the daemon never substitutes the core data directory. - Drills restore core and audit, check three invariants, sign the report and always clean up scratch clusters. - Policy changes through core require maker-checker; the daemon endpoint itself does not. ## 5. Data / API / config / deployment surface | Group | Keys | | :--- | :--- | | Engine/encryption | `BACKUP_ENGINE_MODE`, `BACKUP_COMPRESSION`, `BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX`, `BACKUP_ALLOW_INSECURE_HTTP`, `BACKUP_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS` | | S3/secondary | `BACKUP_PRIMARY_S3_ENDPOINT`, `BACKUP_PRIMARY_S3_BUCKET`, `BACKUP_PRIMARY_S3_ACCESS_KEY`, `BACKUP_PRIMARY_S3_SECRET_KEY`, `BACKUP_CORE_S3_PREFIX`, `BACKUP_AUDIT_S3_PREFIX`, `BACKUP_SECONDARY_SSH_TARGET` | | Schedule/retention | `BACKUP_FULL_CRON`, `BACKUP_DELTA_CRON`, `BACKUP_DRILL_CRON`, `BACKUP_RETENTION_FULL_COUNT`, `BACKUP_RETENTION_WAL_DAYS`, `BACKUP_ALERT_LAG_SECONDS`, `SCHEDULER_ENABLED`, `SCHEDULER_TICK_MS` | | Listener/mTLS | `BACKUP_DAEMON_PORT`, `BACKUP_DAEMON_BIND_HOST`, `BACKUP_DAEMON_CERT_PATH`, `BACKUP_DAEMON_KEY_PATH`, `BACKUP_DAEMON_CA_CERT_PATH` | | PostgreSQL | `PG_PRIMARY_HOST`, `PG_PRIMARY_PORT`, `PG_PRIMARY_USER`, `PG_PRIMARY_PASSWORD`, `PG_PRIMARY_DB_NAME`, `PG_AUDIT_DB_NAME`, `PG_REPLICA_NODES`, `PG_DATA_DIR`, `PG_AUDIT_DATA_DIR`, `PG_BIN_DIR` | | Catalog/scratch | `BACKUP_CATALOG_PATH`, `BACKUP_SCRATCH_DIR`, `BACKUP_SCRATCH_PORT`, `BACKUP_SCRATCH_AUDIT_DIR`, `BACKUP_SCRATCH_AUDIT_PORT`, `PGPASSFILE` | | Binaries | `WALG_BIN`, `BARMAN_BIN`, `BARMAN_CLOUD_BIN`, `BARMAN_SERVER`, `BARMAN_AUDIT_SERVER` | | Redis | `REDIS_URL`, `REDIS_CLI_BIN` | `BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX` must be hex, at least 16 bytes and even length; the deploy requires exactly 64 hex characters. `backup.env.example` is a local/troubleshooting reference; a deployment generates `/etc/pg-backup/backup.env` from `deploy.env`. ## 6. Operational usage ```bash cd deploy/backup-daemon bun install bun run start bun test bun run typecheck ``` On a deployed host, use `systemctl status pg-backup-daemon`, `journalctl -u pg-backup-daemon`, and a curl request with `internal-ca.crt`, `backup-client.crt` and `backup-client.key` to `/v1/overview`. Admin triggers and policy changes go through core; policy changes require a second user. ## 7. Status and deviations ### Implemented - WAL-G/Barman full/delta backup, listing, restore, verification and cloud copy. - Optional Redis snapshot. - S3 primary and optional secondary mirror for WAL-G. - In-process cron scheduler with policy reload and overlap skipping. - Atomic JSON catalog with in-memory fallback. - Core+audit drill with double-entry, balance parity and audit-chain checks and HMAC-signed reports. - mTLS server with client-certificate verification and secret redaction. - Core proxy/approval integration and admin edge routes. - Provisioner-generated env, systemd unit, cron and source deployment. ### Partial - Barman health depends on WAL-G for the S3 target. - No per-CN daemon authorization. - The shell drill is narrower than the in-process drill. - The catalog is one unencrypted JSON file with count-based retention. ### Missing / deferred - Log-database backup target. - HTTP trigger serialization/backpressure. - Automatic certificate/key ownership correction for `pgbackup`. - Catalog backup and encryption. - A verify-only restore mode. ### Known bugs / risks - `all` includes `audit_db` without checking whether audit is configured; WAL-G needs `PG_AUDIT_DATA_DIR` and Barman needs an audit server. - A Barman-only installation reports the primary S3 target unhealthy because health uses WAL-G. - The backup cert/key may be root-owned and unreadable by `pgbackup`, preventing mTLS startup and failing the deploy probe. - Any CA-signed certificate can call the policy endpoint directly and bypass maker-checker. - Concurrent HTTP triggers are not serialized. - The drill requires audit recovery even for a core-only intent. - An interrupted cleanup can leave scratch clusters/directories. - The catalog may contain host/run metadata and is not encrypted. ## 8. Purpose and scope This part documents the end-to-end verification performed by the deploy engine, the release layout used for rollback, the rollback procedure and its limits, common failure modes and the security constraints around recovery. It does not own the application health payloads, the storage provisioners or the backup daemon's internal drill. It records how deployment observes them and what an operator can safely do when something fails. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The design requires verification stronger than "the process is running": - every core node answers `/health` over mTLS; - every edge host completes a mutually authenticated TLS 1.3 handshake with a core node on its own channel; - every edge backend and public vhost answers; - PostgreSQL primary/replicas, PgBouncer, Redis, audit/log databases and the backup daemon are reachable; - a failed rolling batch stops the deploy, leaving the previous release on disk for rollback; - releases are immutable and `current` is a symlink, so rollback is a pointer change; - recovery from a bad deploy is possible without rebuilding from scratch. The design describes zero-downtime rolling updates. The code provides rolling batches with health gates but not connection draining or automatic compensation. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 Core health `GET /health` in `core-back/index.ts`: - is reachable without authentication (but the TLS listener still requires a client certificate); - reads the background-job queue health when workers are enabled; - returns `msg: "OK"`, `status: "ok"` when workers are enabled, the queue is reachable and the oldest job is below the threshold; - returns `msg: "DEGRADED"`, `status: "degraded"` when workers are disabled, the queue cannot be inspected, or the oldest queued job exceeds the threshold; - stays reachable when the database cannot be read, with `queue.degraded=true` and `QUEUE_HEALTH_UNAVAILABLE`. `probeCoreHealth()` and `probeCoreService()` run on the core host and use `curl` with the CA and the core certificate as both server and client material. They pass when the body contains `"msg":"OK"` or the literal `OK`. A degraded core fails the probe. The core certificate also carries clientAuth so this loopback probe can present it. ### 3.2 Edge health Each edge `GET /health` is unauthenticated and returns `{ status: "ok", service, uptime }`. It does not query core, the database or any dependency. `probeEdgeService()` and `probeEdgeBackend()` call this endpoint over `http://127.0.0.1:/health` with a 10-second timeout. They pass on `"status":"ok"` or the literal `ok`. A running edge with a broken core pool therefore passes its local health check; core/SAN/certificate problems are caught only by the cross-host probe or final verification, so the rolling batch gate for edges is liveness, not readiness. ### 3.3 Edge-to-core mTLS `probeEdgeToCore()` runs on each edge host with that host's own client certificate: - for each of `admin`, `merchant`, `checkout` present on the host; - for every derived core URL; - calls `/internal//health` with `--cacert`, `--cert` and `--key`. The core channel health routes return `{ status: "ok", channel: "" }` after the CN guard. The probe passes on `ok` or the channel marker. This is the critical cross-host check. It verifies: - DNS/route/reachability to every core node; - TLS 1.3 handshake and CA trust; - the server SAN contains the core private IP; - the client certificate is accepted; - the CN matches the channel; - the core process is up. It does not verify business authorization, database writes or a specific gateway flow. ### 3.4 Public and Fake Rails vhosts `probePublicVhost()` runs on the edge host and probes every Nginx site except the admin LAN site: - scheme from the site's `ssl` flag; - `-k` for self-signed certificates; - `/health` first, then `/` with an HTTP status fallback; - passes when any non-empty body is returned. Fake Rails gets backend and vhost `/health` probes, with `-k` when SSL is enabled. The admin LAN vhost is covered by the edge backend probe; the deploy does not probe it through Nginx. ### 3.5 Storage and backup probes `probeStorage()` includes: | Target | Probe | | :--- | :--- | | PostgreSQL primary | `pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -p ` and `psql SELECT 1` with the application user/password. | | PostgreSQL replicas | Same two probes per replica. | | PgBouncer | `psql SELECT 1` on `PGBOUNCER_PORT` with the application user/password. | | Redis | `REDISCLI_AUTH= redis-cli -h 127.0.0.1 -p PING`, expecting `PONG`. | | Audit DB | `psql SELECT 1` with the audit user/password. | | Log DB | `psql SELECT 1` with the log user/password. | | Backup daemon | HTTPS `/health` with the CA and the `backup-daemon` certificate/key, expecting `"status":"ok"` or `ok`. | The backup probe uses the daemon's server certificate (which also has clientAuth) rather than `backup-client`. It depends on the daemon being able to read its own 0600 key; if the key is root-owned and the daemon runs as `pgbackup`, the probe fails. ### 3.6 Verification aggregation `verifyDeployment()`: - probes every core node; - probes each Fake Rails host; - for each edge host, probes the edge backends, the edge-to-core handshake for every core URL and the public vhosts; - appends storage probes; - returns `{ ok, results }`. `deploy.ts` prints `PASS`/`FAIL` per result and throws if any result fails. The error message says the previous release is still on disk. It does not switch back automatically. `--skip-verify` and `--dry-run` skip the step. ### 3.7 Rolling batch gates For steps 6-10, after deploying every unit in a batch: - core units use `probeCoreService()`: loopback mTLS `/health` on that service port; - edge units use `probeEdgeService()`: loopback HTTP `/health`. A failed probe throws immediately. The cross-host mTLS, public vhost and storage checks run only in step 12 after all roles are deployed. This means a batch can be declared healthy while the edge cannot reach core, or while the core cannot reach the database. The final verification is the real gate. ### 3.8 Release layout ```text / ├── releases// │ ├── / # source, dependencies, .env symlink │ └── /dist/ # edge hosts ├── shared/ │ ├── .env # 0600 │ ├── certs/ │ ├── backups/ │ ├── pm2/.config.cjs │ └── data/ └── current -> releases/ ``` - Releases are immutable. - `current` is the only release pointer. - Nginx static roots use `/current//dist`. - The inline PM2 ecosystem uses an **absolute** `cwd` and script path inside ``, not the `current` symlink. - Environment and certificate paths in the service env are absolute after `absoluteEnv()`. The PM2 detail matters for rollback: changing `current` changes Nginx static assets immediately, but a `pm2 restart ` reuses the absolute script/cwd from the process's original start. It does not automatically follow the new symlink. ## 4. Contracts and invariants - Verification runs after all deployments and before the deploy is declared successful. - Any failed probe aborts the run with a non-zero exit. - A core `/health` response of `DEGRADED` is a failure. - Edge `/health` success is not a readiness guarantee for core connectivity. - A batch is not a full verification; step 12 is. - `KEEP_RELEASES` controls how many release directories remain; pruning happens inside `deployService`. - Rollback does not revert database migrations or restore the pre-migration dump. ## 5. Data / API / config / deployment surface ### Verification commands - `curl --cacert ... --cert ... --key ... https://127.0.0.1:/health` - `curl http://127.0.0.1:/health` - `curl ... https://:/internal//health` - `curl -k https://127.0.0.1:/health` for self-signed public vhosts - `pg_isready`, `psql SELECT 1`, `redis-cli PING` ### Release paths | Role | Default remote directory | | :--- | :--- | | core | `/var/www/pg-core` | | admin | `/var/www/pg-admin` | | merchant | `/var/www/pg-merchant` | | checkout | `/var/www/pg-checkout` | | Fake Rails | `/var/www/pg-fake-rails` | ### Flags | Flag | Effect on verification/recovery | | :--- | :--- | | `--skip-verify` | Skips step 12. | | `--dry-run` | Prints probes as commands, executes none. | | `--keep=` | Changes how many releases remain for rollback. | | `--fresh` | Bootstraps hosts; no pre-migration dump. | ## 6. Operational usage ### Normal verification Run the deploy without `--skip-verify`. The output lists every PASS/FAIL with host and check. Treat any FAIL as a release blocker even if the process started. ### Manual rollback of one host 1. List releases: ```bash ssh ls -1dt /var/www/pg-/releases/*/ ``` -2. Choose the previous timestamp and confirm its `shared` environment is compatible. The release-specific app directory has an `.env` symlink to `/shared/.env`; the shared env is current, not historical. If the env changed, the old code may not match it. +2. Choose the previous timestamp and confirm its `shared` environment is compatible. The release-specific app directory has an `.env` symlink to `/shared/.env` (or `shared/.env.` on a multi-node tier); the shared env is current, not historical. If the env changed, the old code may not match it. 3. Stop and restart the service from the target release, not with `pm2 restart`: ```bash TARGET=/var/www/pg-/releases/ ln -sfn "$TARGET" /var/www/pg-/current "$HOME/.bun/bin/pm2" delete || true cd "$TARGET/" PATH="$HOME/.bun/bin:/usr/local/bin:$PATH" pm2 start pm2-compatible-start.js --name --interpreter /usr/local/bin/bun --update-env "$HOME/.bun/bin/pm2" save ``` The shared PM2 config is regenerated on every deploy and points at the latest release. A plain `pm2 restart` is not sufficient because it reuses the absolute path of the currently running release. Re-running the deploy from the previous commit is the cleanest whole-role rollback. 4. Nginx static files follow `current` immediately; verify the vhost after the switch. 5. Re-run verification for that host or role. ### Rollback of the whole deployment The reliable path is to check out the previous commit and re-run `./deploy/deploy.sh --update --only=`. Releases are immutable, but the shared `.env`, PM2 config and Nginx config are rewritten by the new run. ### Database recovery The pre-migration dump is a `pg_dump -Fc` file in `/shared/backups/pre-migrate-.dump`. It is not restored automatically. Recovery requires an operator decision, a target database and a compatible schema. Migrations are forward-only; restoring an old code release against a migrated schema can fail. ### Backup drill recovery Use the backup daemon's `/v1/drills/run` or the admin backup control to verify a restore. The drill restores into scratch directories and removes them; it does not restore the live database. ### Common failures | Symptom | Likely cause | | :--- | :--- | | `SSH key ... does not exist` | The `*_SSH_KEY_PATH` is wrong or missing on the workstation. | | `core /health (mTLS) FAIL` | Core did not start, DB credentials are wrong, or workers/queue are degraded. | | `mTLS -> core /internal/... FAIL` | Wrong client CN/cert, core SAN missing the target IP, or core down. | | `backup-daemon /health FAIL` | Certificate ownership, missing S3/Barman prerequisite, or daemon config. | | Pre-migration dump fails | `pg_dump` is absent on the core host or the primary is unreachable. | | PgBouncer connection fails | No `[databases]` mapping in the generated `pgbouncer.ini`. | ### Security notes - Keep `deploy.env` at 0600 and `deploy/.certs` private; the CA key never leaves the workstation. Secrets are streamed over SSH stdin, but the pre-migration `PGPASSWORD` is embedded in the verbose command and may appear in logs. - The core port is private and mTLS-only; edge hosts never receive `DATABASE_URL` or `KMS_MASTER_KEY`. - Protect the edge host and make the backup key readable by `pgbackup`. - The deploy's `--skip-verify` is not a security control and should not be used for production acceptance. ## 7. Status and deviations ### Implemented - Core loopback mTLS health. - Edge local health. - Edge-to-core mTLS channel health across every core URL. - Public merchant/checkout vhost probes. - Fake Rails backend and vhost probes. - PostgreSQL, PgBouncer, Redis, audit/log and backup-daemon probes. - Batch-level health gate and final fail-fast verification. - Immutable release layout and `current` pointer. - Pre-migration dump artifact. ### Partial - Batch gates are liveness-only for edges and do not test cross-host mTLS. - The guide's symlink + `pm2 restart` rollback is incomplete for backend processes. ### Missing / deferred - Automatic rollback on a failed batch or failed verification. - Connection draining and a zero-downtime single-node switch. - Blue/green or canary routing. - Database down-migrations or an automated point-in-time restore path. - Post-deploy alerting or a health history. ### Known bugs, risks and limits - A single-node service has a restart gap; a core restart can make all edges fail for the cooldown window. - A failed verification leaves the new release as `current` on every deployed host. - `--skip-verify` can report success with a broken core/edge path. - Shared `.env` is not versioned per release; backup probe failures can be cert ownership. ## 8. Purpose and scope This part defines how the monorepo is verified: the test philosophy, the gate progression, database and Redis expectations, the zero-tautology rule, and which suites currently skip, mock or fail to exist. It does not list every test file or count (see `testing.suites`), the fixture and live-stack wiring (see `testing.fixtures`) or the benchmark gates (see `testing.benchmarks`). Per-workspace test evidence is repeated in each workspace part. ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The exhaustive test plan was written to prevent a small happy-path suite from missing intersection defects: rounding remainders, confirmation races, SSRF notations, JSX binding failures and seeded historical attempts that fail when an operator clicks Inquire or Refund. Its non-negotiable rules are: 1. **Zero-tautology.** Every test must invoke the real production module, real Express router, real PostgreSQL constraint or rendered Vue DOM. `expect(true).toBe(true)` and mock-against-mock tests are forbidden. 2. **Combinatorial and property-based generation.** Use data-driven Cartesian products and a seeded PRNG so permutations are named and reproducible. 3. **Continuous double-entry invariant.** Every database suite runs the ledger invariant after writes and requires `drift === "0.0000"`. 4. **Fail-fast gate progression.** Implement and pass suites `T-EX-01` through `T-EX-11` in order; fix production defects before advancing. 5. **Fail loudly when the environment is absent.** A suite that needs PostgreSQL, Redis or a live host either skips with a named reason or fails; it must not silently pass against a stub. The plan targets 38,500 or more assertions across eleven suites, plus a unified runner. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 Test roots | Root | Runner | Primary scope | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `core-back/test` | `bun test` | Unit, route, engine, ledger, storage, exhaustive | | `admin-back/test` | `bun test` | Edge contract, mTLS, env isolation, admin surface | | `merchant-back/test` | `bun test` | Edge contract, forwarding, KYB/external surface | | `checkout-back/test` | `bun test` | Zero-trust checkout, mTLS, env isolation | | `fake-rails-back/test` | `bun test` | Real Express app over SQLite | | `deploy/test` | `bun test` | Config, host planning, PKI, firewall, pipeline | | `deploy/backup-daemon/test` | `bun test` | Backup engine, catalog, scheduler, restore drill | | `tests/e2e` | Playwright | Portal geometry, auth, dialogs, mocked API surface | | `tests/e2e-live` | Playwright | Deployed-stack smoke journeys | | `tests/unit` | Vitest | Frontend utility and authority helpers | `tests/run-playwright.sh` is the Playwright wrapper used by local runs. `scripts/run-exhaustive-suite.sh` is the master gate runner and forces one Bun worker for database suites. ### 3.2 The zero-tautology rule in practice The core exhaustive suites are structurally honest about production code: - `core-back/test/exhaustive/_harness.ts` drives real Prisma clients, real schema files and real production services. It says explicitly that it only provisions fixtures and reads metadata. - `_dbFactory.ts` builds rows from the real `schema.prisma` and live catalog; it does not replace constraints. - Suite 01 reads `information_schema`, `pg_catalog`, `pg_indexes` and real constraint metadata. - Suite 02 invokes `LedgerPoster.validateTemplate` and real `buildLedgerTemplate` output. - Suite 03 invokes the real transform, canonicalisation, signing and Vault code. - Suite 04 invokes `DynamicRailEngine` through `_engineHarness.ts`, not the live fake-rails HTTP tier. - Suite 05 drives real authority/session helpers and the real list-query parser. - Suite 06 uses live PostgreSQL concurrency primitives. - Suite 07 uses real parsers, KYB sniffers, AML rules and go-live validators. - Suite 08 uses real SSRF/URL/response-hardening helpers. The UI and edge tests are weaker: - `tests/e2e/fixtures.ts` `mockApi()` fulfills every `/api/v1/**` call with `{}` or a small fixture. The exhaustive surface tests only assert rendering, layout, direction and theme. - Auth tests intercept the login endpoint and return a fixture session; they assert the shape of the posted body, not a real login. - The fake-rails surface test mocks every `/portal-api/**` and only visits `/login`. - `tests/unit` tests real frontend utility functions, not the full pages. These are useful regression tests, but they do not satisfy the design's zero-tautology claim for UI behaviour. ### 3.3 Gate progression `scripts/run-exhaustive-suite.sh` implements this sequence: | Gate | Command target | Notes | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `T-EX-01` | `core-back/test/exhaustive/01-schema` | Live PostgreSQL required for most tests | | `T-EX-02` | `core-back/test/exhaustive/02-ledger` | Some tests are pure; checkpoints need PostgreSQL | | `T-EX-03` | `core-back/test/exhaustive/03-transforms-crypto` | Pure | | `T-EX-04` | `core-back/test/exhaustive/04-rail-engine` | Pure engine harness | | `T-EX-05` | core plus all edge backends plus fake rails plus deploy | Mixed Bun suites | | `T-EX-06` | `core-back/test/exhaustive/06-concurrency` | Live PostgreSQL | | `T-EX-07` | `core-back/test/exhaustive/07-workflows` | Mostly pure | | `T-EX-08` | `core-back/test/exhaustive/08-security-edge` | Pure | | `T-EX-09` | `core-back/test/storage-engine`, `test/backup-admin`, backup daemon | There is no `09-storage-backup` directory | | `T-EX-09b` | `tests` unit plus exhaustive Playwright | Mocked UI | | `T-EX-10` | `10-seeder-and-deploy` plus optional cross-service journeys | Journeys skip without `E2E_LIVE=1` | | Final | `core-back bun test` | Full regression | The design's numbering differs from the runner: the runner calls the UI matrix `T-EX-09b` and the seeder/deploy suite `T-EX-10`, while the design calls them Suite 10 and Suite 11. ### 3.4 Database provisioning There is no single test database configuration. The suites use these variables: | Variable | Default | Used by | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `DATABASE_URL` | `postgresql://postgres@127.0.0.1:55432/payment_gateway_monolith_test` | `test/setup.ts`, storage helpers, postgres payment test | | `POSTGRES_TEST_DATABASE_URL` | fallback | Postgres payment test, exhaustive harness fallback | | `EXHAUSTIVE_DATABASE_URL` | fallback to `POSTGRES_TEST_DATABASE_URL` | Exhaustive harness | | `STORAGE_TEST_DATABASE_URL` | fallback to `DATABASE_URL` | Storage-engine helpers | | `STORAGE_TEST_REDIS_URL` | `redis://127.0.0.1:56379` | Cache/velocity and performance | | `REDIS_URL` | `redis://127.0.0.1:56379` | Storage performance and production adapters | The expected local server is PostgreSQL 18 on port 55432 and Redis on 56379, not the default service ports. The test database must already be migrated (`bun run migrate-deploy`) before the DB-backed suites run. `_harness.ts` uses a dedicated Prisma client so it does not share the cached application client. The storage helpers create dedicated schemas or sandboxes with `search_path` so files can run in parallel. `bun test --parallel=1` is mandatory for the database suites in the runner because they share one database and the invariant hook. ### 3.5 Double-entry invariant `_harness.ts` exposes `verifyInvariant()` and `assertZeroDrift()`, which wrap the production `InvariantVerifier`. Suite 02 and the storage write-path suites use it after batches. A non-zero drift throws with left/right sides and drift printed. The invariant hook is not applied to every file that touches the database. The runner enforces one worker, but not a universal `afterEach` hook. ### 3.6 Skipping behaviour Current named skips: - `describeDatabase` becomes `describe.skip` when `SELECT 1` fails against the storage database. - `describeRedis` becomes `describe.skip` when the Redis connection or `PING` fails. - Storage files register a `test.skip("... requires the live database")` placeholder so a skipped file is still visible. - `core-back/test/e2e/postgres-payment.test.ts` uses `test.skipIf(!reachable)` for every payment test. - `write-path.integration.test.ts`, `uow.test.ts`, `ledger-shards.test.ts`, `audit-chain.test.ts`, `outbox-workers.test.ts`, `engine-factory.test.ts` and `performance/*.test.ts` have explicit skips. - `tests/e2e/exhaustive/full-platform-lifecycle-journeys.spec.ts` skips unless `E2E_LIVE=1`. - The link-journey test also skips unless `E2E_LINK_KEY` is set. - `tests/e2e-live/live.spec.ts` has no skip guard; it fails if the deployed host is unreachable. No suite currently sets a CI fail-on-skip policy. A run can be green with most DB or live coverage skipped. ### 3.7 Mocked surfaces | Surface | Mocking approach | Consequence | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Admin UI | `mockApi()` intercepts every `/api/v1/**` call | No real permissions, validation or data flow | | Merchant UI | Same | Same | | Checkout UI | Route intercepts `/api/v1/pay/**` | No real payment state machine | | Fake-rails UI | Route intercepts `/portal-api/**` and `/hosted/**` | Only login geometry is tested | | Login flows | Route intercept returns fixture session | Body-shape assertions only | | Edge BFF tests | Real Express routers with fake core clients in places | Contract coverage, not live mTLS | | Engine suite 04 | In-process harness with scripted step results | Deterministic and broad, not live fake-rails | | Seeder safety | Fake Prisma objects and stubbed handshake | Gate logic only | ## 4. Contracts and invariants 1. **A test that asserts only on a stub is not acceptance evidence.** Behaviour claims need a real module or live service. 2. **A skipped DB suite is not a passing DB suite.** Reports must name the skip reason. 3. **The test database is disposable.** Tests must not depend on rows left by another file; use unique references and clean up. 4. **Money invariants are checked after database writes.** Any suite that posts ledger entries must verify zero drift. 5. **Seeded PRNGs must be fixed and named.** A failure must be reproducible from the printed seed. 6. **Live credentials belong in the environment, not in source.** This invariant is currently violated by `tests/e2e-live/live.spec.ts`. 7. **The runner must fail when a required gate fails.** It currently does so for command failures, but not for skips. ## 5. Purpose and scope This part documents the performance measurements that actually exist, the thresholds they enforce, the runner they use, and the missing benchmarks needed to support the platform's scaling and restore claims. It covers storage write-path, storage primitives, outbox, shard reads, audit-chain, Redis velocity and the backup/restore test surface. It does not cover correctness suites (`testing.suites`) or fixtures (`testing.fixtures`). ## 2. Design intent (extracted and synthesized from ./design) The storage design targets: - 50 million to 500 million+ financial records. - 1,000+ sustained transactions per second. - Sub-5 ms read latency. - Horizontal scaling from one to N nodes per tier. - LSN-aware replica reads with primary fallback. - 16-way GL shard locking without hot-row deadlocks. - A SHA-256 audit chain and a non-blocking log sink. - Backup/restore drills that verify double-entry zero drift, shard parity and audit-chain integrity. The exhaustive plan's Suite 09 asks for about 900 tests covering unit-of-work atomicity, shard concurrency, LSN routing, Redis velocity, audit/log databases, backup control and a scratch restore drill. The plan requires tests that need a replica or daemon to skip explicitly, not pass silently. ## 3. As-built architecture ### 3.1 Runner `scripts/run-benchmarks.sh`: - Requires `DATABASE_URL`, `POSTGRES_TEST_DATABASE_URL` or `STORAGE_TEST_DATABASE_URL`; exits 2 otherwise. - Optionally honours `BENCHMARK_FILTER`. - Runs `bun test test/storage-engine/performance` (or filtered). - Runs `bun test test/storage-engine` as a full regression. - Runs `bun test test/backup-admin`. - Does **not** run the backup daemon, the frontend, the seeder, search or the fake rails tier. - Does **not** accept a Redis URL argument; Redis is read from `STORAGE_TEST_REDIS_URL` (default 56379). The script prints p50/p95 where the tests do and summarizes the result. It does not compare against a stored baseline, fail on regression beyond the hard-coded bounds, or persist a report. ### 3.2 Write-path benchmark `core-back/test/storage-engine/performance/write-path-benchmark.test.ts` runs only with a reachable PostgreSQL: | Test | Assertion | Reported value | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | 300 transactional audit writes with `audit_outbox` | Under 10 s | `[benchmark] 300 writeAudit (audit_log + audit_outbox)` | | Shard balance reads for a 16-shard account, 120 posts, 50 samples | p95 under 25 ms | `[benchmark] shard balance read p95 (two accounts)` | It uses real `writeAudit`, `createLedgerPoster` and `loadShardBalanceRows`. It cleans audit rows and ledger data in `finally`. ### 3.3 Storage primitive performance `core-back/test/storage-engine/performance/storage-performance.test.ts` has a pure section that runs without a database: | Test | Assertion | Reported value | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `compareLsn` 1,000,000 operations | Median under 1,000 ms | `[perf] compareLsn 1M median` | | `uuidv7` 100,000 ids | Median under 2,000 ms | `[perf] uuidv7 100k median` | | `stableJson` 10,000 rows | Median under 2,000 ms | `[perf] stableJson 10k median` | | Memory cache sliding-window evaluation 10,000 times | Median under 2,000 ms | `[perf] memory velocity 10k median` | | Read-store routing selection 100,000 times with 3 fake replicas | Median under 1,000 ms | `[perf] read routing 100k median` | The read-routing test uses empty client objects. It measures selection arithmetic, not a database read or replica network hop. ### 3.4 PostgreSQL storage performance With a reachable database, the same file measures: | Test | Assertion | Reported value | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | 500 sequential unit-of-work transactions with outbox and audit | Under 10 s | `[perf] UoW 500 sequential` | | 50 concurrent unit-of-work transactions | p95 under 500 ms | `[perf] UoW 50 concurrent p95` | | Outbox drain of 1,000 events | Under 5 s | `[perf] outbox drain 1000` | | 16 shard rows load plus EXPLAIN | Median under 50 ms and no sequential scan | `[perf] shard 16-row query median` | | 1,000-row audit hash-chain append plus verification | Under 5 s | `[perf] audit 1000 append+verify` | The outbox test inserts 1,000 rows in four raw batches and runs `OutboxRelayWorker.drain()`. The shard test runs `EXPLAIN` and requires an index scan or bitmap scan. The audit test uses the dedicated audit sandbox driver. ### 3.5 Redis performance With a reachable Redis: | Test | Assertion | Reported value | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | 1,000 sliding-window evaluations via `RedisCacheAdapter` | Under 3 s | `[perf] redis velocity 1k` | ### 3.6 Replica and backup tests that are not benchmarks `core-back/test/storage-engine/read-store.test.ts` has a broad correctness suite for: - Primary reads. - Healthy replica selection and lag reporting. - Round-robin across replicas. - Lag-threshold rejection and primary fallback. - `{ atLeastLsn }` selection. - Watermark waiting with a timeout. - Mid-flight replica error, unhealthy marking and fallback. - Empty replica pool. - Watermark parsing and two-failure degradation. These are fake-replica unit tests. They do not measure real replication lag or failover time. `deploy/backup-daemon/test/restoreDrillRunner.test.ts` (10 declarations) verifies drill orchestration and report logic. It does not measure restore duration, WAL replay time or backup throughput. ### 3.7 What is not measured The following design claims have no benchmark or load test: - **1,000+ sustained TPS.** No multi-process or multi-connection throughput harness. - **50M-500M row performance.** Tests use small synthetic batches (hundreds to thousands). - **Sub-5 ms read latency.** No p50/p95 measurement of real list, dashboard or search queries at volume. - **Replica reads.** Only `pickHealthyReplica` arithmetic and fake clients are measured; no live streaming replica. - **Deep search.** No trigram index, plug-in fan-out, Arabic normalisation or relevance-latency benchmark. - **Restore drills.** No timed scratch restore, no WAL replay measurement, no backup upload/download throughput. - **Backup daemon.** No benchmark of pgBackRest/WAL-G/Barman invocation, compression, encryption or retention pruning. - **Synthetic seeder.** No measurement of 3.5-year history generation, batch size, memory, or bulk-sync runtime. - **Fake rails.** No throughput or webhook-delivery benchmark. - **Frontends.** No bundle-size, first-render, search-index build or table-render benchmark beyond Playwright geometry. - **Concurrency soak.** No long-running mixed workload, connection-pool exhaustion, lock-wait percentile or deadlock-rate test. ### 3.8 Strategy to add the missing benchmarks Add benchmarks in this order so each one answers a real capacity question rather than inflating the suite: 1. **Throughput harness.** Create a dedicated load script (not a `bun test` file) that drives mixed checkout writes, webhook intake, list reads and ledger posts for 10-30 minutes at increasing concurrency. Record p50/p95/p99 latency, achieved TPS, error rate, connection-pool saturation and PostgreSQL CPU/WAL. Acceptance: a repeatable profile with a 1,000 TPS target and a documented hardware baseline. 2. **Volume dataset.** Seed a staging database with at least 10 million attempts and journal lines, then measure the hot list, dashboard, search and reconciliation queries. Acceptance: p95 read latency and query plans recorded at 10M and 100M rows. 3. **Replica benchmark.** Provision one or more real streaming replicas. Measure replication lag, `{ atLeastLsn }` wait time, fallback rate and failover duration under write load. Acceptance: a live-replica report; fake handles no longer count as replica evidence. 4. **Deep search.** Build the trigram indexes and all search plugins, then measure build time, index size, p50/p95 query time and top-k relevance for English and Arabic queries at 1M/10M merchants and attempts. Acceptance: a relevance fixture and latency thresholds. 5. **Restore drill.** Time a scratch restore from each backup target, including WAL replay, then run ledger invariant, shard parity and audit hash-chain verification. Acceptance: a signed report with duration, replayed LSN, row counts and pass/fail. 6. **Seeder and fake rails.** Measure seeder generation and fake-rails bulk sync at COMPACT, STANDARD and profile volumes; measure webhook queue drain and duplicate delivery. Acceptance: a per-profile runtime and memory report. 7. **Frontend budgets.** Add bundle-size, first-contentful-paint, search-index build and large-table render budgets to the UI suite. Acceptance: CI-enforced budgets, not only geometry checks. Each benchmark must print a machine-readable report (JSON) in addition to console output, and CI must store it as an artifact. A skipped or missing database must fail a release-candidate gate, not silently pass. ## 4. Contracts and invariants 1. **A benchmark requires a real database.** The runner refuses to start without a database URL. 2. **Redis performance is optional.** It skips when Redis is absent, and the skip is printed by Bun's runner. 3. **Thresholds are generous regression guards, not capacity claims.** Passing them does not prove the design's TPS or scale targets. 4. **Reported values must be compared across runs on the same hardware.** No baseline file exists. 5. **Benchmarks must clean up.** Each DB test removes its ledger/outbox/audit rows or uses a sandbox schema. 6. **A skipped benchmark is not a passing benchmark.** CI must report it. ## 5. Status and deviations ### Implemented - A dedicated storage benchmark runner with DB URL guards. - Write-path audit and shard-read thresholds. - Pure primitive microbenchmarks. - UoW sequential/concurrent, outbox drain, shard query-plan and audit-chain measurements. - Redis velocity measurement. - Replica-routing correctness tests with fake replicas. - Backup/restore drill logic tests. ### Partial - The benchmark set covers storage only. - Replica routing is measured only as selection arithmetic. - Backup tests assert logic, not duration or throughput. - The runner does not execute the backup daemon, deploy, seeder or search. - Thresholds are absolute, not baseline-relative. ### Missing / deferred - Sustained TPS/throughput harness with mixed read/write traffic. - Large-volume dataset benchmark (millions of ledger rows, partitioned journals, trigram search). - Live replica failover, LSN wait and lag percentile benchmark. - Deep-search p50/p95 and relevance benchmark across all plugin groups. - Timed scratch restore drill with WAL replay, invariant, shard parity and audit-chain checks. - Backup daemon throughput, compression, encryption, retention and pruning benchmark. - Synthetic-seeder volume/runtime benchmark. - Fake-rails webhook throughput and queue-drain benchmark. - Frontend bundle, first-render and search-index build benchmarks. ### Known bugs / risks - **False capacity claim:** the design's 1,000+ TPS and sub-5 ms read targets are not tested. - **False green:** DB/Redis benchmarks skip when services are absent; the runner still exits successfully. - **Regression blindness:** no stored baselines or statistical comparison. - **Environment sensitivity:** thresholds are generous enough that a 5-10x regression on a fast machine may still pass. ## 8. They are not run by this documentation task. - `write-path-benchmark.test.ts` — 2 tests, both DB-gated. - `storage-performance.test.ts` — 5 pure tests, 6 DB tests and 1 Redis test, with explicit skip placeholders. - `read-store.test.ts` — correctness, not timing. - `uow.test.ts` — correctness plus two local timing assertions without a hard threshold. - `restoreDrillRunner.test.ts` — drill logic.
